title: You’re No Good
note: Written by the Californian blues and one-man-band performer Jesse Fuller, it opens Dylan's first album, played on acoustic guitar and harmonica.
preview: A man complains, half in fun, about a woman who has done him nothing but wrong.
summary: A lover's grievance played for laughs: the singer lists the ways a woman has treated him badly and decides she is simply no good. It moves fast, with little build, each verse another complaint thrown off with a grin. Dylan's version is loose and rough-voiced, a young singer hamming up an older man's blues. It sets the tone for an album of borrowed songs sung with more nerve than polish.

title: In My Time of Dyin’
note: A traditional gospel blues best known from Blind Willie Johnson's 1927 recording, which Dylan sings with slide guitar on his first album.
preview: A dying man asks for the comfort of his faith and to be laid to rest in peace.
summary: A deathbed song: the speaker faces his last hour and asks that heaven make his passing easy. It is built on repetition, the same plea returning as the verses circle the moment of death. Dylan sings it with a hoarse urgency far older than his years, over a sliding, moaning guitar line. Like much of the album, it shows a twenty-year-old singer drawn again and again to songs about dying.

title: Man of Constant Sorrow
note: A traditional Appalachian song popularised by the Stanley Brothers; Dylan's early arrangement appears on his 1962 debut album.
preview: A wanderer who has known nothing but trouble says farewell to his home and the people he loved.
summary: The speaker is a man marked by sorrow all his life, about to leave the place he grew up and go wandering. It unfolds as a farewell, each verse another goodbye to home, friends and a sweetheart he may never see again. Dylan slows it down and sings it with a mournful drawl over guitar and harmonica, turning a mountain lament into something closer to a blues.

title: Fixin’ to Die
note: A Delta blues written and first recorded by Bukka White in 1940, given a ferocious, gravel-voiced reading on Dylan's first album.
preview: A man who senses death is close worries less about himself than about the children he will leave behind.
summary: The singer feels death coming and cannot stop thinking about it, though what troubles him most is leaving his children alone. The verses return to that one fear with little relief, the beat driving on as if there were no time to waste. Dylan attacks it with a rasping, exaggerated growl and hard-strummed guitar, one of the most intense performances on a record full of songs about mortality.

title: Pretty Peggy‐O
note: A traditional ballad descended from the Scottish song The Bonnie Lass o' Fyvie, which Dylan sings in a playful, exaggerated style on his debut.
preview: A soldier courts a girl in a town his company passes through, and the story ends with his death.
summary: An old soldier's ballad: a captain passing through a town falls for a local girl and asks her to come away with him, but she turns him down. The story moves quickly from courtship to his death far away. Dylan sings it with a mock-hillbilly swagger and whoops, treating a sad old ballad almost as a romp, which makes its sudden ending land all the harder.

title: Highway 51
note: Adapted from Curtis Jones's 1938 Highway 51 Blues, it is a fast, hard-strummed road blues on Dylan's first album.
preview: A man stands by a long southern highway, thinking of the woman who left along it and the road that may carry him too.
summary: The highway of the title runs north and south through the country, and the singer stands beside it thinking of someone who has gone. It is a road song and a lost-love song at once, the highway both what took her and what might take him. Dylan drives it hard with a pounding guitar rhythm that owes something to rockabilly, a hint of the louder music to come.

title: Gospel Plow
note: A traditional spiritual, also sung as Keep Your Hand on the Plow, given a fast, raucous treatment on Dylan's first album.
preview: A short, driving spiritual urging the faithful to keep working toward heaven and not look back.
summary: A gospel song about perseverance: the believer is told to keep going, hold steady and stay fixed on the reward ahead. It draws on Bible stories in quick verses around a repeated call to hold on. Dylan turns it into a breathless, under-two-minute burst of guitar and harmonica, closer in spirit to a hoedown than a church hymn.

title: Baby, Let Me Follow You Down
note: A traditional blues Dylan says in its spoken introduction he learned from Ric Von Schmidt in Cambridge; he later played it electric with the Hawks in 1966.
preview: A man pleads with a woman to let him go wherever she goes, promising to do anything for her.
summary: A simple, good-humoured courting song: the singer will do whatever it takes if she will just let him follow her. It repeats its single plea over a rolling fingerpicked pattern, warm rather than desperate. Dylan opens with a chatty spoken introduction crediting where he learned it, one of the few moments on the album where his offhand personality comes through between songs.

title: Freight Train Blues
note: An old country song recorded by Roy Acuff among others; on Dylan's first album it is a fast yodelling showcase with one famously long held note.
preview: A man born to the railroad says he cannot rest, because the sound of a passing freight train always calls him away.
summary: The singer was raised around trains and the railroad is in his blood; whenever a freight goes by, he has to go with it. Each verse adds more of his restless life, always ending at the pull of the tracks. Dylan sings it at a gallop with harmonica and a held, stretched-out note that shows off his lungs, a comic, high-spirited take on the hobo song.

title: See That My Grave Is Kept Clean
note: Written and recorded by Blind Lemon Jefferson in the late 1920s, it closes Dylan's first album as a slow, solemn blues.
preview: A dying man's single last request is that his grave be looked after once he is gone.
summary: A man thinks about his funeral and asks only one favour of those he leaves behind: that his resting place be cared for. The song lingers on images of burial, slow and grave, with the request returning as a refrain. Dylan ends his debut with it, singing in a weary, aged voice over steady guitar, a final note on the album's preoccupation with death.

title: Down The Highway
note: A Dylan original on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, a solo acoustic blues written while his girlfriend Suze Rotolo was away studying in Italy.
preview: A man whose lover has gone far across the sea takes to the highway, lonely and unsure she will return.
summary: The singer's woman has gone overseas and taken his heart with her, and all he can do is walk the road alone. It is a straight twelve-bar blues in form, with verses that move between loneliness and grim humour. Dylan plays it with a hard, choppy guitar and sings in a tough, clipped voice, a personal blues dressed in the traditional style he had been studying.

title: Bob Dylan's Blues
note: A short comic song on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, opened by a spoken introduction poking fun at songs written in Tin Pan Alley.
preview: A light, rambling joke song about the singer going his own way and keeping clear of fads and fakes.
summary: After a deadpan spoken introduction mocking the songwriting factories of New York, Dylan offers a loose, improvised-sounding song about himself. Its verses wander through jokes and small boasts, with no real story and no pretensions. Played on guitar with harmonica, it sounds tossed off in a single take, a breather between the heavier songs on the album.

title: Talking World War III Blues
note: A talking blues on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, in the comic spoken style of Woody Guthrie, about a dream of surviving a nuclear war.
preview: A man tells a doctor about his dream of wandering an empty city after the bombs, and finds everyone else has the same dream.
summary: Framed as a visit to a psychiatrist, the song recounts a dream in which the speaker survives atomic war and roams a deserted America looking for anyone else alive. It is told in the half-spoken talking-blues form, each episode ending on a punchline. The comedy carries real Cold War dread underneath, and the ending turns the joke on the listener: everyone, it seems, is having the same nightmare.

title: Corrina, Corrina
note: A traditional blues first recorded in the late 1920s, it is the one track on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan with a backing band.
preview: A man misses the woman who has gone and says he cannot rest until she comes back to him.
summary: The singer's lover is gone, and the song is his gentle, persistent wish that she would return. It moves through a few short verses with the same yearning refrain, never angry, only patient and sad. Dylan sings it softly over a quiet band shuffle, a warm, unhurried recording that stands out among the album's solo performances.

title: Honey, Just Allow Me One More Chance
note: A fast, comic song on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, adapted from a 1920s recording by the songster Henry Thomas.
preview: A man begs a woman for just one more chance, in a lighthearted song that never quite sounds heartbroken.
summary: The singer asks to be forgiven and taken back, though he sounds more cheerful than repentant. It is brief and bouncing, little more than a refrain and a couple of verses, with whoops and harmonica breaks between them. Dylan plays it for fun, the kind of jaunty old-time number that lightened his live sets of the time.

title: I Shall Be Free
note: The closing track of The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan, a rambling comic song loosely modelled on Lead Belly's We Shall Be Free.
preview: A string of tall tales and jokes about politicians, women and celebrities from a singer who insists he will be free.
summary: A series of absurd vignettes: the singer finds himself in improbable situations with famous and ordinary people, each verse ending in a punchline. Between them a refrain promises that he will be free. The tone is satirical and goofy, poking at the news and the culture of the early sixties. It ends the album on a laugh after its protests and love songs.

title: All I Really Want to Do
note: The opening track of Another Side of Bob Dylan; the Byrds and Cher both released versions in 1965.
preview: A man assures a woman that he wants nothing from her except friendship, with no demands and no games.
summary: The singer runs through a long list of things he will not do to the woman he is addressing, all the ways he will not try to change, trap or own her. The list keeps growing, each line a playful denial, before returning to the simple refrain of what he does want. Dylan sings it with yodels and laughter breaking through, a buoyant opening that announces the lighter, more personal record.

title: Black Crow Blues
note: A slow blues on Another Side of Bob Dylan, notable as one of the album's tracks on which Dylan plays piano rather than guitar.
preview: A lonely man waits and frets for a woman who has gone, uneasy and unable to settle.
summary: The singer is restless and alone, missing a woman who is not coming back soon, and everything around him seems to mirror his gloom. The song circles in short verses with harmonica breaks, a mood more than a story. Dylan plays a rolling, barrelhouse-style piano, giving the record an unexpected texture between its guitar songs.

title: Spanish Harlem Incident
note: A short love song on Another Side of Bob Dylan, later recorded by the Byrds on their 1965 debut album.
preview: A man is dazzled by a gypsy woman he meets in the city and asks her to tell him who he is.
summary: The singer is captivated by a woman in Spanish Harlem, and the song is his rush of attraction, part flirtation and part surrender. It is brief and impressionistic, three verses of heat and colour with no resolution. Dylan sings it quickly over guitar, a sketch of infatuation rather than a story.

title: I Shall Be Free No. 10
note: A comic follow-up to I Shall Be Free from Freewheelin', it sits in the middle of Another Side of Bob Dylan.
preview: A rambling, joking song in which the singer mocks himself, his critics and the world around him.
summary: Like its predecessor, it strings together absurd scenes and wisecracks, each verse a fresh joke about boxing, politics, fame or his neighbours. There is no plot, just a running stream of nonsense delivered with a straight face and a refrain of freedom. Dylan plays it on guitar and harmonica, sounding relaxed and amused, a sign of the less earnest songwriter on this album.

title: To Ramona
note: A gentle waltz on Another Side of Bob Dylan, with a lilting, Mexican-flavoured rhythm on acoustic guitar.
preview: A man tenderly tells a troubled woman she is being misled by others and should trust her own way.
summary: The singer addresses a woman who is unhappy and confused, pulled by voices telling her how to live. He offers comfort and advice, but admits he may be no wiser, and in the end leaves the choice to her. The song sways in three-four time with a soft, consoling tone. It is one of Dylan's most tender early songs, sung quietly over a swaying guitar.

title: Motorpsycho Nitemare
note: A comic talking song on Another Side of Bob Dylan that parodies the old farmer's daughter joke and Hitchcock's film Psycho.
preview: A traveller asks for a bed at a farmhouse and ends up fleeing a farmer, his daughter and a shotgun.
summary: A wanderer knocks at a farmhouse door and is given shelter on condition he leaves the daughter alone. Things go wrong from there in a chain of slapstick events, with nods to horror films and Cold War politics along the way. It is told in a fast, half-spoken style with harmonica, a satire of small-town suspicion played entirely for laughs.

title: I Don’t Believe You (She Acts Like We Never Have Met)
note: A song from Another Side of Bob Dylan that he later transformed into a loud electric number on his 1966 tour with the Hawks.
preview: A man is baffled that a woman he spent a night with now behaves as though she has never seen him.
summary: The singer cannot understand the cold shoulder he is getting from a woman who, not long ago, was close to him. He moves between hurt, disbelief and wry humour, going over what happened and what has changed. The original is a brisk acoustic performance with a catch in the voice, wry rather than bitter.

title: Ballad in Plain D
note: A long confessional ballad near the end of Another Side of Bob Dylan, about the end of his relationship with Suze Rotolo; he later said he regretted it.
preview: A man recounts the bitter end of a love affair, the quarrels around it, and the guilt and freedom left behind.
summary: A narrative song looking back at a broken relationship: the singer tells how he fell for a young woman, how tensions with her family grew, and how a final fight ended it. It runs through many verses in a slow, steady waltz, more diary than ballad. The tone is raw and self-accusing, with a closing reflection on whether he is truly free. Its bluntness makes it one of his most personal early songs.

title: One Too Many Mornings
note: A quiet acoustic song from The Times They Are a-Changin' that Dylan later turned into a loud full-band number on his 1966 tour.
preview: A man stepping away from a lover at daybreak admits that neither of them is wrong, yet he cannot stay.
summary: The singer stands at the edge of a parting, looking back at the house and the woman he is leaving as night turns to morning. There is no quarrel and no blame; each verse settles on the idea that two people can both be right and still be finished. The mood is tired and tender rather than bitter. Dylan sings it softly over his guitar, with harmonica breaks that stretch the stillness.

title: North Country Blues
note: A ballad in the voice of a woman from an iron-mining town, drawing on the Minnesota iron range where Dylan grew up.
preview: A miner's widow traces how her town and family fall apart as the mines close and the work goes overseas.
summary: A woman tells her own life story from childhood to middle age in a northern mining town. Her family is lost one by one, her husband's work disappears when the company finds cheaper ore abroad, and her household slowly empties. The song moves in plain, unhurried verses, each a step further into hardship, with no chorus to relieve it. Dylan sings it alone with guitar, in a flat, steady voice that lets the story carry the anger.

title: She Belongs to Me
note: The second track on Bringing It All Back Home, played softly by a small electric band; Rick Nelson recorded it in 1969.
preview: A portrait of a self-possessed artist woman who belongs to no one, watched by a man half in awe.
summary: Despite its title, the song is about a woman nobody can own. The singer describes an artist who answers to herself alone, who sees through everyone around her and keeps them at a distance, while he and others hover around her in admiration and some fear. The tone is wry and affectionate, with a hint of mockery aimed at the men who court her. The gentle electric backing and harmonica make it one of the album's calmest moments.

title: Outlaw Blues
note: A rough electric blues on the first side of Bringing It All Back Home, the rock-and-roll half of the album.
preview: A restless, rough-edged blues in which the singer casts himself as a hunted man who trusts nobody.
summary: The singer pictures himself as an outlaw, on the run and on edge, keeping his head down and his guard up. The verses are a string of half-comic, half-menacing images rather than a story, delivered in a loose twelve-bar shape. Dylan sounds gleeful in the role, growling over a stomping band. The guitar is ragged and the rhythm heavy, and the whole thing has the feel of a live take caught on the run.

title: On the Road Again
note: A fast electric blues near the end of side one of Bringing It All Back Home.
preview: A man lists the absurd horrors of his girlfriend's household and wonders why she expects him to move in.
summary: The singer describes visiting the home of the woman he is seeing, where every room and every relative is stranger than the last. Each verse piles up another grotesque or ridiculous detail of the family's daily life, and each ends with him turning to her in disbelief at the idea that he could live there. It is a comic song, close to a cartoon, sung with mock exasperation over a jaunty, rattling band and bursts of harmonica.

title: Bob Dylan's 115th Dream
note: Closes the first side of Bringing It All Back Home and opens with a false start that collapses into laughter before the band comes in.
preview: A sailor's absurd dream of landing in America and being met by a parade of rude, ridiculous Americans.
summary: The song is a long comic tall tale in which the narrator sails to America, steps ashore and stumbles from one misadventure to the next, meeting a string of hostile, greedy or baffling locals before fleeing back to sea. It plays on the story of discovery, turning the arrival in the New World into slapstick. The verses tumble on without a chorus, and Dylan sings it with a grin over a loose, galloping band after the opening breakdown.

title: It Takes a Lot to Laugh, It Takes a Train to Cry
note: A slow piano blues on Highway 61 Revisited; an earlier, much faster version was recorded under the title Phantom Engineer.
preview: A weary traveller, borne along by a train through the night, longs to be with the woman he loves.
summary: The singer is on the move, tired and far from home, and the train becomes the image for his longing and his patience. Rather than a story, the verses gather railway and nighttime pictures around a quiet wish to reach the woman waiting for him. The tone is relaxed and a little melancholy, a pause after the album's harder songs. A rolling piano and an easy shuffle give it the feel of an old blues record.

title: From a Buick 6
note: A fast twelve-bar blues near the end of the first side of Highway 61 Revisited.
preview: A man in a hard, dangerous life praises the one woman who looks after him and will stand by him.
summary: The singer describes a woman who is his refuge in a rough world, someone who protects and steadies him while everything around him threatens. The verses are a series of quick, tough images of danger and death, each turning back to her loyalty. It is boastful and grateful at once, more celebration than romance. The band races through it with a driving organ and bass, and Dylan's harmonica squeals over the top.

title: Pledging My Time
note: The second track on Blonde on Blonde, a slow Chicago-style blues led by harmonica.
preview: A man in a bad way promises his devotion to a woman and hopes she will come through for him.
summary: The singer speaks to a woman he wants, offering her his loyalty while hinting at the trouble and sickness all around him. The song is a slow, swaggering blues built on repeated pledges, with dark asides about danger slipping between them. The mood is smoky and late-night rather than romantic. Electric guitar and heavy drums lumber along, and Dylan's harmonica wails between the verses.

title: One of Us Must Know (Sooner or Later)
note: Closes the first side of Blonde on Blonde and was the only track on the album recorded in New York rather than Nashville.
preview: A man explains to a former lover that he never meant to hurt her and that their whole affair was a misunderstanding.
summary: The singer looks back on a relationship that ended badly and tries to set the record straight with the woman he hurt. He insists he did not understand her and did not mean what she took from him, while admitting she saw through him. Each verse builds to a big, pleading chorus. The sound swells from a quiet start into a crashing wall of piano, organ and drums, with Dylan straining against it.

title: Leopard-Skin Pill-Box Hat
note: A twelve-bar Chicago-style blues on side two of Blonde on Blonde, released as a single in 1967.
preview: A jilted man mocks the trendy hat his former girlfriend wears and the new man she has taken up with.
summary: The singer fixes on a woman's fashionable hat and turns it into a running joke about vanity, status and his own jealousy. Each verse finds him admiring, envying or teasing her as she moves on to someone else, always circling back to the hat. It is pure comedy, sharp but not cruel. The band plays a stinging, stop-start blues with stabbing electric guitar, and Dylan delivers it with deadpan timing.

title: Most Likely You Go Your Way and I'll Go Mine
note: Opens the third side of Blonde on Blonde; Dylan and the Band played it to open their 1974 tour, heard on Before the Flood.
preview: A man tells a lover who has deceived him that they are better off going their separate ways.
summary: The singer has had enough of a relationship full of games and false promises, and he says so plainly. The verses list her tricks and his tiredness, and the chorus answers each with the same cool conclusion that they should part. It is less heartbroken than relieved, with a cocky, almost cheerful air. A brassy, stomping arrangement with horns punching the rhythm makes the farewell sound like a celebration.

title: Temporary Like Achilles
note: A slow piano blues on the third side of Blonde on Blonde.
preview: A man shut out by the woman he wants complains that she keeps him waiting while another stands guard over her.
summary: The singer stands outside a woman's door, wanting to be let in and growing weary of her coldness. He describes her as hard to reach and protected by a rival who acts as her guard, someone only briefly invincible. The song is a lament with a sly wit, moving at a slow, rolling pace. A barrelhouse piano leads the way, with harmonica answering Dylan's drawled, frustrated vocal.

title: Absolutely Sweet Marie
note: An upbeat organ-driven rocker on the third side of Blonde on Blonde.
preview: A man stuck waiting for an absent woman wonders where she is and why she has left him hanging.
summary: The singer has been waiting for a woman who never shows up, and the song is a string of his complaints and puzzled questions. The images are of being locked out, held up and left behind, mixed with odd pieces of wisdom about honesty and living by your own rules. Despite the frustration, the mood is bright and energetic. A pumping organ and quick beat drive it, and Dylan's harmonica rings out between verses.

title: Obviously Five Believers
note: A fast Chicago-style blues that closes the third side of Blonde on Blonde, listed on the album as Obviously 5 Believers.
preview: A man pleads with his baby to come back to him as soon as she can, promising to be waiting.
summary: This is one of the simplest songs on the album, a straight call to a woman to return to him. The singer begs, coaxes and reassures, with each verse repeating his longing over a tight, insistent groove. It draws openly on the Chicago electric blues records of the 1950s. Driving guitar riffs and a shrill harmonica keep it tense and fast, and the band sounds loose and joyful.

title: The Ballad of Frankie Lee and Judas Priest
note: The longest song on John Wesley Harding, a parable sung over a sparse acoustic backing that ends with a plainly stated moral.
preview: Two friends, one a tempter, test each other over money and desire in a parable that ends in a death.
summary: The song tells the story of two friends: a gambler and a cunning companion who offers him money and leads him toward a house of temptation. The gambler gives in, and his craving costs him his life, while his friend watches. It unfolds like a biblical parable or an old ballad, verse after verse without a chorus, before closing with a plainly stated lesson. Dylan sings it at a brisk, even pace over guitar, bass and drums.

title: Dear Landlord
note: Built around Dylan's piano, it sits on the second side of John Wesley Harding; Joe Cocker recorded it in 1969.
preview: A man asks the landlord who holds power over him not to judge him too harshly or reduce him to what he owes.
summary: The singer addresses a landlord, though the figure seems to stand for anyone with a hold over him. He asks for patience and fair treatment, admits his own weaknesses, and suggests that both of them are struggling in their own ways. The tone is calm, dignified and slightly weary, more a request for mutual respect than a protest. Dylan's piano and a plain rhythm section give it a hymn-like steadiness.

title: I Am a Lonesome Hobo
note: A short, sombre story-song on the second side of John Wesley Harding.
preview: A wandering hobo confesses the greed and crimes that brought him low and warns others to live better.
summary: The narrator is a homeless wanderer who once had wealth and status and lost everything through his own dishonesty and greed. He looks back without self-pity and turns his story into advice for whoever is listening, urging honesty and generosity. It moves like a sermon in miniature, steady and grave. The spare backing of acoustic guitar, bass, drums and harmonica keeps the focus on the confession.

title: I Pity the Poor Immigrant
note: Its tune is close to the Scottish folk song Come All You Tramps and Hawkers; Joan Baez recorded it on her 1968 album Any Day Now.
preview: A grave lament for a newcomer whose greed and selfishness leave him empty even in a land of plenty.
summary: The singer looks with pity, not anger, on an immigrant who arrives seeking a better life but lives only for gain and harms others along the way. The verses list his failings in a solemn, almost biblical voice, and the song suggests his dreams will bring him no peace. Its mood is mournful and reflective, a moral portrait more than a story. Dylan sings it slowly over acoustic guitar and harmonica.

title: Down Along the Cove
note: The second-to-last track on John Wesley Harding, one of two bright country love songs that close the album with pedal steel guitar.
preview: A happy man walks by the water with the woman he loves and everyone can see how good they are together.
summary: After an album of dark parables, the singer suddenly sounds content: he is out walking with his lover and delighted to be seen with her. There is no conflict, only simple affection and pride. It is a short, easy blues with a cheerful lope and a country lilt. Dylan's piano and the pedal steel guitar give it a relaxed, sunny warmth that points toward his next album.

title: Peggy Day
note: A light, jaunty love song that closes the first side of Nashville Skyline, sung in the soft croon that marks the whole album.
preview: A playful, grinning tribute to a girl the singer is glad to spend his days and nights with.
summary: The singer sings the praises of a girl named Peggy, cheerfully admitting how much he enjoys her company. There is no conflict and no heartbreak, only a happy man trading a couple of verses of good-humoured devotion. Its bouncy rhythm and slightly old-fashioned, music-hall feel make it one of the sunniest moments on the album. The ending shifts into a slower, mock-grand coda that adds a wink to the whole thing.

title: One More Night
note: An upbeat country song on the second side of Nashville Skyline, following Lay Lady Lay, with a brisk shuffle under a lonely lyric.
preview: A man alone under the night sky mourns a woman who has left him and wonders how he failed her.
summary: The singer is out under a clear, moonlit sky, but the beauty of the night only reminds him that his love has gone. He blames himself for not being the kind of man she needed, and the song circles back to his solitude. The words are sad, yet the band plays a quick, cheerful country shuffle, so grief and good spirits sit side by side. It is a short, plain-spoken lament in classic country style.

title: Country Pie
note: One of the shortest songs on Nashville Skyline, running under two minutes, it sits just before the closing Tonight I'll Be Staying Here with You.
preview: A rollicking celebration of simple pleasures, using a list of fruit pies as a happy stand-in for country music and life.
summary: This is a song of pure enjoyment: the singer declares his appetite for country pie, reeling off one kind of fruit after another. The pie works as a cheerful metaphor for the down-home music and easy living he loves, and he wants nothing fancier. It moves fast and never slows down, with a loose, rocking country band and a lively guitar. It is a throwaway in the best sense, a burst of fun on a gentle album.

title: Time Passes Slowly
note: One of the songs Dylan wrote in 1970 for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch, it became the third track on New Morning.
preview: A reflection on quiet country days, where time seems to stand still and the singer is content to stay put.
summary: The singer looks at a slow, settled life in the hills, where days drift by and nothing much needs to happen. He pictures himself at home with someone he loves, far from the pressures of the wider world, and seems torn between contentment and a faint unease. The song moves at an unhurried pace, built around Dylan's own piano. It catches the domestic, rural mood that runs through New Morning.

title: Went to See the Gypsy
note: A piano-led New Morning song set in a hotel, often read by listeners as a veiled account of a meeting with Elvis Presley.
preview: A traveller goes to see a famous fortune-teller in a big hotel, but the encounter slips away like a dream.
summary: The singer visits a celebrated figure called the gypsy, who is staying in a grand hotel, and finds himself welcomed but uncertain what passed between them. When he returns, the gypsy has gone, and he wanders out into a quiet small-town dawn. The song has a hazy, dreamlike quality, with hints of a pilgrimage that ends in anticlimax. A rolling piano and a relaxed band keep it gently mysterious.

title: Winterlude
note: A crooned waltz on New Morning, its old-fashioned melody recalling the softer singing Dylan had used on Nashville Skyline.
preview: A sweet, old-fashioned winter romance in which the singer invites his sweetheart to enjoy the snow and each other.
summary: Addressed to a girl the singer is courting, the song paints a cosy winter scene of snow, a chapel and evenings spent together. Its tone is warm and slightly tongue-in-cheek, like a sentimental popular song from an earlier era. Dylan sings it as a lilting waltz in a soft, crooning voice. It is one of the most deliberately gentle and nostalgic moments on New Morning, a valentine to simple happiness.

title: If Dogs Run Free
note: A jazzy New Morning track that Dylan half-recites over a loose cocktail-lounge band, with a woman's wordless scat singing weaving around him.
preview: A musing on freedom and acceptance, asking why we should not let all creatures, and ourselves, live as we please.
summary: The song is less a story than a philosophical drift: the singer muses on letting things be as they are and on a kind of unforced harmony. Dylan delivers it in a relaxed, almost spoken style rather than a tune, sounding like a beat poet in a late-night club. Behind him, piano and brushed drums swing softly while a female singer scats freely. It is one of the strangest and most playful recordings of his early 1970s work.

title: New Morning
note: The title track of the album, written for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch, it is one of the most joyful songs Dylan recorded in this period.
preview: Waking to a bright country morning, the singer rejoices in nature, renewal and simply being with the one he loves.
summary: The singer greets a fresh day in the countryside, noticing small signs of life around him and feeling his spirits lift. The morning stands for a new beginning, and he shares it with someone close to him. The song builds on an exuberant, horn-touched arrangement and a big, open chorus. Its uncomplicated happiness made it the emblem of the album that critics welcomed as Dylan's return to form.

title: Sign on the Window
note: A slow piano ballad near the middle of New Morning, often counted among the album's finest and most personal songs.
preview: After a lonely winter and a broken romance, the singer imagines settling down to a quiet family life.
summary: The song opens in loneliness: rain, a deserted town and a love that has gone elsewhere. Gradually the singer turns from what he has lost toward a modest dream of marriage, children and a home far away from it all, and wonders if that might be the real meaning of happiness. Dylan sings it slowly over his own piano, and the arrangement grows fuller as hope enters. Its mood moves from melancholy to hopeful calm.

title: One More Weekend
note: A bluesy, good-natured rocker on New Morning, one of the album's few uptempo numbers.
preview: A husband begs his wife to slip away with him for a weekend alone, leaving the children and everyday life behind.
summary: The singer is eager for a getaway with his partner, just the two of them, somewhere they can forget their responsibilities for a while. It is a playful, affectionate song about married love rather than new romance. The band plays a loose, rolling twelve-bar blues with a strutting guitar, and Dylan sings with obvious relish. Light and humorous, it shows the domestic contentment that runs through New Morning in a more raucous key.

title: Three Angels
note: A spoken-word piece on New Morning, Dylan reciting rather than singing over organ and a soft gospel-style chorus.
preview: Three angel decorations look down over a busy city street while ordinary people hurry past without noticing them.
summary: Dylan describes a winter street scene in a city, where three angels sit high above the sidewalk playing their horns. Below them, all kinds of people go about their business, and none seems to look up or hear. The piece asks quietly whether anyone is listening to the heavenly music around them. Delivered as a calm recitation over swelling organ and wordless voices, it sounds like a short hymn or parable.

title: Father of Night
note: The closing track of New Morning, a short piano hymn also written for Archibald MacLeish's play Scratch; Manfred Mann's Earth Band later recorded an extended version.
preview: A brief, intense prayer praising God as the maker of night and day, of love and of the whole natural world.
summary: The song is a hymn of praise addressed directly to God, naming him as the creator of the darkness, the seasons and the things of the earth. It draws on the shape of Jewish and Christian prayer, piling up images of creation in a steady chant. Dylan sings it over his own rolling piano with backing singers, and it lasts only about a minute and a half. It ends New Morning on a note of devotion.

title: Alberta
note: A traditional folk blues that Dylan recorded in two versions, Alberta #1 opening Self Portrait and Alberta #2 closing it.
preview: A man calls out to a woman named Alberta, longing for her and wondering where she has gone.
summary: This old song, sung by many folk and blues performers before Dylan, is a plea addressed to Alberta, a woman the singer misses and wants to come back to him. It is simple and repetitive, more a mood of longing than a story. Self Portrait frames the album with two different takes: the first gentle and folky with female backing voices, the second fuller and more upbeat. Both carry an easy, unhurried charm.

title: I Forgot More Than You’ll Ever Know
note: A country song written by Cecil Null and a 1953 hit for the Davis Sisters, which Dylan recorded in Nashville for Self Portrait.
preview: A jilted lover tells the new partner of his former sweetheart that he knows her far better than they ever will.
summary: The singer addresses the person who has taken his love away, warning them that his memories of her run deeper than anything they will share. It is a classic country lament, bitter but dignified, built on a single sharp idea. Dylan sings it in the mellow, crooning voice of his Nashville period, backed by steel guitar and soft harmony vocals. His version treats it as a straightforward tribute to the country tradition he admired.

title: Days of 49
note: A traditional ballad of the California Gold Rush, credited on Self Portrait as arranged by Alan Lomax, John Lomax and Frank Warner.
preview: An old prospector looks back on the wild days of the gold rush and the rough companions now long gone.
summary: The song is a monologue from an aging forty-niner, recalling the gamblers, brawlers and dreamers who chased gold with him in California. One by one he tells how each came to a bad end, until he alone remains, poor and forgotten. Dylan sings it in a rough, weathered voice that suits the old man telling it. His reading leans into the ballad's mix of humour and melancholy about the American frontier.

title: Early Mornin’ Rain
note: Written by Gordon Lightfoot and recorded by Ian and Sylvia and Peter, Paul and Mary before Dylan cut it for Self Portrait.
preview: A broke, stranded man at an airport watches a plane take off toward home, unable to follow it.
summary: The singer stands on a cold, wet morning near an airfield, far from home with no money in his pocket. He watches a jet climb away and thinks of the place it is headed, where he longs to be. It is a song of homesickness and helplessness, quiet rather than angry. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, sung in his softer 1970 voice over acoustic guitar, staying close to the folk style of the song.

title: In Search of Little Sadie
note: The first of two versions of the traditional murder ballad on Self Portrait, its tempo and key lurching unpredictably from verse to verse.
preview: A man shoots a woman named Sadie, flees across the country, and is caught and brought to trial.
summary: This old American ballad is narrated by the killer himself, who tells plainly how he shot Sadie, ran away and was finally arrested and sentenced. Dylan treats the song as an experiment, with the guitar and rhythm shifting abruptly so that the story seems to stagger and restart. The effect is disorienting, almost like a sketch of the song being worked out. Its companion, Little Sadie, follows later with a steadier take.

title: Let It Be Me
note: An English version of Gilbert Bécaud's French song Je t'appartiens, made famous by the Everly Brothers in 1960 and recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait.
preview: A tender plea from a lover who asks to be the one person their beloved always turns to.
summary: The song is a vow of devotion: the singer asks to be the one who stays by his love's side for good, offering faithfulness above everything. It is gentle and earnest, without any hint of irony. Dylan sings it softly with female backing voices, in the smooth style he adopted around Nashville Skyline. His version is a straight, affectionate tribute to a well-loved standard rather than a reinvention of it.

title: Little Sadie
note: The second, straightforward version of the traditional murder ballad on Self Portrait, played at a brisk, even pace.
preview: The killer of a woman named Sadie tells of his crime, his flight and his capture and sentence.
summary: The song is a first-person confession: the narrator shoots Sadie, runs off, and is eventually tracked down and brought before a judge. He tells the story with little emotion, which makes it all the more chilling. Unlike the shifting In Search of Little Sadie, this version moves at a steady clip on acoustic guitar, much as a folk singer would play it. Placed together, the two takes show Dylan approaching the same old ballad from opposite directions.

title: Woogie Boogie
note: A short instrumental on Self Portrait, a loose boogie-woogie jam credited to Dylan.
preview: A brisk, good-time boogie-woogie romp led by rolling piano and a bright, bouncing band.
summary: This is a wordless jam built on the old boogie-woogie piano pattern, with the band falling in behind a steady, driving rhythm. It sounds informal, like a warm-up captured on tape rather than a polished composition. Over its brief running time it never changes much, keeping a cheerful, toe-tapping groove from start to finish. On an album full of covers and oddities, it works as a light musical interlude.

title: Belle Isle
note: A traditional ballad from the British Isles and Newfoundland, recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait with strings added afterwards.
preview: A returning young man tests his sweetheart's faithfulness while in disguise, then reveals himself when she stays true.
summary: The song tells an old ballad story: a man meets a young woman by the shore and, without saying who he is, asks for her hand. She refuses, explaining that she is waiting for her own love, who has been away. Satisfied of her loyalty, he reveals that he is that very man. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, with a lush string arrangement that some listeners found surprising.

title: Living the Blues
note: A Dylan original that he performed on The Johnny Cash Show in 1969 before recording it for Self Portrait.
preview: A man left behind by his love confesses that he has been sinking into sadness ever since she went away.
summary: The singer is lonely and lovesick, admitting that his life has been nothing but the blues since the woman he loves departed. It is a simple, sincere country lament without much story, built around one feeling. Dylan sings it in the warm, crooning voice of his Nashville period, over a relaxed band with backing voices. It sounds much like a song from the late 1950s, deliberately old-fashioned and unassuming.

title: Gotta Travel On
note: A folk song adapted by Paul Clayton and a 1959 hit for Billy Grammer, recorded by Dylan for Self Portrait.
preview: A restless man feels the pull of the road and knows he must leave town and keep moving.
summary: The song speaks for a wanderer who has stayed too long in one place and now hears the call to move on, despite the people he leaves behind. It is upbeat rather than mournful, treating the urge to go as part of who he is. Dylan's version is a brisk, cheerful country-folk romp with a steady beat and backing voices. It fits the album's mood of revisiting songs he had known for years.

title: Blue Moon
note: Written by Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart in 1934 and recorded by countless singers before Dylan crooned it on Self Portrait.
preview: A lonely singer sees his life changed when the moon that watched over his solitude suddenly brings him love.
summary: This classic popular song tells of a person alone and without hope who unexpectedly finds love, as if the moon itself had answered him. It moves from loneliness to wonder in a few short verses. Dylan sings it in his gentle Nashville croon, with fiddle and a relaxed, easy backing that gives the standard a country lilt. To many listeners at the time, it was the clearest sign of how far Self Portrait strayed from expectations.

title: Take Me as I Am (or Let Me Go)
note: A country ballad written by Boudleaux Bryant and a hit for Ray Price, which Dylan sings in a soft Nashville style on Self Portrait.
preview: A man asks his lover to accept him exactly as he is, or else to set him free.
summary: The singer speaks directly to a woman whose feelings for him have grown uncertain. He makes no promise to change and asks her to decide, either to take him as he stands or to release him. The song moves slowly and plainly, with a patient, pleading tone rather than anger. Dylan sings it in the smooth, crooning voice of his Nashville Skyline period, backed by easy country accompaniment.

title: Take a Message to Mary
note: Written by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant and first a hit for the Everly Brothers, it appears on Self Portrait as a close-harmony country cover.
preview: A man locked away for his crimes asks a friend to hide the truth from the woman he loved.
summary: The speaker is a young outlaw who has been caught and sentenced, and will not be coming home. He sends word to his sweetheart Mary, but asks that she be told a gentler story so she can forget him and go on with her life. The song is a short, story-telling ballad with a sorrowful but restrained tone. Dylan's version keeps the country harmony feel of the original, with backing singers filling out the refrain.

title: It Hurts Me Too
note: An old blues long associated with Tampa Red and Elmore James, which Dylan recorded for Self Portrait as a quiet, mostly acoustic performance.
preview: A man watches the woman he loves suffer at the hands of another, and feels her pain as his own.
summary: The singer loves a woman who belongs to someone else, and that man treats her badly. He urges her to leave and come to him, insisting that whatever wounds her wounds him as well. The song follows the classic blues pattern of repeated lines and a returning refrain, sympathetic more than bitter. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, far from the electric slide-guitar treatment the song is best known for.

title: Wigwam
note: A Dylan instrumental on Self Portrait, carried by a wordless hummed vocal and a slow horn arrangement, later heard in the film "The Royal Tenenbaums".
preview: A lazy, hummed melody drifts over brass, a song without words that feels like a half-remembered tune.
summary: There are no lyrics here; Dylan sings the melody as wordless syllables instead. A brass section answers him, swelling and falling in a stately, slightly woozy procession. The tune repeats in gentle circles without building to any climax, which gives it the feel of a late-night reverie or a memory of an old dance band. It is one of the few Dylan originals on Self Portrait, and its warmth has made it one of the album's best-loved tracks.

title: Sarah Jane
note: A traditional-based song recorded in Dylan's 1970 sessions and released on the 1973 album "Dylan", with female backing singers.
preview: A cheerful man sings of his devotion to Sarah Jane and the happy, crowded home they share.
summary: The singer is a contented family man who describes his life with Sarah Jane and declares his affection for her. It plays as a light, good-humoured folk song rather than a story of trouble or heartbreak. A bouncing rhythm and a chorus of backing voices give it a loose, sing-along feel. Like the rest of the 1973 album, it was put out by Columbia from outtakes, and it sounds like a relaxed studio warm-up.

title: Mr. Bojangles
note: Written by Jerry Jeff Walker and later a hit for the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, it was released on "Dylan", the album Columbia assembled from outtakes.
preview: A narrator remembers meeting an old wandering dancer in a jail cell who told the story of his life.
summary: The narrator recalls a night in jail spent with an aging street performer, a dancer who has travelled the South for decades. The old man talks about his life, the dog he lost, and the drinking that keeps landing him in cells, then dances to lift the room. The song is tender and rueful, built on a gentle waltz feel. Dylan's version, cut in his 1970 sessions with backing singers, is looser and rougher than the well-known recordings.

title: The Ballad of Ira Hayes
note: Written by Peter La Farge and made famous by Johnny Cash, it tells the true story of a Pima Marine who helped raise the flag on Iwo Jima.
preview: A Native American war hero comes home to neglect and drink, and dies forgotten by the country that praised him.
summary: The song tells the life of Ira Hayes, a Pima man from Arizona who fought in the Pacific and was photographed raising the flag at Iwo Jima. Celebrated as a hero, he returns to a reservation stripped of its water and a nation that soon loses interest in him, and he dies alone. It unfolds as a sombre narrative ballad with a bitter refrain. Dylan's outtake, released on the 1973 album, is plain and slow, letting the story carry it.

title: Mary Ann
note: A traditional folk song of a sailor's farewell, recorded by Dylan around 1970 and released on the 1973 Columbia album "Dylan".
preview: A man about to sail away mourns the woman he must leave behind on the shore.
summary: The speaker is a seafaring man parted from the woman he loves, and the song dwells on his sorrow at going and his longing to return. It is a simple, lilting folk tune with a repeated chorus and a wistful tone throughout. There is little story beyond the parting itself, so the feeling rests on the melody. Dylan sings it with backing vocalists in a relaxed, unpolished arrangement typical of the outtakes Columbia gathered for this album.

title: Big Yellow Taxi
note: A cover of Joni Mitchell's 1970 song, recorded by Dylan in his sessions of that era and released on the 1973 album "Dylan".
preview: A bright, catchy complaint that we only value the natural world, and the people we love, once they are gone.
summary: The song looks at a landscape being covered over by development and wonders why people notice what they had only after losing it. It moves from fields, trees and birds to a more personal loss at the end, when a lover leaves. The tone is light and teasing, with a bouncing tune hiding a serious point. Dylan's version, with backing singers, is loose and playful, and he alters some of the details of Mitchell's original.

title: A Fool Such as I
note: Written by Bill Trader and a hit for both Hank Snow and Elvis Presley, it was recorded by Dylan around Self Portrait and released on "Dylan".
preview: A jilted man admits he is still devoted to the woman who left him and will go on loving her.
summary: The singer has been left behind, yet he cannot stop loving the woman who walked away. He addresses her directly, asking what she would want with someone so foolishly faithful, and confessing that he will love her anyway. The song is a classic country weeper, gentle and self-mocking rather than bitter. Dylan sings it in a relaxed, crooning voice over a light country backing.

title: Spanish Is the Loving Tongue
note: A cowboy song set to a poem by Charles Badger Clark, which Dylan recorded more than once; this version is on the 1973 album "Dylan".
preview: A cowboy remembers a Mexican girl he once loved and lost, and still hears her tender words.
summary: The speaker is a rider on the border country who recalls a brief romance with a young Mexican woman. He has long since ridden away, but the memory of her and the warmth of her language stay with him. The song is slow and melancholy, a quiet reflection rather than a story with events. Dylan's version here, from his 1969 and 1970 sessions, is a gentle, unhurried cowboy ballad.

title: Main Title Theme (Billy)
note: The instrumental that opens the soundtrack to Sam Peckinpah's film "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid", built on the melody of the album's song "Billy".
preview: A spare acoustic theme sets a lonesome frontier mood, circling slowly as if over open country.
summary: This is an instrumental with no singing, written to play over the film's opening titles. Acoustic guitars state a simple, mournful melody drawn from the Billy ballad, the album's ballad about the outlaw, and other instruments join quietly around it. It keeps an even, rolling pace and never rises to a big climax. The effect is of a long, dusty ride toward something bad, which suits a film about an old friendship that ends in a killing.

title: Cantina Theme (Workin’ for the Law)
note: An instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, its subtitle pointing to Garrett's turn from outlaw to lawman in the film.
preview: A relaxed, slightly uneasy groove plays like music heard in a frontier saloon.
summary: There are no words here; it is a short piece of incidental music from the film. A loose rhythm and gentle guitar figures create the feel of a smoky cantina, easygoing on the surface but with an undercurrent of tension. The melody turns over and over rather than developing. Its title recalls the story at the heart of the film, of a former outlaw now working for the law and hunting his old friend.

title: Bunkhouse Theme
note: A short acoustic instrumental from the soundtrack to "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid".
preview: Gentle interlocking acoustic guitars play a quiet, homely tune, like evening music in a cowboy bunkhouse.
summary: This brief instrumental sets aside the drama of the film for a moment of calm. Acoustic guitars pick out a soft, folk-like melody that feels intimate and restful, as though played among friends at the end of a day. It does not build or change much, keeping one modest mood from start to finish. On the album it works as a breathing space between the more mournful themes and the songs.

title: River Theme
note: An instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, featuring wordless voices over a slow, flowing accompaniment.
preview: Wordless singing floats over a slow, gentle melody that moves like water drifting past.
summary: Like most of the soundtrack, it has no lyrics; voices hum and sing syllables rather than words. The music moves calmly and evenly, with a sense of drift and stillness that suits its title. Its mood is peaceful but faintly sad, a pause by the water in a story that is heading toward violence. It is a short, atmospheric piece meant to sit under a scene rather than stand alone.

title: Turkey Chase
note: A lively instrumental from the "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid" soundtrack, driven by fiddle and banjo in an old-time country style.
preview: Fiddle and banjo race along in a bright, rollicking old-time tune full of chase and fun.
summary: This is the most high-spirited piece on the soundtrack, an instrumental in the manner of a country hoedown. Fiddle and banjo trade the quick melody over a steady, galloping rhythm, giving it the feel of a frontier romp. Its playful energy stands out against the slow, mournful themes around it. As film music it suggests a moment of horseplay and freedom before the story darkens again.

title: Final Theme
note: The instrumental that closes the soundtrack album for "Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid", returning to the film's mournful main melody.
preview: A slow, stately farewell melody brings the story to a sorrowful close.
summary: This closing instrumental gathers up the mood of the whole soundtrack. A spare, elegiac melody unfolds slowly over a gentle, steady accompaniment, with no singing. It has the feeling of an ending already decided, quiet and resigned rather than dramatic. Placed last on the album, it plays like music for the film's final scenes, after the friendship between the two men has ended in death.

title: Going, Going, Gone
note: A slow song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, notable for Robbie Robertson's stinging guitar answering Dylan's voice.
preview: A man who has reached the end of something resolves to walk away and leave it all behind.
summary: The singer stands at a point of no return, ready to break with a life or a love that has run its course. He speaks of leaving with a mixture of calm resolve and quiet sorrow, and a middle passage recalls advice to follow one's heart. The title phrase works as a refrain, like an auctioneer closing a sale. The Band's playing is spare and moody, with Robertson's guitar lines adding much of the song's ache.

title: Tough Mama
note: A driving rock song on Planet Waves, recorded with The Band in Los Angeles in late 1973.
preview: A man pays tribute to a strong, earthy woman who inspires him and pulls him back into the world.
summary: The singer addresses a powerful woman, part lover and part muse, praising her strength and appetite for life. Around her he gathers striking images and hints of his own wish to return to work and public life after years away. The song charges forward with a hard, rolling groove and an urgent vocal. The Band plays tightly behind him, with Garth Hudson's organ and Robertson's guitar giving it a rough, exciting edge.

title: Hazel
note: A short love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, which Dylan also performed with them in "The Last Waltz".
preview: A man longs for a woman named Hazel and asks her to give him a little of her love.
summary: The singer is drawn to Hazel and describes her in admiring terms while confessing how much he needs her. It is a simple song of yearning, without a story or conflict beyond his desire and hope. The tone is warm and slightly melancholy, and the melody rises and falls gently. The Band supply a soft, rootsy backing that keeps it intimate and unhurried.

title: Something There Is About You
note: A love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, in which Dylan refers to his boyhood in Duluth, Minnesota.
preview: A woman stirs up memories of his youth and a feeling he cannot name, and he pledges himself to her.
summary: The singer tries to explain what it is about a particular woman that moves him so deeply. She seems to awaken his earliest memories, taking him back to his childhood in the north, and he concludes that he is devoted to her. The song mixes nostalgia and romance in a mood that is both tender and restless. Musically it rolls along at a steady mid-tempo, with The Band's organ and guitar weaving around the vocal.

title: Dirge
note: One of the starkest songs on Planet Waves, performed only by Dylan on piano and Robbie Robertson on acoustic guitar.
preview: A man looks back with bitterness and self-disgust on a consuming attachment he is finally ready to leave.
summary: The singer turns on himself, confessing shame for having needed someone or something that brought him only misery. He describes the relationship with a harsh, unforgiving clarity and insists he is done with it. The mood is dark and unrelenting, as the title suggests, with no consoling chorus. Dylan's heavy piano and voice are joined only by Robertson's acoustic guitar, which makes it one of the barest, most intense recordings in his catalogue.

title: You Angel You
note: A cheerful, mid-tempo love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band.
preview: A man is so smitten with a woman that he can think of nothing else and calls her an angel.
summary: The singer simply celebrates the woman he loves, describing how completely she has captivated him. It is a light, happy song with no darker turn, built on a bright refrain that addresses her directly. The tone is playful and easygoing compared with the heavier songs elsewhere on the album. The Band give it a bouncy, rolling arrangement, with organ and guitar keeping it buoyant.

title: Never Say Goodbye
note: A tender love song from Planet Waves, recorded with The Band, set against an image of a wintry northern landscape.
preview: Amid a frozen winter scene, a man asks the woman he loves never to leave him.
summary: The singer looks out on a cold, still winter landscape and turns to the woman he loves, wishing their time together would last. He dreams of the future and asks that there be no parting between them. The song is gentle and wistful, mixing quiet natural imagery with a simple plea. The Band's backing is soft and restrained, letting the mood of hushed affection come through.

title: You’re a Big Girl Now
note: The third track on Blood on the Tracks, and one of the five songs he re-recorded in Minneapolis in December 1974 for the final album.
preview: A man tells a woman who has moved on without him that he sees her growing and wishes he could change.
summary: A man speaks to a former lover who has grown independent and found a life without him. He admits how much the separation hurts and hints that he could become a different man if she would let him. The song moves in long, aching lines, his voice climbing high on each confession, more pleading than bitter. The Minneapolis band gives it a soft, rolling setting of acoustic guitars and organ.

title: Meet Me in the Morning
note: A slow twelve-bar blues that opens the second side of Blood on the Tracks, kept from the New York sessions of September 1974.
preview: A weary man asks a woman to meet him at dawn so they can leave together, though he senses she may not come.
summary: A man calls out to a woman, asking her to meet him in the morning so the two of them can get away. He has been waiting and struggling for a long time, and his images of cold nights and dawn carry more doubt than hope. It is the plainest song on the album, a straight blues sung in a tired, patient voice. Electric guitar answers each line, giving it a smoky, late-night feel.

title: If You See Her, Say Hello
note: The eighth track on Blood on the Tracks, re-recorded in Minneapolis in December 1974; the earlier New York take had a harsher, more wounded tone.
preview: A man asks a friend to pass his greetings to the woman who left him, hiding how much he still misses her.
summary: A man speaks to someone who may run into his former lover, now far away, and asks them to give her his regards. He insists he bears no grudge and respects her choice, yet every message he sends reveals how much he still thinks about her. The song is gentle and controlled on the surface, the hurt showing only at the edges. A quiet acoustic arrangement with mandolin gives it a sad, tender glow.

title: Odds and Ends
note: The opening track of The Basement Tapes, a short, fast rocker recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967.
preview: A man gives up on a careless partner whose broken promises and wasted chances have finally worn out his patience.
summary: A man complains about a lover who keeps letting things spill and slip, leaving him with nothing but scraps and loose ends. He sounds more exasperated than heartbroken, and by the end he is ready to walk away. The song is brief and breezy, built on a driving rock and roll beat with a shouted chorus. It sets the loose, good-humoured tone of the whole collection.

title: Orange Juice Blues (Blues for Breakfast)
note: A Richard Manuel song performed by the Band without Dylan, one of the Band-only tracks added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A lonely man nurses the blues over breakfast, missing a woman who has gone and dreading the long day ahead.
summary: This is the Band's track rather than Dylan's: a slow morning blues about a man left alone with his thoughts. He sits through breakfast feeling sorry for himself, missing someone and unable to shake the gloom. The song unfolds at an easy, sorrowful pace, its mood lifted only slightly by wry humour. Its soulful vocal and warm horns sound closer to rhythm and blues than to the rest of the basement recordings.

title: Million Dollar Bash
note: A Basement Tapes party song recorded with the Band in 1967; Fairport Convention released a cover on their 1969 album Unhalfbricking.
preview: A crowd of oddballs and misfits all gather and stumble toward one wild, enormous party.
summary: The song gathers a cast of strange, comic characters who are all on their way to a big celebration. Each verse adds another absurd figure or mishap, and the chorus keeps returning to the promise of the party itself. It is pure fun, loose and laughing, with the feel of friends playing in a room for each other. The bouncing rhythm and group singing make it one of the most cheerful tracks on the album.

title: Yazoo Street Scandal
note: A Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A rowdy tale of a young man drawn into trouble by a dangerous woman on a disreputable street.
summary: This is one of the Band's own numbers: a rocking story about a seductive woman and the gossip that surrounds her on a notorious stretch of street. The singer is pulled in despite warnings, half thrilled and half afraid. The song moves fast, with a swampy Southern feel and a hard-driving beat. It shows the Band's taste for Southern settings and colourful, slightly lurid storytelling.

title: Goin’ to Acapulco
note: A slow, mournful song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A tired man heads off to Acapulco to see a woman for some fun, though his voice carries more sorrow than pleasure.
summary: A man describes going down to Acapulco to spend time with a woman he knows there, as he does whenever life gets heavy. The words talk of good times, but the music is slow and weary, and his voice sounds resigned, almost grieving. That gap between what he says and how he sounds gives the song its strange power. The Band's organ and steady drums wrap it in a heavy, hymn-like mood.

title: Katie’s Been Gone
note: A Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A man mourns a woman who has left, wondering how long he can stand her absence.
summary: This is a Band track, not a Dylan performance: a gentle lament from a man whose love has gone away. He waits and wonders whether she will come back, his loneliness growing with each verse. The song is soft and unhurried, with a tender, almost fragile vocal. Its quiet piano and organ give it the feel of a late-night ballad.

title: Lo and Behold!
note: A comic travelling song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A restless traveller hops from town to town, meeting strange people and leaving each place with a shout.
summary: A man tells the story of a rambling journey from city to city, each stop bringing an odd encounter or a small comic misfortune. He moves on every time, never settling, and the chorus bursts in with a loud, exclaiming refrain. The song is playful and absurd, more a tall tale than a confession. The Band's rolling rhythm and harmony voices on the chorus make it feel like a group singalong.

title: Bessie Smith
note: A Rick Danko and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A tribute to the great blues singer Bessie Smith, looking back at her world with affection and longing.
summary: This is one of the Band's own songs, named for the classic blues singer Bessie Smith. The singer looks back on her and the vanished world she belonged to, searching for something of her that cannot be found again. The tone is warm and nostalgic rather than mournful. Its relaxed tempo and old-time feel suit its homage to an earlier era of American music.

title: Clothes Line Saga
note: A deadpan story song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions, often heard as a reply to Bobbie Gentry's "Ode to Billie Joe".
preview: A family takes in the washing and trades flat small talk while big news passes by almost unnoticed.
summary: An ordinary household goes through the chore of bringing in the clothes from the line, and the narrator reports every small step. A neighbour mentions startling news from the wider world, but it gets the same shrug as the weather. The joke lies in the flat, matter-of-fact telling, which turns country life into gentle absurdity. The music is slow and plain, letting the storytelling carry the song.

title: Apple Suckling Tree
note: A nonsense song in nursery-rhyme style, recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967 and released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A playful, nonsensical rhyme about meeting someone under a tree, sung for the joy of the sound.
summary: The song is built like a children's rhyme, with a simple question-and-answer pattern and words chosen more for their sound than their sense. It hints at a meeting between two people under a tree, but any story is buried in silliness. Its charm is in its looseness, as if made up on the spot. A bouncing beat and a cheerful, rough-edged vocal keep it light from start to finish.

title: Please, Mrs. Henry
note: A comic barroom song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A drunk, broke man begs a woman named Mrs. Henry to help him out of his sorry state.
summary: A man who has had far too much to drink pleads with Mrs. Henry, who seems to run the place, to take pity on him. He is out of money, uncomfortable and fast losing his dignity, and each verse makes his plight sillier. The song is a broad comic turn, sung with a wobbly, mock-desperate swagger. The Band's slow, swaying accompaniment sounds like a tavern at closing time.

title: Too Much of Nothing
note: Written and recorded at the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band; Peter, Paul and Mary released it as a single later that year.
preview: A brooding warning that emptiness and idleness can make people cruel, restless and lost.
summary: The song reflects on what happens when life holds too little: people grow mean, confused and cut off from one another. It reads like a dark proverb, moving through grim observations about history and human nature. A haunting refrain sends greetings to two absent women, adding a note of mystery. The slow, heavy beat and ghostly harmonies give it one of the most ominous moods on the album.

title: Yea! Heavy and a Bottle of Bread
note: A nonsense song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A jumble of absurd images about packing up and setting off, sung with a straight face.
summary: The song strings together odd, comic images of travel, food and getting ready to leave, without ever settling into a clear story. Its humour comes from how seriously it delivers pure nonsense, as if every detail mattered. The chorus repeats its strange title phrase like a slogan. The music lopes along at a lazy pace, loose and goofy, in the spirit of musicians amusing themselves.

title: Ain’t No More Cane
note: A traditional prison work song about convict labour, performed by the Band without Dylan on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: Prisoners describe the brutal, endless labour of cutting cane under guard, and long for it to be over.
summary: This old work song comes from the convict labour camps of the American South, where prisoners were forced to cut sugar cane. It speaks of the harsh work, cruel overseers and the men who did not survive, along with the hope that such days will end. The Band's version passes the lead between several singers, giving it the feel of a shared lament. Acoustic instruments and rough harmonies keep it close to its folk roots.

title: Crash on the Levee (Down in the Flood)
note: Recorded with the Band in 1967; he re-recorded it as "Down in the Flood" for Bob Dylan's Greatest Hits Vol. II in 1971.
preview: With the water rising and the levee about to break, a man warns a woman she will have to fend for herself.
summary: A man sees a flood coming and warns that the levee is about to give way. In the middle of the disaster, he tells the woman he is with that she will need to find someone else to lean on. The flood works as both a real danger and a picture of a relationship washing away. The song is a tough, rolling blues, delivered with grim good humour over a steady beat.

title: Ruben Remus
note: A Richard Manuel and Robbie Robertson song performed by the Band without Dylan, added to the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: An upbeat, good-time Band number built around a colourful, restless character.
summary: This is one of the Band's own tracks, a lively song centred on a character named Ruben Remus. It has the loose, comic spirit of the basement sessions, telling its story with more energy than detail. The singers trade lines and lean into the fun of the tune. Its bouncing rhythm, piano and horns give it an old-fashioned, rollicking feel.

title: Tiny Montgomery
note: One of the earliest songs from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A roll call of oddball characters, all told to pass the word that Tiny Montgomery is coming back.
summary: The song announces the return of a mysterious figure called Tiny Montgomery and asks a string of strange, comic characters to spread the news. Each verse adds another nickname and another odd errand, building a crowded little world of rogues. It feels like a rumour passing through a small town. The music is loose and chugging, with a sly, half-spoken vocal.

title: Don’t Ya Tell Henry
note: A Dylan song performed by the Band without him on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A comic, rowdy tale of a night of mischief that the singer keeps insisting must be hidden from Henry.
summary: This is the Band's performance of a Dylan song, a comic story of wandering, drinking and strange encounters. After each episode the singer insists that Henry must not hear about any of it, which becomes the running joke. The tone is boisterous and teasing, like a tall tale told in a bar. Horns and a stomping, good-time rhythm make it one of the album's liveliest tracks.

title: Nothing Was Delivered
note: Recorded with the Band near Woodstock in 1967; the Byrds recorded it for their 1968 album Sweetheart of the Rodeo.
preview: A man demands that someone explain why nothing they promised ever arrived, and own up to it.
summary: A man confronts someone who took something on trust and failed to deliver what was promised. He asks for an explanation and an admission, his tone patient but firm, as if the reckoning is overdue. The refrain sounds like a gentle farewell that is also a warning. The slow, rolling piano gives it the feel of an old rhythm and blues ballad.

title: Open the Door, Homer
note: A loose, rambling song from the 1967 Woodstock sessions with the Band, first officially released on The Basement Tapes in 1975.
preview: A man asks a friend to let him in while sharing odd bits of advice about living and forgiving.
summary: The song mixes a simple request to be let in with a string of cryptic sayings passed on from friends. Its advice touches on how to live, how to swim against the current and how to forgive, though it never quite explains itself. The refrain returns as a cheerful, insistent call at the door. The music is easygoing and warm, carried by the Band's relaxed groove and harmony vocals.

title: Long Distance Operator
note: A Dylan blues performed by the Band without him on the 1975 release of The Basement Tapes.
preview: A desperate man pleads with a telephone operator to put his call through to the woman he loves.
summary: This is the Band's recording of a Dylan song: a blues in which a man begs the long distance operator to connect him. He is far from the woman he loves and growing frantic at every delay. The telephone becomes a picture of the distance between them. The Band gives it a heavy electric blues sound, with a raw, pleading vocal.

title: Mozambique
note: Written with Jacques Levy, this short, breezy song sits in the middle of Desire and was also released as a single.
preview: A light invitation to a sunny faraway coast where couples dance and fall in love.
summary: The singer paints the African country of the title as an idyllic seaside place, a travel postcard where lovers meet by the water. It moves in short, lilting verses with no real story, simply luring the listener there with the promise of romance. Its easy tone stands out on an album otherwise full of long dramas and confessions. Scarlet Rivera's violin and Emmylou Harris's harmony give it a bright, swaying lift.

title: Romance in Durango
note: Written with Jacques Levy, it is one of the long story songs on Desire, with a chorus sung partly in Spanish.
preview: An outlaw flees across Mexico with the woman he loves, haunted by the man he has killed.
summary: The narrator is a man on the run in Mexico, riding with his lover after shooting a man, and dreaming of the quiet life they will have once they reach safety. The song unfolds like a western film, with dust, heat, a fiesta and the constant sense of pursuit, until the ending turns dark and uncertain. Its chorus breaks into Spanish as he reassures her. The violin, accordion-like textures and harmonies give it a cinematic, border-town feel.

title: New Pony
note: The opening track of Street-Legal, a heavy blues with the album's gospel-style backing singers answering him throughout.
preview: A sultry, menacing blues in which a man sings about a pony as a thinly veiled stand-in for a lover.
summary: The singer talks about a pony he once had and the new one that has replaced her, using the horse as a barely disguised image of desire and of a woman who has a hold on him. It is built on a slow, grinding blues riff, with the backing singers repeating a churchy call behind his lines. The mood is sexual and a little threatening, with hints of dark magic. Horns and the women's voices make it heavier than a plain twelve-bar blues.

title: No Time to Think
note: One of the longest songs on Street-Legal, a slow waltz packed with abstract nouns and symbolic figures.
preview: A man caught among temptations, duties and lost loves finds he never has a moment to stop and reflect.
summary: The song is a long allegorical journey in which the narrator meets a parade of figures and ideas, from rulers and soldiers to a mysterious woman, each pulling him a different way. Verse after verse in a rolling three-time rhythm, it piles up grand abstractions while a refrain keeps returning to the pressure of having no space to think. The tone is weary and bewildered rather than angry. The violin and backing voices give it a stately, almost hypnotic sway.

title: Baby Stop Crying
note: Released as a single from Street-Legal, it is a slow ballad with the album's gospel-style backing singers.
preview: A man tries to comfort a heartbroken woman and offers to help her if she will let him.
summary: The singer speaks to a woman who is distraught after being hurt by someone else, and he offers himself as a friend and protector.
