Each verse sketches her trouble and his willingness to take her side, returning to a pleading chorus asking her to dry her tears. The tone is tender but also a little helpless, as if he is unsure she wants him. Slow, swelling saxophone and the backing singers give it a soulful, almost doo-wop warmth.

title: True Love Tends to Forget
note: A mid-tempo song on the second side of Street-Legal, built around a hooky chorus with the backing singers.
preview: A man worn down by an unsteady love asks his partner not to deceive him or let him go.
summary: The narrator is in a relationship that leaves him weary and unsure, and he speaks to his lover about his doubts and his fear of being betrayed. The verses describe his exhaustion and restlessness, while the chorus turns his worry into a rueful observation about how love can be careless. The tone is wistful and pleading rather than bitter. The singers and horns give the song a smooth, almost pop sheen.

title: We Better Talk This Over
note: A late track on Street-Legal, a brisk breakup song set to the album's horns and backing singers.
preview: A man suggests to his partner that their relationship is over and they should part without bitterness.
summary: The singer addresses a lover after things have gone wrong between them, proposing that they sit down and settle it before going separate ways. He moves between regret, wry humour and resignation, admitting his own confusion while insisting that staying together would only hurt them both. The song keeps a steady, upbeat pace that contrasts with its sad subject. It plays like a grown-up farewell rather than an angry one.

title: Where Are You Tonight? (Journey Through Dark Heat)
note: The closing track of Street-Legal, a long, dense song that ends the album on a note of hard-won survival.
preview: A man searching for a lost lover through a dark, dreamlike night comes out the other side changed.
summary: The narrator travels through a shadowy landscape of strange figures and painful memories, all the while calling out to a woman who is gone. The verses tumble forward in crowded, symbolic images of struggle and temptation, until near the end he finds he has broken through his ordeal and is free of it, though still without her. The tone moves from anguish to a kind of fierce relief. The full band, horns and singers drive it with urgency.

title: Do Right to Me Baby (Do Unto Others)
note: A gentle, mid-tempo song on Slow Train Coming built around the Golden Rule from the Gospels.
preview: The singer refuses to judge or harm others and asks only to be treated the way he treats them.
summary: The song works through a list of things the narrator will not do to other people, such as judging, cheating or hurting them, and pairs each with the hope that he will be spared the same. Its refrain returns to the Biblical rule of doing unto others as you would have them do unto you. The tone is calm and almost conversational, closer to a personal creed than a sermon. The smooth Muscle Shoals groove keeps it light and easy.

title: A Satisfied Mind
note: Written by Red Hayes and Jack Rhodes and a 1955 country hit for Porter Wagoner, it opens Saved as a short gospel-style performance.
preview: Wealth cannot buy contentment, and a peaceful heart is the only thing worth taking to the grave.
summary: The song reflects on how people chase money and status, and how riches can vanish in a moment while a contented spirit lasts. It ends with the thought that the speaker will leave this life poor in goods but at peace. Dylan's version is brief and stately, sung close to the backing singers in a churchy, almost a cappella style. Placed first on Saved, it works like a quiet prayer before the louder gospel songs that follow.

title: Covenant Woman
note: A slow ballad on Saved that blends a love song with a song of faith.
preview: The singer thanks a woman who has shared his faith and stands beside him in a covenant with God.
summary: The narrator speaks with gratitude to a woman whom he sees as bound with him in a sacred promise, someone who understands him and has helped bring him closer to God. The verses mix personal tenderness with religious language, so that devotion to her and devotion to faith blur together. The tone is warm, humble and steady. A gentle keyboard-led arrangement keeps it intimate compared with the more fiery songs around it.

title: What Can I Do for You?
note: A slow gospel song on Saved, notable for an extended harmonica solo, one of the few on his gospel records.
preview: A grateful believer, aware of all that has been given to him, asks God what he can offer in return.
summary: The song is a prayer addressed directly to God, in which the singer recounts how he has been rescued, guided and forgiven. Each verse adds to the list of gifts, and each time he returns to his humble question of what he could possibly give back. The tone is quiet, devotional and searching. Near the end a long, keening harmonica solo carries the feeling further than the words do.

title: In the Garden
note: A dramatic gospel song on Saved about the life of Jesus, often used to close his gospel-era concerts.
preview: Retelling moments from the life of Jesus, the song asks whether the people around him truly saw who he was.
summary: Starting with the arrest in the Garden of Gethsemane, the song moves through scenes from the Gospels, including miracles and the resurrection. After each scene it asks whether the witnesses understood what they were seeing, building a pattern of repeated questions. The tone is solemn and then increasingly triumphant. The arrangement climbs steadily, with chord changes rising and the backing singers swelling behind him to a powerful finish.

title: Saving Grace
note: A slow, hymn-like song on the second side of Saved.
preview: A humble believer marvels that he has been kept alive and rescued by grace he did not earn.
summary: The narrator looks back on his life, considering the many times he might have died or gone astray, and credits his survival entirely to divine grace. Rather than preaching to others, he sounds grateful and almost surprised to be spared, and he looks ahead calmly to death. The tone is quiet, reverent and personal. The arrangement is spare and hymn-like, with organ and soft backing voices.

title: Are You Ready
note: The closing track of Saved, a gospel song with a call-and-response between Dylan and his backing singers.
preview: The singer asks, again and again, whether the listener is prepared to meet God when the end comes.
summary: The song is built almost entirely from questions put to the listener, and to the singer himself, about being ready for judgment, for the end of the world and for death. The backing singers echo and answer each question, giving it the feel of a church service. The tone is urgent and searching rather than condemning. Its driving rhythm and repeated refrain end Saved on a note of challenge.

title: Heart of Mine
note: Released as a single from Shot of Love, it is a loose, rolling love song rather than a gospel one.
preview: A man warns his own heart not to give itself away to a woman who will only hurt him.
summary: The singer talks to his own heart as if it were a reckless friend, cautioning it to stay quiet and keep its distance from a woman it is drawn to. Each verse lists another warning, while the refrain keeps returning to this odd inner conversation. The tone is wry and self-mocking, as he clearly knows his heart may not listen. The relaxed, ragged band sound gives it a casual, late-night feel.

title: Property of Jesus
note: A hard-edged rock song on Shot of Love, mixing the album's faith themes with sharp defiance.
preview: The singer defends a believer from the mockers around him, insisting he belongs to Jesus and cannot be bought.
summary: The song describes a man of faith who is laughed at, scorned and misunderstood by the people around him. Verse by verse the narrator turns on those mockers, listing their sneers and contrasting their shallow values with the believer's steadfastness. The tone is combative and scornful, closer to his old protest anger than to a hymn. A tough, driving band arrangement with backing singers gives it real bite.

title: Watered‐Down Love
note: An upbeat song on Shot of Love, with a light, bouncy groove and backing singers.
preview: True love is pure, patient and selfless, quite unlike the weak and grasping imitation people settle for.
summary: The song sets out a portrait of real love in the spirit of the famous passage from Corinthians, describing what it does and does not do. Against this ideal, the refrain dismisses the lesser, compromised love the world offers instead. The tone is cheerful and confident, more like a lesson than a confession. The breezy, almost pop arrangement keeps its moral message light on its feet.

title: The Groom's Still Waiting at the Altar
note: First issued as a B-side, this hard-rocking song was added to later editions of Shot of Love.
preview: A man searches for a vanished woman in a world that seems to be falling apart around him.
summary: The narrator is looking for a woman who has disappeared, piecing together rumors of where she might be while the landscape around him grows violent and chaotic. Personal loss and visions of a world near collapse run together, so the song reads as both a love story and an apocalyptic warning. Its refrain returns to the image of a groom left waiting at a wedding. A fierce, driving rock arrangement makes it one of the most energetic tracks of the period.

title: Dead Man, Dead Man
note: A mid-tempo song on Shot of Love with a lightly reggae-flavored rhythm.
preview: The singer confronts a spiritually dead man, perhaps his own old self, and asks when he will finally rise.
summary: The song addresses a dead man who stands for sin, pride and worldliness, and the narrator seems to be wrestling with that part of himself as much as with someone else. The verses describe the man's emptiness and the hold he has, while the refrain asks when he will come back to life. The tone is stern but restless. Its loose, swaying groove keeps the confrontation from becoming a sermon.

title: In the Summertime
note: A gentle, reflective ballad near the end of Shot of Love, with harmonica.
preview: Looking back on a summer long ago, the singer remembers a love or grace that changed him.
summary: The narrator recalls a past summer when someone was close to him and he felt changed, and the song leaves open whether he means a woman, God or both. The verses drift between memory and the present, quietly weighing what was gained and what was lost. The tone is wistful and tender, with none of the album's sharper edges. Soft keyboards and harmonica give it a warm, unhurried glow.

title: Trouble
note: A blues on Shot of Love, placed just before the closing song, Every Grain of Sand.
preview: Trouble is everywhere, in every street, home and institution, and nobody can escape it.
summary: The song is a catalogue of the world's troubles, moving from cities and politics to everyday life, each verse adding another place where misery and danger can be found. The refrain simply repeats the idea that there is trouble everywhere, with no solution offered. The tone is grim and matter-of-fact rather than preachy. It rides on a heavy, straightforward blues groove that suits its plain, relentless message.

title: Man of Peace
note: A Dylan original that opens the second side of Infidels, set to a loping, bluesy groove carried by the Sly Dunbar and Robbie Shakespeare rhythm section.
preview: A warning that evil rarely announces itself and may arrive looking like a gentle, trustworthy peacemaker.
summary: The song is a sermon in disguise, written soon after his gospel years: the devil, it argues, does not appear with horns but in the shape of a charming leader everyone wants to follow. Verse by verse it lists the many guises this figure can wear, and each one returns to the same unsettling refrain. The tone is dry and knowing rather than fiery. The band plays a long, swaying blues that keeps the warning sounding almost casual.

title: Seeing the Real You at Last
note: The opening track of Empire Burlesque, a Dylan original that sets the album's bright, horn-and-drum-machine production from its first bars.
preview: A lover who has finally seen through a partner's act and feels relieved, even liberated, to be done with the illusion.
summary: The singer looks back on a relationship in which he was taken in, and announces that the mask has finally slipped. Rather than grieving, he sounds wry and lightened, as though clear sight is its own reward. The verses are full of the tough-talking, film-noir attitude that runs through the album. The arrangement is punchy mid-1980s rock, with horns, backing singers and a bright, heavy drum sound.

title: I'll Remember You
note: The second track on Empire Burlesque, a Dylan original and one of the album's slower, more tender songs, later a regular in his concerts.
preview: A promise to keep a lost lover in memory long after everything else has faded and the road has moved on.
summary: The song is a farewell that refuses to be a goodbye: the singer admits that life will carry him on, but swears that this one person will stay with him. Its mood is grateful rather than bitter, looking back on what was shared instead of what went wrong. The melody is simple and rises gently into its title line. The recording is a mid-tempo ballad, warmer and less crowded than the rocking tracks around it.

title: Clean Cut Kid
note: A Dylan original first tried during the Infidels sessions and finished for Empire Burlesque, a sardonic rocker about a young American soldier of the Vietnam era.
preview: An ordinary, all-American boy is sent to war and comes home a broken stranger whom no one understands.
summary: The song tells the story of a polite, wholesome young man who did everything his country asked and was sent to fight in Vietnam. On his return he is lost and violent, and the people around him cannot see how the nice boy they knew became this. Dylan tells it with bitter, black humour, piling up ironic details instead of preaching. The music is a fast, rowdy rock shuffle whose cheer sharpens the sting of the story.

title: Never Gonna Be the Same Again
note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a soft soul-pop ballad built around backing singers and a smooth mid-1980s production.
preview: A brief encounter with someone has changed the singer for good, and he admits there is no going back.
summary: The singer addresses a woman whose touch has left him altered, and he confesses it plainly, almost with gratitude. There is little story here; the song lingers on a single feeling of being shaken out of one's old self. Its tone is tender and slightly bashful, apologising and thanking at once. The recording leans on a gentle groove, keyboards and female backing vocals, making it one of the most polished, radio-minded sounds Dylan had attempted.

title: Trust Yourself
note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a funky, chant-like rocker driven by a repeated title hook and loud mid-1980s drums.
preview: Advice to rely on your own judgment rather than on preachers, lovers, experts or anyone else claiming to know best.
summary: The song is a sermon of self-reliance: the singer warns the listener not to hand their life over to someone else's promises or answers. Each verse names another kind of authority to be wary of, and each time the title phrase comes back as the remedy. Its tone is brisk and confident rather than angry. Musically it is built on a tight, funky groove with stabbing guitar and backing vocals answering the lead.

title: Emotionally Yours
note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a slow piano-led love ballad later recorded by the O'Jays as the title track of a 1991 album.
preview: A heartfelt declaration that, whatever happens, the singer belongs to his lover body and soul and will stay that way.
summary: The song is a straightforward love letter, unusually unguarded for Dylan in this period. The singer pleads to be held and understood, and vows a devotion that does not depend on circumstances. It moves slowly, building to the title line at the close of each verse, with a feeling close to a classic pop standard. The recording is spare by the album's standards, carried by keyboards and a gentle rhythm under a tender vocal.

title: Something's Burning, Baby
note: A Dylan original from Empire Burlesque, a dark, slow-marching song that stands out on the album for its ominous drum-led arrangement.
preview: A lover senses that something has gone badly wrong between them and pleads for honesty before it is too late.
summary: The singer speaks to a woman he can feel slipping away, convinced that a crisis is coming even though neither of them will name it. He presses her with questions, by turns suspicious and pleading, while the danger stays vague and smouldering. The mood is tense and foreboding, like a scene from a thriller. The music moves at a heavy, steady march, with a martial drum pattern and backing voices deepening the sense of threat.

title: You Wanna Ramble
note: The opening track of Knocked Out Loaded, a cover of a rhythm and blues number credited to Herman Parker Jr., the Memphis singer known as Junior Parker.
preview: A man warns a restless lover that if she wants to run around, she should not expect him to wait at home.
summary: The song is a jaunty rhythm and blues challenge from a man to a partner who cannot settle down. He lays down his terms with more swagger than heartbreak, half warning and half teasing. It moves on a simple, repeating structure built for dancing rather than storytelling. Dylan's version is a loose, upbeat band performance with backing singers, a light-hearted start to an album made largely of covers and collaborations.

title: Precious Memories
note: A gospel hymn written by J. B. F. Wright in the 1920s and widely sung in Southern churches; Dylan recasts it with a lilting, Caribbean-flavoured rhythm.
preview: Memories of loved ones and of the faith they passed on return unbidden and bring comfort in the night.
summary: The hymn is a meditation on remembrance: the singer finds that memories of parents, home and old worship come back to console him in later life. It is gentle and devotional, moving through short verses to a familiar chorus about those memories lingering. Dylan's recording sets the old church song to a swaying, island-style groove with backing singers, turning a solemn standard into something warm and easy-going. It is one of the few explicitly religious songs on the album.

title: Maybe Someday
note: A Dylan original from Knocked Out Loaded, a fast, crowded rock song with backing singers, one of the few songs on the album he wrote alone.
preview: A spurned lover imagines that someday his former partner will understand what she gave up, though he hardly believes it.
summary: The singer addresses a woman who has left him, and runs through what might happen if she ever thinks better of it. The words tumble out quickly, mixing hurt pride, sarcasm and a lingering wish that she might come back. The title becomes a refrain that sounds less hopeful each time. The recording rushes along at a hectic tempo, with gospel-style backing voices and a busy band nearly overrunning the vocal.

title: Got My Mind Made Up
note: Co-written by Dylan and Tom Petty and recorded with Petty and the Heartbreakers, with whom Dylan was touring in 1986.
preview: A man has decided to leave, and nothing his lover says will talk him out of taking off.
summary: The singer announces that he is going, and the song is all momentum: his bags are packed, his reasons are settled, and the arguments for staying no longer reach him. The mood is restless and defiant, with flashes of humour rather than sorrow. It works like a classic leaving song, one verse of reasons after another. The recording is a tough, straight-ahead rock performance with the Heartbreakers, among the liveliest band tracks on the album.

title: Under Your Spell
note: The closing track of Knocked Out Loaded, co-written by Dylan and the pop lyricist Carole Bayer Sager.
preview: A man under a lover's spell is torn between devotion and the need to break away before he is lost.
wordsBy: Bob Dylan and Carole Bayer Sager
summary: The singer speaks to a woman whose hold over him is almost supernatural, and the song wavers between surrender and resistance. He sounds bewitched and wary at once, promising to return even as he goes. The tone is wistful and slightly mysterious, ending the album on a quieter note than it began. The arrangement is a mid-tempo pop-rock ballad with backing singers and a smooth 1980s sheen.

title: Let's Stick Together
note: Written and first recorded by Wilbert Harrison in 1962, later remade by Bryan Ferry; Dylan's version opens Down in the Groove.
preview: A man urges his wife not to break up their marriage but to stay together for better or worse.
summary: The song is a plea to keep a marriage whole: the singer reminds his partner of the vows they made and argues that splitting up would hurt everyone, the children included. It is direct and good-humoured, more persuasion than lament, with a simple refrain that drives the point home. Dylan's recording is a rough, rocking rhythm and blues romp with harmonica, a loose and energetic start to an album built mostly from other people's songs.

title: When Did You Leave Heaven?
note: A 1936 popular song by Richard Whiting with words by Walter Bullock, introduced in a Hollywood film; Dylan sings it as a slow, crooning ballad.
preview: An admirer marvels at a woman so lovely that she must have come down from heaven, and wonders how.
summary: The song is a classic Tin Pan Alley compliment: the singer treats his beloved as an angel who has strayed to earth and asks, with mock seriousness, how heaven could have let her go. It is sweet, courtly and old-fashioned, built on a gentle melody and a single extended conceit. Dylan sings it softly over a sparse, keyboard-heavy backing, foreshadowing his much later albums of standards from the same era.

title: Sally Sue Brown
note: A rhythm and blues song first recorded by Arthur Alexander, who co-wrote it; Dylan cut it with a rowdy rock band for Down in the Groove.
preview: A man is completely smitten with a girl called Sally Sue Brown and can think of nothing and no one else.
wordsBy: Arthur Alexander, Earl Montgomery and Tom Stafford
summary: The song is a breathless celebration of a girl the singer cannot get out of his head. He sings her praises and admits she has the upper hand, but he is too happy to mind. There is no real story, just infatuation sustained over a bouncing beat. Dylan's version is a ragged, fast rock and roll performance with loud guitars and backing vocals, sounding like a lively bar band rather than a polished studio take.

title: Had a Dream About You, Baby
note: A Dylan original written for the 1987 film Hearts of Fire, in which he also acted, and included on Down in the Groove.
preview: A man cannot shake the dream he had about a woman and is restless with wanting her.
summary: The song is a simple, rocking piece of desire: the singer has dreamed about a woman and wakes up preoccupied with her. He describes her with playful exaggeration and repeats the title as a hook rather than telling a story. The tone is lusty and fun, closer to vintage rock and roll than to his serious songwriting. The recording is a driving guitar rocker, short and loud, made to suit the film's rock-star setting.

title: Ugliest Girl in the World
note: Music by Dylan with words by Robert Hunter, the Grateful Dead lyricist, one of two Hunter collaborations on Down in the Groove.
preview: A man cheerfully admits his girlfriend is no beauty, yet he is devoted to her and cannot live without her.
summary: The song is a comic love song turned upside down: instead of praising his sweetheart's looks, the singer happily lists how plain she is. The joke is that the more he runs her down, the clearer it becomes that he adores her. The tone is good-natured and silly, never cruel. The recording is a bouncy, uptempo rock and roll number that plays the novelty idea for laughs.

title: Ninety Miles an Hour (Down a Dead End Street)
note: A country song by Hal Blair and Don Robertson, recorded by Hank Snow in 1963; Dylan sings it as a slow, hushed duet-style ballad.
preview: Two people know their forbidden affair can only end badly, yet they keep racing toward it anyway.
summary: The song pictures an illicit love affair as a car speeding toward a wall: both lovers can see the crash coming but neither will brake. The singer is resigned rather than defiant, admitting guilt and inevitability in the same breath. It is a classic country cheating song, built on a single strong image. Dylan's recording slows it right down, with a gentle band and harmony voices, giving it a mournful, almost gospel calm.

title: Shenandoah
note: A traditional American folk song dating from the nineteenth century, often sung as a sea shanty; it closes Down in the Groove.
preview: A wanderer far from home longs for a river, a valley and a love he has left behind across the wide country.
summary: The song is one of the oldest and best-loved American folk tunes, a slow lament from someone travelling away from a beloved place and person, with the Shenandoah and Missouri rivers standing for home and distance. Its long, rolling melody gives it a sense of vast space. Dylan sings it with a full chorus of backing singers and a stately rhythm, ending an uneven album on a solemn, old-time note.

title: Where Teardrops Fall
note: The second track on Oh Mercy, a slow and tender ballad set apart by its soft saxophone and accordion.
preview: A man offers comfort and devotion to someone in a place of sorrow, promising to meet her there.
summary: The singer speaks to a woman he loves, picturing a distant place where grief gathers and pledging to find her there. Around that promise he sets night images, passing time and an awareness that the world is unsettled. The tone is hushed and patient rather than pleading. Musically it is one of the gentlest moments on the album, a slow sway with saxophone and accordion drifting under his voice.

title: Disease of Conceit
note: A slow, piano-led song near the end of Oh Mercy, close in spirit to a sermon.
preview: Pride is pictured as an epidemic sweeping the land, wrecking lives and blinding people to their own ruin.
summary: Dylan treats conceit as a sickness spreading from person to person across the country, more dangerous than any physical plague. He describes what it does to people: it inflates them, isolates them and finally brings them down. The song moves like a stern moral lesson delivered with sorrow rather than anger. Its stately piano and sombre singing give it the feel of a hymn sung in a darkened church.

title: What Was It You Wanted
note: The ninth and penultimate track on Oh Mercy, a murky, slow-moving song of suspicion with drifting harmonica.
preview: A man keeps asking someone what they really want from him, never quite trusting the answer.
summary: The whole song is a string of questions put to someone who has approached the singer, perhaps a lover, perhaps a fan or a hanger-on. He wonders what they came for, whether he has already given it and whether he heard them right. The repeated questioning turns wary and faintly mocking, with a sense that the relationship is a game neither side admits to. The sound is swampy and hazy, typical of the album's night-time atmosphere.

title: Unbelievable
note: The third track on Under the Red Sky, a brisk rock song issued as a single from the album.
preview: A narrator marvels at a world where greed and wrongdoing go unpunished and nothing makes sense anymore.
summary: The singer looks around at a society that seems to run on money, deceit and empty promises, and keeps declaring how hard it is to believe. Each verse adds another absurdity, delivered with a shrug as much as a protest. The refrain turns disbelief into a running joke. The band plays a bright, driving rock arrangement that sits in wry contrast to the bleak picture the words paint.

title: T.V. Talkin' Song
note: The fifth track on Under the Red Sky, a story song delivered in a half-spoken style over a loping groove.
preview: At a London speakers' corner, a man rails against television until the crowd turns ugly and the scene ends up on the news.
summary: The narrator wanders into a park where a street preacher is warning a crowd about the evils of television and what it does to families and minds. As the speech goes on, the audience grows restless and a riot breaks out. In a closing twist, the narrator later watches the whole commotion broadcast on TV. Told with deadpan humour, it is both a satire of media and a gentle mockery of the preacher himself.

title: 10,000 Men
note: The sixth track on Under the Red Sky, a slow blues built from repeated, nursery-rhyme style lines.
preview: An army of ten thousand men passes by in a series of strange, fable-like images.
summary: The song paints a procession of ten thousand men, sometimes soldiers on a hill, sometimes figures in an odd dream, each verse adding a new detail in the manner of a counting rhyme. Between these images the singer turns to address a woman at home. The effect is playful and ominous at once, like a children's chant with something dark underneath. The band settles into a heavy, unhurried blues groove.

title: 2 X 2
note: The seventh track on Under the Red Sky, a counting song that echoes the story of Noah's ark.
preview: Pairs, then larger groups, march forward in a counting rhyme that hints at the flood and the end of things.
summary: Built like a children's counting game, the song lines figures up two by two, three by three and onward, recalling the animals entering the ark. As the numbers climb, the questions it asks grow more uneasy: where are they all going, and what is waiting for them. The simple structure carries a sense of judgment and passing time. It moves at a gentle, rolling pace with a soft, repeating melody.

title: God Knows
note: The eighth track on Under the Red Sky, a song of faith that builds from quiet to a full band.
preview: The singer finds comfort in the belief that God sees everything, including the troubles between people.
summary: Addressed partly to a lover and partly to the world, the song rests on the idea that God understands what people cannot say or fix themselves. It acknowledges hardship, separation and a world that may end, yet holds to a steady trust. Each verse returns to that refrain of divine knowledge. The recording starts sparse and gathers force, ending in a rousing, rock-driven finish.

title: Handy Dandy
note: The ninth track on Under the Red Sky, a character sketch carried by a prominent organ and a swinging band groove.
preview: A portrait of a charming, careless man surrounded by admirers, whose easy life hides something hollow.
summary: The song circles a figure called Handy Dandy, a carefree ladies' man who seems to have everything and to owe nothing to anyone. Scenes of parties, women and idle talk pass by as the narrator watches him with amusement and a hint of judgment. The name itself, taken from an old children's guessing game, suggests a trickster. The band plays a loose, jaunty groove dominated by a bright organ.

title: Cat's in the Well
note: The closing track of Under the Red Sky, a driving blues that ends the album on an apocalyptic note.
preview: A nursery-rhyme image of a cat in a well opens a vision of a world sliding toward ruin.
summary: Taking its title from an old children's rhyme, the song pictures a world in which danger is close and nobody is coming to help. Images of decline pile up, from neglected homes to an approaching sense of doom, delivered with a calm, almost matter-of-fact voice. It closes with a plea for mercy from above, turning the song into a prayer. The band drives it as a tough, rocking shuffle.

title: Jim Jones
note: A traditional Australian convict ballad, the second track on Good as I Been to You, sung over intricate fingerpicked guitar.
preview: A convict sentenced to transportation to Australia vows to break free and take revenge on his jailers.
summary: Jim Jones is a prisoner shipped from England to the penal colony at Botany Bay. The song follows his voyage and his harsh treatment, and ends with his resolve to escape, join the outlaws in the bush and turn on those who held him. It is a song of defiance more than despair. Dylan sings it alone with acoustic guitar, in a measured, weathered voice that suits the old story.

title: Blackjack Davey
note: A version of the old British ballad also known as Gypsy Davy, the third track on Good as I Been to You.
preview: A married woman leaves her home and husband to ride away with a wandering gypsy.
summary: The ballad tells of a charming traveller who sings at a lady's door and wins her over. She leaves her comfortable house, her husband and her fine clothes to go with him, and when her husband rides after her she refuses to come back. It celebrates choosing freedom and passion over wealth and duty. Dylan performs it solo with a steady, rolling guitar pattern.

title: Canadee-i-o
note: A traditional sailing ballad, the fourth track on Good as I Been to You, performed with voice and fingerpicked guitar.
preview: A young woman disguises herself as a sailor to cross the sea, and wins a surprising fortune.
summary: A girl dresses as a sailor so she can board a ship bound for Canada. When the crew discovers she is a woman they turn against her, but the captain protects her, and by the end she has married him and settled in the new land. It is a tale of courage and luck told in a long, flowing narrative. Dylan sings it gently over a delicate, ringing guitar part.

title: Sittin’ on Top of the World
note: A blues first recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks in 1930, which Dylan sings solo on Good as I Been to You.
preview: A man whose lover has left him insists he is doing just fine without her.
summary: The singer has been abandoned by a lover who went away and did not come back. Rather than mourn, he claims to be doing better than ever, though the boast carries a clear trace of hurt. The song is built on a simple, repeated refrain that turns heartbreak into stubborn pride. Dylan plays it as a relaxed country blues with guitar and harmonica, an old standard handed down through many singers.

title: Little Maggie
note: A traditional Appalachian song, usually played on banjo, that Dylan adapts to solo guitar on Good as I Been to You.
preview: A man watches the woman he loves drink, gamble and give her heart to someone else.
summary: The singer describes Maggie, a lively and reckless woman he cannot stop loving even as she spends her time drinking and going with other men. He turns between admiration, jealousy and resignation, and thinks of leaving. The song is short and quick, built on a driving rhythm taken from mountain music. Dylan delivers it in a rough, urgent voice over fast strummed guitar.

title: Hard Times
note: Stephen Foster wrote this parlour song, known in full as "Hard Times Come Again No More", in the 1850s.
preview: A plea on behalf of the poor and suffering, asking that hard times stop coming back.
summary: The song asks listeners to pause amid their own comfort and remember those who are hungry, weary and poor. Its refrain is a quiet wish that hardship would leave and not return, sung on behalf of everyone who suffers. Written as a gentle, hymn-like piece, it has outlasted its century as a standard of compassion. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly with acoustic guitar, letting its sorrow carry it.

title: Step It Up and Go
note: An upbeat Piedmont blues associated with Blind Boy Fuller, one of the liveliest tracks on Good as I Been to You.
preview: A good-humoured blues full of comic scenes, urging everyone to quicken their step and get moving.
summary: This is a jaunty, ragtime-flavoured blues made of short, comic verses about people and their foibles, each one capped by the title as a refrain. There is little story; the fun lies in the rhythm and the wit. Dylan plays it fast with a bouncing fingerpicked guitar, singing with obvious enjoyment, a brief burst of energy among the album's darker ballads.

title: Tomorrow Night
note: Written by Sam Coslow and Will Grosz in 1939, it became a hit for Lonnie Johnson and was later recorded by Elvis Presley.
preview: A lover wonders whether tonight's tenderness will still be there tomorrow.
summary: The singer is with someone he loves and is happy tonight, but he cannot stop worrying about tomorrow and whether her feelings will last. The song is a soft, romantic pop ballad from before the rock and roll era, built on that single fear. Dylan gives it a crooning, intimate reading with just his guitar, an early sign of his later love for old popular standards.

title: You’re Gonna Quit Me
note: A country blues recorded by Blind Blake in the 1920s, sung by Dylan with guitar on Good as I Been to You.
preview: A man senses that the woman he loves is about to leave him and asks her not to.
summary: The singer can tell that his partner is preparing to walk away, and he pleads, half resigned and half hopeful, for her to stay. The song turns on that single fear, returning to it again and again in the manner of a classic blues. It is short and spare. Dylan plays it with a nimble fingerpicked guitar and sings it with a worn, close-up intimacy.

title: Diamond Joe
note: A traditional cowboy song, near the end of Good as I Been to You, which Dylan also sang in the film Masked and Anonymous.
preview: A hired hand complains about working for a stingy, cruel boss and longs to get away from him.
summary: The narrator has signed on to work for a man named Diamond Joe, and soon regrets it: the food is poor, the pay is meagre and the work is hard. He tells his story with a wry, weary humour, warning others not to make his mistake and dreaming of escape. It is an old western work song of grievance. Dylan sings it solo in a rugged voice over a steady strum.

title: Love Henry
note: A traditional murder ballad descended from the old British ballad known as "Young Hunting", it is the second track on World Gone Wrong.
preview: A jealous woman kills the man who means to leave her for another, and a bird witnesses the crime.
summary: An old ballad of love turned to murder: a man arrives to tell a woman he loves someone else, and she kills him and hides his body. A talking bird has seen everything and refuses to keep her secret. Dylan sings it slowly and flatly, letting the cold facts carry the horror. It is just his worn voice and a single acoustic guitar.

title: Ragged & Dirty
note: A country blues sung to his own acoustic guitar, it is the third track on World Gone Wrong.
preview: A down-and-out man, turned away and left with nothing, asks a woman to take him in anyway.
summary: A plain-spoken blues from a man who has been thrown out and is broke, shabby and alone, pleading with a woman to let him back in. The verses circle around the same situation rather than telling a story, in the way of old country blues. Dylan plays it with a loose, rolling guitar pattern and sings with a rough, unhurried patience.

title: Blood in My Eyes
note: A song first recorded by the Mississippi Sheiks in the early 1930s; Dylan's version on World Gone Wrong was given a black-and-white video filmed in London.
preview: A man burns with desire for a woman and keeps trying to win her, even as she slips away.
summary: A blues about longing: a man is so taken with a woman that he can think of nothing else, and he offers what little he has to win her over. It repeats its situation like a lament rather than moving forward, and its mood is weary more than lustful. Dylan slows the original's string-band lilt into a dark, deliberate solo performance on acoustic guitar.

title: Broke Down Engine
note: A blues by Blind Willie McTell, who recorded it in the early 1930s; Dylan sings it alone with acoustic guitar on World Gone Wrong.
preview: A man compares himself to a worn-out engine that no longer runs, abandoned and begging his woman to return.
summary: A man left by his lover describes himself as a broken-down machine, out of power and useless without her. He prays and pleads for her to come back, his bad luck piling up as he goes. Dylan's version is fierce and percussive, with hard-strummed guitar and a hoarse vocal that turns McTell's lament into something close to a shout.

title: Two Soldiers
note: A traditional song from the time of the American Civil War, sung by Dylan to acoustic guitar on World Gone Wrong.
preview: Two young soldiers, one leaving people behind and one with no one, march into battle, and neither returns.
summary: A ballad about two soldiers before a battle: one has family waiting at home, the other has no one who will miss him. They make promises to one another about who will carry word home, and then the fighting takes them both. Dylan sings it gently and without drama, letting the quiet telling make the loss feel heavier.

title: Jack‐a‐Roe
note: An old ballad, also known as Jackaroe, that Joan Baez and the Grateful Dead also recorded; it is the second-to-last track on World Gone Wrong.
preview: A wealthy merchant's daughter disguises herself as a man and follows her sweetheart to war.
summary: A ballad about a rich young woman whose sweetheart is sent off to war against her parents' wishes. She dresses as a man, enlists under a false name and goes after him, finding him wounded on the battlefield and nursing him back to health before they marry. Dylan tells the story briskly and plainly, sounding like a storyteller passing on something old.

title: Lone Pilgrim
note: An old American hymn that Doc Watson had recorded, it closes World Gone Wrong.
preview: A traveler finds the grave of a pilgrim who died far from home, and the dead man speaks of peace.
summary: A hymn in which a visitor stands at the grave of a stranger who died while journeying, and the dead pilgrim answers, telling him not to grieve because he is at rest and at home. It turns a lonely death into a calm acceptance. Dylan sings it quietly and tenderly, a soft ending to an album full of murder and misfortune.

title: Dirt Road Blues
note: The second track on Time Out of Mind, a short, rockabilly-tinged shuffle that follows the opener "Love Sick".
preview: A man walks a dusty road looking for a lost love, hoping something will change.
summary: A man on foot along a country road keeps moving, waiting for a woman to come back and wondering if she ever will. The song is short and repetitive, more a mood than a story, with the road standing in for a restless, unsettled mind. Its sound is lo-fi and echoing, a bouncing old-time rhythm under Dylan's distant, roughened voice.

title: Million Miles
note: A slow, smoky blues near the middle of Time Out of Mind, the album's fourth track.
preview: A man feels endlessly far from the woman he loves, even as he tries to get closer.
summary: A man speaks to a woman who seems impossibly distant from him, though he keeps telling himself he is getting nearer. The song drifts through scraps of thought, regret and wry asides, its refrain measuring the gap between them. The band plays a low, loping groove with organ and guitar, and Dylan's voice sounds tired and sly at once.

title: 'til I Fell in Love With You
note: A heavy, stomping blues that is the sixth track on Time Out of Mind.
preview: A man says love has wrecked him, leaving him sleepless, sick and unable to go on as before.
summary: A man describes how falling in love has left him worn out and damaged, unable to rest or think clearly, with his life falling apart around him. Each verse adds another sign of his decline, and the refrain blames it all on love. The tone is grim but wryly funny, set over a grinding blues groove with a thick, murky sound.

title: Can't Wait
note: A slow, brooding blues near the end of Time Out of Mind; alternate versions were later released on Tell Tale Signs.
preview: A man consumed by longing for a woman says he cannot keep waiting for her much longer.
summary: A man tormented by desire tells a woman that he is running out of patience and running out of time, haunted by thoughts of her day and night. The song moves with a heavy, dragging gait, its refrain pressing the same urgency again and again. Organ and a dark, rumbling band surround Dylan's weathered voice, giving it the feel of a late-night confession.

title: Bye and Bye
note: A light, crooning swing number, the fourth track on "Love and Theft", in the style of prewar popular song.
preview: A man woos a woman in a gentle, easygoing way, though a hint of menace hides under the charm.
summary: A man courts a woman with a relaxed, sweet-talking manner, saying he is in no hurry and enjoying himself. But beneath the charm the singer drops darker hints about his past and his intentions, so the courtship never feels quite innocent. Dylan croons it softly over a lilting swing arrangement that recalls the popular ballads of the 1930s.

title: Lonesome Day Blues
note: A long, driving electric blues, the fifth track on "Love and Theft".
preview: A lonely, embittered man moves through a bleak day, nursing grief and threatening those who wronged him.
summary: A man having a dreadful, lonely day pours out a string of grievances, losses and boasts, moving from family memories to threats against his enemies. The verses pile up loosely, as in old blues, mixing sorrow, humor and menace. A tough, relentless band groove pushes it along, and Dylan sings in a gravelly growl that keeps the mood both mournful and defiant.

title: Floater (Too Much to Ask)
note: A gently swinging song on "Love and Theft" that later drew attention for borrowing lines from Junichi Saga's book Confessions of a Yakuza.
preview: An aging man drifts through memories of family, love and small-town life with dry, rambling humor.
summary: An older narrator muses about his family, his youth, a romance and the passing of time, wandering from topic to topic like a man fishing on a lazy afternoon. His wit is dry and sometimes unsettling, with flashes of violence under the calm. The music is a lilting, old-fashioned swing with fiddle, giving the song the easy feel of a porch tune.

title: Moonlight
note: A soft, old-fashioned crooner's ballad, the eighth track on "Love and Theft".
preview: A man gently invites a woman to come and meet him under the moon.
summary: A man speaks tenderly to a woman, asking her to meet him in the evening and painting a lush, romantic picture of nature at dusk. Each verse returns to the same invitation, so the song feels like a patient serenade. Dylan sings it in a light, crooning style over a lilting arrangement, sounding like a parlour song from long before rock and roll.

title: Cry a While
note: A blues near the end of "Love and Theft" that switches between a slow, swaggering pace and a fast, driving shuffle.
preview: A man who once wept over a woman now tells her it is her turn to suffer.
summary: A man who was hurt in love turns the tables, telling the woman who treated him badly that now she will be the one crying. The verses are full of sardonic asides and tough talk. The song alternates between a slow, menacing blues and sudden bursts of a fast shuffle, giving it a lurching, unpredictable energy.

title: Beyond the Horizon
note: A lilting love song on Modern Times whose melody draws on the 1930s popular song "Red Sails in the Sunset".
preview: A man promises that love and peace wait somewhere past the horizon, beyond the troubles of now.
summary: A man speaks to someone he loves, assuring them that something better lies past the horizon, beyond the world's troubles. The song is a gentle reverie, blending romance with a quiet sense of faith in what lies ahead. Its arrangement is soft and swaying, like an old dance-band ballad, and Dylan sings it with an unexpected tenderness.

title: Nettie Moore
note: A slow, solemn song on Modern Times whose refrain draws on the 1857 parlour song "Gentle Nettie Moore".
preview: A man mourns a lost love while moving through a hard, disordered world of trouble and judgment.
summary: A man longs for a woman named Nettie Moore, who seems lost to him, while describing a world full of danger, hardship and approaching judgment. The verses roam between grief, scripture, blues images and wry asides before returning to the sorrowful refrain. The arrangement is sparse and stately, built on a slow, thudding beat, with Dylan sounding grave and reflective.

title: The Levee’s Gonna Break
note: A rocking blues on Modern Times based on "When the Levee Breaks", the 1929 song by Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie.
preview: A man warns that the floodwaters are rising and the levee is about to give way.
summary: A man watches as the river rises and warns that the levee is about to fail, the coming flood standing for both natural disaster and a life spinning out of control. Released the year after Hurricane Katrina, it inevitably recalled that flood. The verses toss together worry, love and sardonic remarks over a fast, rolling boogie driven by the road band.

title: Do You Hear What I Hear?
note: Written in 1962 by Noël Regney and Gloria Shayne as a plea for peace during the Cuban missile crisis, it is the second track on Christmas in the Heart.
preview: News of a newborn child passes from the night wind to a lamb, a shepherd and a king, until it reaches everyone.
summary: The song is a chain of messages: each figure hears or sees something and passes it on to the next, from the smallest creature up to a mighty ruler. It grows step by step, each verse a little grander, until the closing call is for peace and goodness for all. Dylan takes it straight and earnest, his rough voice set against a warm, old-fashioned arrangement with backing singers.

title: Winter Wonderland
note: A 1934 standard with words by Richard B. Smith and music by Felix Bernard, here played as a bright, bouncy number early on Christmas in the Heart.
preview: A couple walks through a snowy landscape, building a snowman and dreaming happily about their future together.
summary: The song follows two sweethearts out in the snow, delighting in sleigh bells, a snowman and the cold that sends them back by the fire. It is less about Christmas itself than about winter romance, and its mood is light and playful throughout. Dylan gives it a brisk, cheerful swing with a chorus of backing voices, and his gravelly delivery makes its innocence sound both sincere and a little comic.

title: Hark the Herald Angels Sing
note: An eighteenth-century hymn with words by Charles Wesley, sung to a melody adapted from Felix Mendelssohn, it is one of the album's traditional carols.
preview: Angels announce the birth of Christ and call on every nation to join their song of praise.
summary: This is a hymn of proclamation: the angels' message of a newborn king is relayed to the world, and the listener is asked to join in. Its verses move from the birth itself to what it means for believers, ending in joyful praise. Dylan sings it plainly and reverently, letting the choir carry much of the melody, and makes no attempt to dress up a song meant for a congregation.

title: I'll Be Home for Christmas
note: Written in 1943 by Kim Gannon and Walter Kent and made famous by Bing Crosby, it spoke for soldiers away from home during the Second World War.
preview: Someone far away promises to come home for the holiday, then admits it may only happen in a dream.
summary: The singer is writing home, perhaps a soldier, asking for snow, mistletoe and presents to be ready for a homecoming. Only at the end does the twist arrive: the reunion may happen only in dreams. The song is short and gentle, its warmth shadowed by distance. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, and his worn voice brings out the longing beneath its holiday cheer.

title: Little Drummer Boy
note: A carol written by Katherine Kennison Davis in 1941 and popularised by the Harry Simeone Chorale, it sits near the middle of Christmas in the Heart.
preview: A poor boy with nothing to give the newborn Christ offers the only gift he has: his drumming.
summary: The song tells of a boy summoned to see the infant Jesus who has no fine present to bring, so he plays his drum for the child instead. Its refrain imitates the beat of the drum, and the story ends with the baby smiling at him. The point is humility: the gift that matters is the one honestly given. Dylan's version keeps a steady marching beat and a soft choir behind his voice.

title: O' Come All Ye Faithful (Adeste Fideles)
note: An old Latin hymn, usually credited to John Francis Wade in the eighteenth century, which Dylan sings partly in Latin before switching to English.
preview: The faithful are invited to come to Bethlehem, see the newborn Christ and worship him.
summary: The hymn is an invitation: believers are called to travel to Bethlehem and adore the child born there. Each verse repeats the call, building to a rousing refrain of worship. Dylan opens in Latin, a nod to the song's origins, then carries on in English with a choir behind him. His grainy, unpolished voice against the stately hymn tune gives the track an unusual, heartfelt character.

title: Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas
note: Written by Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane for the 1944 film Meet Me in St. Louis, where Judy Garland sang it, it became a holiday standard.
preview: A wish that this Christmas may be bright, with troubles set aside and friends gathered close again.
summary: The singer comforts someone, hoping the coming holiday brings relief from the year's worries and a return of old friends. Beneath its warmth lies a quiet sadness: the good times are hoped for rather than promised. The song moves slowly and tenderly, a lullaby more than a celebration. Dylan croons it gently over a soft, old-fashioned band arrangement, sounding both tender and weathered.

title: Silver Bells
note: Written by Jay Livingston and Ray Evans for the 1951 film The Lemon Drop Kid, it is a Christmas song about the city rather than the countryside.
preview: Busy city streets fill with shoppers, lights and the sound of bells as Christmas draws near.
summary: The song paints a crowded city at holiday time: sidewalks full of people, shop windows lit, children laughing and bells ringing on every corner. It is a picture of urban bustle turned festive, with a gentle refrain about the bells. Dylan sings it in an easy, swaying style with backing singers, treating it as an affectionate snapshot of an old-time American Christmas.

title: The First Noel
note: A traditional English carol of uncertain age, first printed in the early nineteenth century, sung here with a choir late in Christmas in the Heart.
preview: Shepherds watch their flocks and wise men follow a star to find the newborn king.
summary: The carol retells the Nativity story: angels appear to shepherds in the fields, a star rises in the east, and wise men travel to bring gifts to the child. Each verse ends with the same joyful refrain. It is calm and narrative, less a celebration than a recounting. Dylan's version leans on its choir, his voice blending into a slow, reverent arrangement.

title: Christmas Island
note: Written by Lyle Moraine and recorded in 1946 by the Andrews Sisters with Guy Lombardo, it is a lighthearted island novelty near the end of the album.
preview: The singer invites someone to spend Christmas on a tropical island, swapping snow for sunshine and palm trees.
summary: This is a playful daydream: rather than a snowy holiday, the singer imagines Christmas on a warm island, with Santa arriving by canoe and the season spent under the palms. The tone is breezy and romantic, closer to a holiday postcard than a carol. Dylan gives it a relaxed, swaying feel with a Hawaiian-style lilt, one of the album's lightest moments.

title: The Christmas Song
note: Written in 1945 by Mel Tormé and Bob Wells and made famous by Nat King Cole, it is the penultimate track on Christmas in the Heart.
preview: Familiar winter comforts and children's excitement make up a simple, warm wish for a merry Christmas.
summary: The song is a string of cozy images: roasting chestnuts, carols, decorations and children waiting for Santa, rounded off with a wish that everyone has a good holiday. It is unhurried and intimate, more a mood than a story. Dylan sings it slowly over a soft jazz-tinged arrangement, and his cracked voice gives a song associated with velvet crooners a more fragile, human sound.

title: O' Little Town of Bethlehem
note: A hymn written by Phillips Brooks in 1868, it closes Christmas in the Heart on a quiet, reverent note.
preview: A quiet town sleeps under the stars on the night a holy child is born there.
summary: The hymn looks on Bethlehem at night, still and silent, as the birth of Christ takes place unnoticed by the world. Later verses turn the scene into a prayer that the same presence might be born in the believer's heart. It is hushed and contemplative throughout. Dylan sings it simply with a choir, ending the album in reverence rather than celebration.

title: My Wife's Home Town
note: Written with Robert Hunter and credited also to Willie Dixon, since it is built on his blues "I Just Want to Make Love to You".
preview: A man grumbles, half in jest, that his wife's home town is the root of all his troubles.
wordsBy: Bob Dylan, Robert Hunter and Willie Dixon
summary: The singer complains about the place his wife comes from, blaming it for everything that goes wrong and casting it as something close to hell. The humor is dark and deadpan, a classic blues grievance played for laughs and menace at once. It moves on a slow, heavy Chicago blues riff, with accordion and growling guitar, and Dylan delivers it with a gruff, sly relish.

title: If You Ever Go to Houston
note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a mid-tempo Texas song driven by accordion, the album's border-town sound at its plainest.
preview: A traveler offers advice to anyone heading to Houston and other Texas towns, remembering people and places he knew.
summary: The singer speaks as someone who has been around Texas, handing out tips on how to carry yourself in Houston and asking to be remembered to people there. Between the advice come hints of an old love and unfinished business. It rolls along at an easy, swinging pace, and the accordion gives it the feel of a Tex-Mex dance hall, with Dylan sounding wry and worn.

title: Forgetful Heart
note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a slow, minor-key ballad and one of the darkest songs on Together Through Life.
preview: A man speaks to his own heart, which has let go of a love he still cannot forget.
summary: The singer addresses his heart directly, as if it were a companion that has drifted off and lost the memory of a past love. He is left behind, lonely and sleepless, while the love fades into the past. The song is brooding and spare, built on a slow, haunting groove with mournful accordion and violin, and Dylan sings it in a low, ghostly voice.

title: Jolene
note: Written with Robert Hunter and not the Dolly Parton song of the same name, it is a stomping blues number in the middle of the album.
preview: A swaggering man declares his devotion to a woman named Jolene and boasts of his own power.
summary: The singer is a confident rambler who names his woman as his queen and himself as king, mixing devotion with bravado. The repeated name serves as the song's hook, coming back after every short verse. It is loose and rough, a road-house shuffle with crunching guitar and accordion, and Dylan sings it with a grin in his voice.

title: This Dream of You
note: The only song on Together Through Life that Dylan wrote without Robert Hunter, it has a Tex-Mex lilt with accordion and violin.
preview: A lonely man clings to a dream of the woman he loves, the one thing keeping him going.
summary: The singer is alone, uncertain and tired of the world, and what holds him up is a vision of someone he loves, whether real or only remembered. He fears what will happen if the dream fades. The song sways gently like a border waltz, with accordion and fiddle carrying a sweet, melancholy tune, and Dylan sings it with weary tenderness.

title: Shake Shake Mama
note: Written with Robert Hunter, it is a raw, fast blues shuffle in the second half of Together Through Life.
preview: A restless man urges a woman to dance and shake, mixing lust with grumbling about his troubles.
summary: The song is a party blues: the singer calls on a woman to move, while slipping in boasts and complaints about his own hard situation. Its verses are short and punchy, each returning to the title cry. The music is a rough, driving shuffle with stinging guitar and accordion, and Dylan growls through it in the spirit of old Chicago and Memphis records.

title: It's All Good
note: Written with Robert Hunter, it closes Together Through Life with a jaunty tune that turns a cheerful catchphrase into irony.
preview: Amid broken homes, corruption and decay, the singer keeps insisting with a straight face that everything is fine.
summary: The song surveys a world going wrong, marriages failing, the powerful lying, towns falling apart, and answers each bad sign with the same breezy reassurance of its title. The gap between the grim pictures and the upbeat refrain is the joke, and the bite. It bounces along on a bright, swinging groove with accordion, and Dylan sounds amused and knowing.

title: Soon After Midnight
note: The second track on Tempest, a slow and gentle ballad with a lilting, old-fashioned doo-wop feel.
preview: A late-night love song from a man who sounds tender and patient, though a quiet menace keeps slipping in.
summary: A man awake in the small hours waits for a woman and tells her how devoted he is. The song moves at an easy, swaying pace, sweet on the surface, but darker hints of jealousy and violence surface between the romantic lines, so the tenderness never feels entirely safe. The band plays softly behind a croon that is half lullaby, half warning, which makes it one of the gentlest and strangest moments on a dark record.

title: Narrow Way
note: The third track on Tempest, a long, hard-driving blues built on a repeating riff.
preview: A weary, stubborn man insists that one day he and the woman he wants will finally meet halfway.
summary: A narrator who has wandered and suffered addresses a woman who keeps her distance, swearing that if he cannot climb up to her, she will one day have to come down to him. Verse after verse returns to that promise as a refrain, mixing boasts, grievances and stray images of hardship and travel. The groove barely changes, rolling forward relentlessly, and the song's length turns it into an endurance test of longing and pride.

title: Long and Wasted Years
note: The fourth track on Tempest, a mid-tempo song delivered in a rough, half-spoken voice over a circling guitar figure.
preview: A man talks to a former partner about the years they let slip away and the distance now between them.
summary: Addressed to someone the narrator once loved, the song looks back over a broken relationship and the time both of them squandered. Its tone is regretful but also defensive and bitter, moving between apology, accusation and resignation without settling. The verses are short and conversational, almost like a man thinking aloud. A repeating guitar pattern carries it forward steadily, and Dylan's growled delivery makes the regret sound lived-in rather than sentimental.

title: Pay in Blood
note: The fifth track on Tempest, a snarling mid-tempo rocker driven by piano and guitar.
preview: A furious, vengeful voice declares that he settles every debt with violence rather than with money.
summary: The speaker is a hard, menacing figure who seems to have seen corruption and cruelty everywhere and answers it with threats of his own. Each verse piles up insults, boasts and grim pronouncements, and the refrain returns to the idea that his payment comes in blood. The music is jaunty and polished, which makes the venom in the vocal even more unsettling. It is one of the angriest songs on an already violent album.

title: Scarlet Town
note: The sixth track on Tempest; Scarlet Town is the setting of the old ballad "Barbara Allen".
preview: A portrait of a decaying, haunted town where love, sin and death sit side by side.
summary: The song describes a strange town drawn from old folk balladry, a place full of mourners, sinners, beauty and ruin. Rather than tell a single story, it moves from scene to scene, sketching characters and images in a slow, hypnotic procession. The mood is mournful and eerie, like a ghost story set to a dirge. Banjo and fiddle give it an old-time sound, as if a centuries-old ballad has been reopened and filled with new shadows.

title: Early Roman Kings
note: The seventh track on Tempest, a heavy blues built on the stop-time riff familiar from Muddy Waters' "Mannish Boy".
preview: A swaggering portrait of brutal, powerful men who rule by force and fear no one.
summary: The song describes a gang of arrogant, well-dressed strongmen, part ancient emperors and part modern hoodlums, and the narrator sometimes seems to speak as one of them. It unfolds as a series of boasts and threats over a single stomping riff that never lets up. The tone is darkly comic and menacing at once. An accordion adds a dusty, border-town color to the grinding Chicago-style blues underneath.

title: Tin Angel
note: The eighth track on Tempest, a long narrative ballad that runs for roughly nine minutes.
preview: A husband pursues his runaway wife and her lover, and the confrontation ends in death for all three.
summary: A man comes home to find his wife has left with another man, and he sets out after them. The song tells the story in many verses like an old murder ballad, with dialogue between the three characters as the chase reaches its violent end. There is no chorus, just the steady unfolding of the plot over a dark, repetitive acoustic groove. Its tone is fatalistic, as if the tragedy were written long before it began.

title: The Night We Called It a Day
note: Written by Matt Dennis and Tom Adair in 1941 and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1942; the second track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: A lover remembers the night a romance ended and how the whole world seemed to darken with it.
summary: The singer recalls the evening a love affair came to an end, when even nature seemed to share in the sorrow. It is a classic torch song, quiet and wistful, dwelling on a single remembered moment rather than telling a long story. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly, without the polish of a crooner, and his small band plays softly with pedal steel guitar standing in for the lush strings of the original arrangements.

title: Stay With Me
note: Written by Jerome Moross and Carolyn Leigh for the 1963 film "The Cardinal" and recorded by Frank Sinatra; the third track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: A humble prayer asking God for guidance, comfort and companionship through doubt and darkness.
summary: Unlike most songs on the album, this one is addressed to God rather than to a lover. The singer confesses to feeling lost and unworthy and asks for a guiding presence to stay close. It moves slowly and solemnly, like a hymn, with no real refrain beyond its repeated plea. Dylan's recording is hushed and spare, his voice exposed and fragile over a soft, sparse band.

title: Autumn Leaves
note: A French song by Joseph Kosma and Jacques Prévert, with English words by Johnny Mercer; the fourth track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: Falling leaves in autumn bring back memories of a summer love that is now gone for good.
summary: The singer watches the leaves drift past a window and is reminded of a lover who has left, and of the summer they shared. It is a short, simple song built on the image of the changing season as a measure of passing time and fading love. Dylan sings it very slowly and quietly, letting the melody carry the sadness, while the band keeps to a soft, sparse accompaniment.

title: Why Try to Change Me Now
note: Written by Cy Coleman and Joseph McCarthy and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1952; the fifth track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: A dreamy, unconventional man asks the woman he loves to accept him as he is rather than reform him.
summary: The singer admits he has always been a bit odd and out of step, and asks his lover why she would want to change him after all this time. The song has a gentle, self-mocking humor and a tone of quiet pleading. It moves easily through its verses without a big climax. Dylan's plain, weathered voice suits the idea of a man set in his ways, and the band's soft, slow arrangement keeps it intimate.

title: Some Enchanted Evening
note: Written by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II for the 1949 Broadway musical "South Pacific"; the sixth track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: Advice to seize love the moment you meet it, because such a chance may never come again.
summary: The singer describes seeing a stranger across a crowded room and knowing at once that this is the person meant for you. The song urges the listener to act on that feeling before it slips away. In the musical it is a grand, operatic showpiece, but Dylan's version strips it down to a slow, almost conversational reading, with steel guitar and quiet bass, making it sound more like a private memory than a declaration.

title: Where Are You?
note: Written by Jimmy McHugh and Harold Adamson in 1937 and the title song of a 1957 Frank Sinatra album; eighth on Shadows in the Night.
preview: An abandoned lover asks where the one who left has gone and why their love came to nothing.
summary: The singer is left alone after a lover's departure and keeps asking where that person has gone and what became of the promises they shared. It is a pure lament, built on repeated questions that get no answers. The mood is lonely and still. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly over a hushed arrangement, letting long pauses and the drifting pedal steel fill the empty space the song describes.

title: What'll I Do
note: Written by Irving Berlin in 1923 and recorded by Frank Sinatra; the ninth track on Shadows in the Night.
preview: A lonely lover wonders how to go on now that the person who mattered most is gone.
summary: The singer has lost someone and can only imagine the empty days ahead, filled with memories and photographs instead of company. The song is a waltz built around a series of quiet, helpless questions. Its tone is tender and resigned rather than dramatic. Dylan's version is slow and unadorned, with the band barely above a whisper, so the old melody and his worn voice carry all the feeling.

title: Maybe You'll Be There
note: A 1940s ballad by Rube Bloom and Sammy Gallop; the second track on Fallen Angels.
preview: A lonely singer clings to the hope that a lost love might be waiting somewhere ahead.
summary: The singer is alone, looking back on a love that slipped away and imagining that one day, somewhere, that person may turn up again. It is a quiet torch song where hope and doubt are mixed in equal measure. The melody rises gently and falls back without resolving. Dylan sings it softly with his touring band, keeping the arrangement light and unhurried so the wistful mood can settle.

title: Polka Dots and Moonbeams
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke in 1940 and recorded by Frank Sinatra with Tommy Dorsey; the third track on Fallen Angels.
preview: A sweet story of a young man meeting a girl at a country dance and falling in love.
summary: The song tells a small, storybook romance: a chance meeting at a dance, an instant attraction, and a happy future that follows. Its images are whimsical and gentle, and its tone is warm and a little nostalgic. Unlike many of the sad ballads on these standards albums, it is light and charming. Dylan's band plays it at an easy, swaying tempo, and his voice treats it fondly, like a memory of a simpler time.

title: Skylark
note: Written by Hoagy Carmichael with words by Johnny Mercer in 1941; the fifth track on Fallen Angels.
preview: A lonely singer asks a skylark whether it has seen anywhere the love they are longing for.
summary: The singer speaks to a bird in flight, asking it to carry news of a love that might be waiting in some faraway place. The song is full of yearning and imagery of open skies, distant meadows and night. Its long, winding melody is famously demanding to sing. Dylan takes it slowly and carefully, his band playing a soft, airy backing that leaves room for the melody's wandering phrases.

title: Nevertheless
note: Written by Bert Kalmar and Harry Ruby in 1931 and recorded by Frank Sinatra in 1950; the sixth track on Fallen Angels.
preview: Someone admits that falling in love may end badly, but chooses to fall anyway.
summary: The singer knows that this romance could bring heartbreak and that friends would advise caution, yet admits to being hopelessly in love regardless. The song is light and good-humored, more amused than anguished about its own foolishness. It moves at an easy, strolling pace. Dylan's version is relaxed and affectionate, with the band's gentle swing and steel guitar giving it a soft, slightly old-fashioned glow.

title: All or Nothing at All
note: Written by Arthur Altman and Jack Lawrence and first recorded by Frank Sinatra with Harry James in 1939; the seventh track on Fallen Angels.
preview: A lover refuses to settle for half a romance: it must be complete devotion or nothing.
summary: The singer lays down terms to a would-be partner, insisting that a half-hearted love is worse than none and that only total commitment will do. Beneath the demand is a fear of being hurt, which gives the song its tension. The melody builds with a slow, insistent pulse. Dylan's band plays it with a darker, Latin-tinged rhythm than most of the album, and his delivery is firm rather than pleading.

title: On a Little Street in Singapore
note: Written by Peter DeRose and Billy Hill in 1938 and recorded by Frank Sinatra with Harry James; the eighth track on Fallen Angels.
preview: A secret romance unfolds in a far-off port city, where two lovers meet in hiding.
summary: The singer describes a clandestine love affair set on a quiet street in a distant Asian port, with moonlight, exotic surroundings and a sense of danger. It is a piece of old Hollywood-style romantic escapism, more about atmosphere than story. The tune sways lazily, evoking a faraway night. Dylan's version is gentle and unhurried, his band adding a soft, slightly mysterious color that suits the song's dreamlike setting.

title: It Had to Be You
note: Written by Isham Jones and Gus Kahn in 1924, one of the most recorded songs of its era; the ninth track on Fallen Angels.
preview: Only one person, flaws and all, could ever win this singer's heart.
summary: The singer explains that many others might have seemed better suited, yet none could hold their interest the way this one person does, even with all their faults. It is affectionate and lightly teasing, a song of contented love rather than longing. The melody is bouncy and familiar. Dylan's band gives it a relaxed, easy swing, and his voice treats the old standard with an unforced warmth.

title: That Old Black Magic
note: Written by Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer for the 1942 film "Star Spangled Rhythm"; the eleventh track on Fallen Angels.
preview: Falling in love feels like being under a spell the singer cannot and does not want to break.
summary: The singer describes love as a kind of sorcery that sets them spinning and burning whenever their lover is near. The song piles up images of enchantment, fire and helpless surrender, and its long, climbing melody mirrors the feeling of being swept away. It is one of the most upbeat songs on the album. Dylan's band plays it with a brisk, loping swing, giving the record a lively change of pace.

title: Come Rain or Come Shine
note: Written by Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer for the 1946 Broadway musical "St. Louis Woman"; it closes Fallen Angels.
preview: A promise of lasting love, whatever luck, weather or fortune may bring to the couple.
summary: The singer vows steady devotion through good times and bad, rich or poor, happy or troubled. It is a vow song, calm and certain rather than anxious, built on a simple contrast between fair and foul weather. Placed at the end of the album, it closes the record on a note of commitment. Dylan sings it slowly and earnestly, with his band's soft, warm backing giving the promise a sense of quiet dignity.

title: I Guess I’ll Have to Change My Plans
note: Written by Arthur Schwartz and Howard Dietz in 1929, it opens the first of Triplicate's three discs.
preview: A man who had his future mapped out with someone learns she is gone and must start over.
summary: A man discovers that the person he was building his life around has moved on, and he takes the news with a rueful shrug rather than a scene. The song is light on its feet, turning heartbreak into a wry admission that the plans have to change. Dylan sings it with a relaxed, conversational phrasing over his touring band, setting the easygoing, late-night tone for the three discs that follow.

title: I Could Have Told You
note: A torch ballad from the 1950s songbook that Frank Sinatra recorded, sitting early on the first disc of Triplicate.
preview: Someone who watched a lover leave says he saw it coming all along and was hurt anyway.
summary: The singer looks back on a love that ended the way he always suspected it would, and he speaks with more weariness than bitterness. The song is a slow, brooding ballad, built on the gap between knowing and still being unable to stop yourself. Dylan takes it at a patient pace with a muted band, letting his weathered voice carry the sense of someone who learned nothing from his own warnings.

title: Once Upon a Time
note: Written by Charles Strouse and Lee Adams for the 1962 Broadway musical All American, later recorded by Tony Bennett and Frank Sinatra.
preview: An older man remembers a youthful, carefree love and the world it belonged to, both now long gone.
summary: An older narrator recalls a time when he was young, in love and sure the world was his, and sets it against the quieter present. The song moves like a fairy tale turned inside out, its gentle opening giving way to the sadness of things that did not last. Dylan sings it slowly and tenderly, and his aged voice gives the memory of youth a real distance.

title: This Nearly Was Mine
note: A Rodgers and Hammerstein song from South Pacific (1949), where the French planter Emile de Becque sings it; here a slow waltz on Triplicate.
preview: A man mourns a love he held almost in his hands before it slipped away.
summary: Written for a character who believes he has lost the woman he loves, the song is a lament for something that was close enough to touch and is now out of reach. It is a sweeping waltz in its stage form, full of grand longing. Dylan pares it down, with pedal steel and brushed rhythm under his voice, so the regret sounds private and late rather than operatic.

title: That Old Feeling
note: Written by Sammy Fain and Lew Brown in 1937 for the film Vogues of 1938, it became a standard sung by many jazz and pop singers.
preview: Seeing a former love again, a man finds the old attraction comes straight back.
summary: The singer runs into someone he once loved and realises his feelings never went away, however much time has passed.
