The song is bright and swinging rather than mournful, treating the rekindled spark as both a surprise and a small helplessness. Dylan's version moves at an easy mid-tempo, with his band giving it a loose, small-combo bounce among the slower ballads around it.

title: It Gets Lonely Early
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Sammy Cahn and recorded by Frank Sinatra on his 1965 album September of My Years.
preview: A man living alone after a breakup finds the evenings start too soon and stretch too long.
summary: The song is about the empty hours after a relationship ends, when the night seems to arrive early and there is no one to share it with. It is a quiet, reflective ballad about ageing and solitude rather than fresh heartbreak. Dylan sings it gently over a spare arrangement, and the slow tempo lets the loneliness settle in rather than being declared.

title: My One and Only Love
note: Written by Guy Wood and Robert Mellin in the early 1950s, famously recorded by Frank Sinatra and later by John Coltrane with Johnny Hartman.
preview: A man tells the woman he loves that she is the only one, and describes how she moves him.
summary: This is a straightforward love song, addressed directly to one person and full of quiet wonder at what she means to the singer. It unfolds slowly, more a hushed confession than a declaration. Dylan treats it with restraint, his voice low and close over soft steel guitar and bass, making it one of the most tender moments on the first disc.

title: Trade Winds
note: Written by Cliff Friend and Charles Tobias and a 1940 hit for Bing Crosby; it closes the first disc of Triplicate.
preview: On a tropical shore, the warm winds bring back memories of a lover who is no longer there.
summary: Set somewhere in the islands, the song has the singer listening to the winds off the sea and thinking of a romance that once happened there. It is dreamy and exotic in the manner of its era, with a gentle sway that suggests palms and water. Dylan's band gives it a soft, drifting arrangement with steel guitar, ending the first disc on a wistful, faraway note.

title: Braggin’
note: A little-known 1940s swing number, Braggin' opens the second disc of Triplicate at a jaunty tempo.
preview: A man playfully boasts about his sweetheart while admitting he may be bragging a bit too much.
summary: The song is a light, teasing piece in which the singer cannot stop showing off about the person he loves. It is one of the more upbeat tracks on the album, built on a bouncing swing rhythm and a sense of humour about its own boasting. Dylan sounds amused and relaxed, and the band keeps the groove brisk, a cheerful start to a disc that soon turns darker.

title: Imagination
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke in 1940, it was a hit for the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra with Frank Sinatra and for Glenn Miller.
preview: A man reflects on how the imagination can make a lover seem perfect, and wonders if it is fooling him.
summary: The song considers how the mind dresses up love, conjuring a perfect partner and making a person believe what they want to believe. It moves between wonder and gentle doubt, never quite settling which one wins. Dylan sings it as a slow, thoughtful ballad, his phrasing unhurried, with the band sketching a soft late-night backdrop behind him.

title: How Deep Is the Ocean
note: Written by Irving Berlin in 1932, it has been recorded by countless singers and is one of his best-known ballads.
preview: A lover answers the question of how much he cares by pointing to the depth of the sea and the height of the sky.
summary: The whole song is built on a series of questions about the size of the singer's love, each answered with an image from nature that has no measurable end. It is simple and devotional, a pledge made through comparisons rather than promises. Dylan takes it slowly and plainly, letting the questions hang in the air over a hushed band.

title: P.S. I Love You
note: Written by Gordon Jenkins with words by Johnny Mercer in 1934; not the Beatles song of the same name.
preview: A man away from home writes a letter to the woman he loves, filling it with small news and his longing.
summary: The song takes the form of a letter from someone separated from his partner, passing on everyday details about how he is getting on before coming to the real point at the end. Its charm lies in that homely, chatty tone, with the feeling held back until the closing line. Dylan delivers it like someone reading his own note aloud, warm and slightly shy, over a gentle arrangement.

title: The Best Is Yet to Come
note: Written by Cy Coleman and Carolyn Leigh in 1959 and made famous by Frank Sinatra with Count Basie's orchestra in 1964.
preview: A man courting someone promises that their romance has only just begun and its best days lie ahead.
summary: The singer is wooing someone and assures them that everything so far is merely a warm-up for what is coming. It is a confident, swaggering song, full of anticipation and a little flirtation. Dylan's version swings at a steady, unhurried pace, and his older voice gives the promise an amused, knowing edge that a young singer could not bring to it.

title: But Beautiful
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke for the 1947 Bing Crosby and Bob Hope film Road to Rio.
preview: Love is described as a tangle of opposites, funny and sad, calm and wild, but always beautiful.
summary: The song tries to pin down what love is and keeps finding contradictions: it can be one thing and its opposite in the same moment. It is a reflective ballad more than a personal story, a meditation in the form of a love song. Dylan sings it softly, almost musing to himself, with spare guitar and steel shading the melody.

title: Here’s That Rainy Day
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke for the 1953 Broadway musical Carnival in Flanders, later a jazz standard.
preview: Someone who once laughed off talk of hard times finds that the hard times have finally arrived.
summary: The singer looks back at a carefree past when love seemed endless and any thought of trouble could be brushed aside, then admits that the day he never planned for has come. It is a sorrowful ballad about the cost of not saving anything for later, emotionally speaking. Dylan's slow, rueful reading suits a song about hindsight, and his band keeps the arrangement grey and still.

title: Where Is the One
note: Written by Alec Wilder and Edwin Finckel and recorded by Frank Sinatra on his 1957 album Where Are You?
preview: A lonely man asks where the person meant for him is, and whether he will ever find her.
summary: The song is a search with no answer: the singer wonders aloud where his true love might be and why she has not appeared. It is a melancholy, searching ballad with an unusual, winding melody. Dylan sings it with quiet resignation over a subdued arrangement, letting the unanswered question stand at the centre of a disc full of lonely late-night songs.

title: There’s a Flaw in My Flue
note: Written by Jimmy Van Heusen and Johnny Burke; Frank Sinatra recorded it in 1956, and it closes the second disc of Triplicate.
preview: A man alone by a smoky fireplace keeps seeing the face of a lost love whenever the chimney acts up.
summary: The song mixes comedy and heartbreak: the singer sits by a faulty fireplace, and every time it smokes and sputters he is reminded of the person he has lost. The domestic, slightly absurd image sits against a genuinely sad feeling. Dylan plays it straight, as a slow ballad, which makes the oddness of the conceit all the more touching.

title: Day In, Day Out
note: Written by Rube Bloom with words by Johnny Mercer in 1939, it opens the third disc of Triplicate.
preview: Every day the same overwhelming feeling returns, the thrill of being in love that never wears off.
summary: The singer describes a love that keeps hitting him with the same force every single day, as if it were brand new each time. It is an energetic, driving song, its rhythm suggesting a pulse that will not slow down. Dylan's version moves along at a steady, swinging clip, a lively opening to the album's final disc.

title: I Couldn’t Sleep a Wink Last Night
note: Written by Jimmy McHugh and Harold Adamson for Higher and Higher (1943), a film in which Frank Sinatra sang it.
preview: After a quarrel with his sweetheart, a man lies awake all night until he can set things right.
summary: The singer has had a falling-out with someone he loves and spent a sleepless night worrying, wanting only to make up. It is a tender, slightly anxious song, more sweet than sad, and it resolves with the hope of reconciliation. Dylan sings it softly and earnestly, the band giving it a gentle sway that suits a song about a restless night.

title: Sentimental Journey
note: Written by Les Brown, Ben Homer and Bud Green; Doris Day's 1945 recording with Les Brown's band became a symbol of soldiers coming home.
preview: A traveller sets off by train for home, eager to return to the places and people of the past.
summary: The song is about heading home after a long time away, with the train journey itself becoming a way to recover old memories. It caught the mood of the end of the Second World War, when many were making exactly that trip. Dylan gives it an easy, rolling rhythm and a warm, nostalgic tone, as if he were looking out of a train window himself.

title: Somewhere Along the Way
note: Written by Kurt Adams with words by Sammy Gallop; Nat King Cole had a hit with it in 1952.
preview: A man realises that at some point on the road of life he lost the person he loved.
summary: The singer looks back over a shared life and finds that the love slipped away at a moment he cannot pin down, somewhere between then and now. The song is regretful and searching, more puzzled than angry. Dylan sings it slowly, with a gentle, wistful arrangement that suits its sense of something lost without anyone quite noticing.

title: When the World Was Young
note: Based on a French song by Philippe-Gérard, with English words by Johnny Mercer; Frank Sinatra and Peggy Lee recorded it.
preview: A worldly, older man looks back with longing on the innocent days of his youth.
summary: A sophisticated figure who seems to have everything admits he misses the simple pleasures and first loves of his younger years. The song sets the glamour of a grown-up life against memories of a more innocent time, and the memories win. Dylan's slow, rueful reading turns it into a portrait of an old man counting what he gave up.

title: These Foolish Things
note: Written in 1936 by Jack Strachey with words by Eric Maschwitz, it is a British song that became an American standard.
preview: Small everyday objects and moments keep reminding a man of a lover who is gone.
summary: The song is built from a list of tiny, ordinary things that bring a lost love back to mind, each one trivial on its own and painful in sum. It is affectionate and bittersweet rather than despairing. Dylan takes it gently, letting the band play a soft, swaying accompaniment while his voice lingers over the memories.

title: You Go to My Head
note: Written by J. Fred Coots with words by Haven Gillespie in 1938, it was recorded by Billie Holiday and many others.
preview: A lover compares the giddy effect of the person he adores to being intoxicated.
summary: The singer describes being so taken with someone that it feels like drinking too much, a pleasant dizziness he cannot shake off. The song is sensual and a little woozy, full of images of intoxication. Dylan's version is slow and smoky, with the band laying down a hushed backdrop that suits its late-night, slightly tipsy mood.

title: Stardust
note: Hoagy Carmichael's 1927 melody, later given words by Mitchell Parish, became one of the most recorded songs of the century; Dylan sings it near the end of Triplicate.
preview: Alone at nightfall, a man remembers a love that has ended and finds the memory itself is all he has left.
summary: A lonely singer looks up at the evening sky and drifts back to a romance that is long over. The song moves from a reflective, half-spoken opening into its famous soaring melody, where the memory of the affair becomes something to treasure in its own right. Its mood is wistful rather than bitter, more about the beauty of remembering than the pain of losing. Dylan takes it slowly and plainly, letting the tune carry the feeling, with a small band behind him.

title: It’s Funny to Everyone but Me
note: A 1939 ballad by Jack Lawrence, recorded early on by Frank Sinatra with Harry James; Dylan places it next to last on Triplicate.
preview: A man whose heart has been broken notices that his misery amuses everyone around him except himself.
summary: A jilted lover talks about being left behind while the people around him treat his heartbreak as a joke. The song turns on that gap between how his sorrow looks from outside and how it feels to him, mixing a little self-mockery into its sadness. It stays small and confiding, a single complaint told quietly rather than a grand lament. Dylan sings it as an unhurried late-night ballad, close and resigned.

title: Why Was I Born
note: Written by Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II for the 1929 Broadway show Sweet Adeline, it closes Triplicate and with it Dylan's run of standards albums.
preview: Someone devoted to a lover who does not return the feeling asks what the point of their own life can be.
summary: A person in love with someone who does not love them back wonders aloud why they were ever born, if it was only to want what they cannot have. The song is built as a chain of plain, aching questions that never receive an answer. Its tone is torch-song despair softened by tenderness. As the final track of Triplicate, Dylan's slow, worn reading turns it into a quiet farewell to the whole songbook project.

title: I’ve Made Up My Mind to Give Myself to You
note: The fourth track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, a gentle, slow love song that stands apart from the darker, wordier pieces around it.
preview: An older man, having travelled and seen enough, decides calmly to commit himself completely to the one he loves.
summary: A man who has lived a long, restless life speaks to the woman he loves and tells her he has finally settled his mind on giving himself to her. The song unfolds patiently, each verse returning to the same quiet resolution, as he looks back over his wandering and finds it led here. Its tone is tender and unhurried, with no irony at all. The arrangement is soft and lilting, close to a lullaby.

title: Black Rider
note: The fifth track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, one of the sparest arrangements on the album, built mostly on quiet guitar.
preview: A man speaks to a dark, shadowy rider who stalks him and tells him to keep his distance.
summary: The singer addresses a mysterious black rider who has been following him, a figure who reads as death, temptation or a darker side of himself. He warns the rider off, mixing defiance with weariness and the odd flash of dry humour. The song moves slowly and quietly, never raising its voice, which makes it all the more menacing. Its sound is hushed and bare, with gentle guitar and soft accompaniment around Dylan's close, low vocal.

title: Mother of Muses
note: The seventh track on Rough and Rowdy Ways, a slow hymn-like invocation of the muse that also salutes Second World War generals.
preview: An aging singer calls on the mother of the muses for inspiration and honours those who fought and marched before him.
summary: Like an ancient poet, the singer opens by calling on the goddess who mothers the muses, asking her to help him sing. He then pays tribute to generals who cleared the way in the Second World War and to figures such as Elvis Presley and Martin Luther King, before turning to his own love for one of the muses and to his sense of age. The tone is solemn, grateful and personal. The music is slow and stately, almost a hymn.

title: The Mighty Quinn (Quinn the Eskimo)
note: Written during the 1967 Basement Tapes sessions and a 1968 hit for Manfred Mann; Self Portrait has it live from the 1969 Isle of Wight festival with the Band.
preview: Everyone is restless and stuck until the mysterious Quinn arrives, and then the whole crowd comes joyfully alive.
summary: The song describes a gloomy, idle crowd waiting for something to happen, and a strange figure called Quinn the Eskimo whose arrival will change everything. Its verses sketch odd, comic scenes of boredom and frustration, and its big singalong chorus celebrates the coming of the hero. It is playful and nonsensical rather than serious, a party song with a hint of a parable. The Isle of Wight performance with the Band is loose, rough and good-humoured.

title: Minstrel Boy
note: A Dylan song from the 1967 basement period, not the old Irish ballad; Self Portrait's version is live from the 1969 Isle of Wight festival with the Band.
preview: A worn-out travelling minstrel keeps rolling on, and the song asks whether anyone will help or reward him.
summary: The song is about a wandering musician who has travelled a long way and grown tired, still on the move with no one to ease his load. It asks, again and again in its chorus, who will offer him some kindness for his trouble. The tone is affectionate and a little mournful, a portrait of the performer as a lonely drifter. The live Isle of Wight recording leans on the Band's harmony voices, giving it a ragged, gospel-tinged warmth.

title: John Wesley Harding
note: The title track is loosely based on the Texas outlaw John Wesley Hardin, with an extra letter added to the name.
preview: A brisk ballad painting an outlaw as a friend of the poor who was never pinned down by the law.
summary: A narrator tells the legend of a frontier gunman in the manner of an old outlaw ballad, casting him as a protector of ordinary people rather than a villain. The song sketches his reputation in quick strokes, a man with a gun in each hand who helps the honest and slips away whenever the lawmen close in. There is no real plot or reckoning, only the myth retold. It moves at a brisk, steady clip on acoustic guitar, harmonica, bass and drums.

title: As I Went Out One Morning
note: Like most of the album, it was cut in Nashville in late 1967 with just bass, drums and Dylan's guitar and harmonica.
preview: A walker meets a captive young woman who begs to go south with him, until a figure of authority intervenes.
summary: This short ballad is told by a man out walking who comes upon a young woman bound in chains. She pleads to run off south with him, and he turns her down, wary of what she wants, until the figure of Tom Paine hurries up to apologize for her and take charge. It reads like an allegory about freedom and its claims, told in a cool, deadpan voice. The arrangement is spare, just bass, drums, guitar and harmonica, like most of the album.

title: I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine
note: Its title and opening echo the labor ballad about the union organizer Joe Hill.
preview: A dream of a grieving saint ends with the dreamer waking in shame over his own part in the saint's fate.
summary: Borrowing the dream framing of the old labor ballad about Joe Hill, the singer describes seeing the saint alive, moving among the crowds in sorrow and calling out to people who have lost their way. The dream then darkens as the singer realizes he was among those who put the saint to death. He wakes in fear and shame, and the song ends in grief. Its tone is quiet and confessional, set over the sparse acoustic backing of the album.

title: All Along the Watchtower
note: It became Dylan's most performed song in concert, usually played in the hard-rock arrangement Hendrix gave it.
preview: Two outsiders talk on the road while, from a high lookout, the powerful watch riders approaching through the wind.
summary: A terse parable, the song opens with two outsiders, a joker and a thief, talking about a world where the powerful take what others make and understand nothing of its worth. Their talk gives way to a wide view from a fortress lookout, where princes keep watch as two riders approach and the weather turns. It stops on the brink of something rather than its arrival, leaving a mood of dread. The original is spare and acoustic, though Dylan later adopted the hard-rock arrangement Hendrix gave it.

title: Drifter’s Escape
note: A three-minute parable that closes the first side of the original LP.
preview: A bewildered man on trial slips away when a bolt from the sky strikes the courthouse.
summary: A drifter stands trial for reasons he cannot grasp, while the judge seems sympathetic yet powerless and the jury and crowd grow hostile around him. Just as the case turns against him, lightning strikes the courthouse, and in the confusion he slips away. Brief and told like a parable, it has a tense, almost biblical feel and leaves the meaning of both the crime and the escape open. It closes the first side of the original LP at a brisk three minutes.

title: The Wicked Messenger
note: At about two minutes it is one of the shortest songs on the album.
preview: A messenger who twists every report is told to bring only good news if he must speak at all.
summary: This is a dark parable about a messenger who cannot carry a message straight. Told in the voice of an ancient scripture, the song describes a man who exaggerates and distorts everything he reports, until the people he serves finally rebuke him and tell him that if he must speak, he should bring only good tidings. It is terse and ominous, with no chorus and no wasted line, and it ends abruptly. A tight, insistent bass line drives it from start to finish.

title: I’ll Be Your Baby Tonight
note: Pete Drake's pedal steel on the closing track pointed toward the country sound of Nashville Skyline.
preview: A relaxed invitation to drop all worries and spend the night together.
summary: A lover speaks gently to his partner, urging her to set aside her worries and the outside world and simply settle in for the night together. It is short and untroubled, with a lazy, good-humored charm and one warm promise at its heart that keeps returning. After the stern parables elsewhere on John Wesley Harding, it closes the album on a note of ease. The pedal steel of Pete Drake gives it a soft country lilt that pointed ahead to Nashville Skyline.

title: Girl From the North Country
note: Dylan re-recorded his 1963 song as a duet with Johnny Cash in Nashville, and it opens the album.
preview: Two old voices recall a lost love up north and ask a traveler to check that she is warm and well.
summary: Two singers send a request with someone heading north: look in on a woman one of them once loved and make sure she is safe and comfortable. The song is tender and wistful rather than bitter, a memory of a love that ended long ago but still matters. Here Dylan and Johnny Cash trade and share the verses, their voices not always in step, which gives the duet a loose, warm, unpolished charm. The backing is a gentle Nashville country arrangement.

title: Nashville Skyline Rag
note: An instrumental that lets the Nashville session players take the spotlight.
preview: A wordless, upbeat country romp built around picking solos.
summary: This track has no words at all. It is a lively country instrumental that hands the spotlight to the Nashville session musicians, who take turns soloing on guitar, banjo, piano and other instruments over a bright, bouncing rhythm. The tone is playful and relaxed, like a band enjoying itself at the end of a long day. Short and cheerful, it serves as a light breather on the album between the more personal love songs.

title: To Be Alone With You
note: A spoken aside from Dylan to producer Bob Johnston was left in at the start of the track.
preview: A cheerful song of counting down the day until the singer can be alone with his sweetheart.
summary: A man spends the day thinking about the evening, when the work is done and he can finally be alone with the woman he loves. The mood is light and affectionate, with no conflict at all, just eager anticipation and simple contentment. The song is short and bouncy, built on a jaunty piano and a loose country rhythm. A brief spoken remark from Dylan to his producer before the music starts adds a casual, studio-floor feel.

title: I Threw It All Away
note: Dylan sang it on the premiere episode of The Johnny Cash Show in 1969.
preview: A man admits he carelessly gave up the love he had and warns others not to do the same.
summary: A man looks back on a love he once held and admits, without excuses, that he let it go through his own carelessness and pride. The regret is plain and personal, and from it he draws a lesson for the listener: treasure love while you have it, because it may not come again. The song is short and direct, a confession turned into advice. It is sung in the smooth, mellow voice of the Nashville Skyline period, over organ and a soft country band.

title: Lay Lady Lay
note: Released as a single, it reached the US top ten in 1969.
preview: A soft, crooned plea for a lover to stay the night.
summary: A man asks a woman to stay with him through the night, coaxing her gently rather than demanding. The song is tender and sensual, a slow seduction in which he tells her there is no reason to leave and that he wants her near until morning. Its verses circle back to the same plea, building patience instead of urgency. Dylan sings in a soft, low croon over pedal steel guitar and an unusual, clip-clopping percussion part.

title: Tell Me That It Isn't True
note: It was recorded in Nashville in February 1969 with Bob Johnston producing.
preview: A man hears rumors that his lover has left him for someone else and begs her to deny them.
summary: A man has heard talk around town that the woman he loves has found someone new and is ready to leave him. He does not accuse her; instead he pleads with her to say the stories are false, his worry growing as the gossip piles up. The song stays in that anxious, hopeful moment of not yet knowing. It is a gentle, mid-tempo country ballad, sung in a smooth voice over piano, organ and a relaxed Nashville band.

title: Tonight I'll Be Staying Here With You
note: It closes the album and was also issued as a single.
preview: A traveler throws away his ticket and decides to stay with the woman he loves instead of moving on.
summary: A man who has always been ready to leave finally decides not to. Speaking to the woman beside him, he gives up his travel plans and lets the train go without him, choosing one night of closeness over the open road. The mood is relaxed and quietly happy, with no regret in it. Sung in the mellow, warm voice of the Nashville Skyline period, it closes the album on an easy country shuffle.

title: All the Tired Horses
note: The album's opening track is sung entirely by female backing singers, with no lead vocal from Dylan.
preview: A short, repeated chant about a rider unable to get going while the day passes.
summary: This is barely a song at all, more a brief, hypnotic chant. A lone rider is stuck, unable to get moving, while the hours slip away. The same couple of lines are repeated over and over by a choir of women, with lush strings swelling behind them, and Dylan himself never sings. Opening Self Portrait this way felt like a puzzle or a joke to many listeners, yet it has a dreamy, drifting beauty.

title: Copper Kettle
note: A 1950s song by Albert Frank Beddoe about making moonshine, earlier recorded by Joan Baez.
preview: An old-timer praises brewing whiskey in the hills, far from tax collectors.
summary: An old mountain dweller speaks fondly of making whiskey the traditional way, out in the hills where nobody comes to collect taxes. He treats the craft as an inheritance passed down from his elders and as a quiet act of independence from the government. The tone is slow, proud and gently defiant rather than rowdy. Dylan sings it tenderly over soft guitar and a hushed backing, one of the more admired tracks on Self Portrait.

title: The Boxer
note: Dylan covered Paul Simon's song by harmonizing with his own overdubbed voice in two different singing styles.
preview: A poor young man who came to the city looking for work tells of hard times while a fighter keeps going despite every blow.
summary: Dylan takes on Paul Simon's well-known story of a poor young man who leaves home for the city, finds little work and much loneliness, and thinks about going back. The song ends on the figure of a fighter who refuses to quit despite all the punishment he has taken. Dylan sings it as a duet with himself, one track in his smooth country voice and one in his rougher older style, slightly out of step with each other. Many hear it as strange or even playful.

title: If Not for You
note: George Harrison recorded it the same year for All Things Must Pass.
preview: A grateful love song saying the world would be gray and empty without the beloved.
summary: A plain, grateful love song in which the singer tells his partner how lost he would be without her. He pictures a life gone dull and cold, unable to find his way, then sets it against the warmth she brings. Each verse returns to the same thankful idea, so the song works almost as a simple refrain. Bright and unhurried, it opens New Morning with a light, homespun country-folk feel.

title: Day of the Locusts
note: It recalls the day he accepted an honorary degree at Princeton in June 1970, when cicadas filled the air.
preview: An uneasy man sits through a stuffy ceremony and is glad to escape back to the hills with his love.
summary: Dylan looks back on a day spent being honored by a famous university, and he plainly would rather be anywhere else. He describes the stiff hall, the solemn faces and his own nervous discomfort, while the loud buzzing of insects outside seems to mock the ceremony. The turn comes when he gets away and drives off toward the hills with the woman he loves. Wry and self-mocking, it is a small comic portrait of fame feeling like a trap.

title: The Man in Me
note: It plays over the opening credits of the 1998 film The Big Lebowski.
preview: A man says only the right woman can see past his defenses to who he really is.
summary: A man admits that he hides behind a tough or distant front, and that only the woman he loves has the patience to see through it. Addressed to her, the song is a warm thank-you for being understood. It is short and easygoing, with a wordless vocal hook that comes back again and again. A rolling piano and gospel-tinged backing singers give it a loose, contented swing.

note: The Jimi Hendrix Experience's version on Electric Ladyland became a hit single in 1968.

note: The Byrds included it on their 1965 debut album Mr. Tambourine Man and released it as a single that summer.

note: Cher's version was her first solo hit, reaching the US top twenty in 1965.

note: The Byrds recorded it for their 1965 debut album Mr. Tambourine Man.

note: Rick Nelson's country-rock version with the Stone Canyon Band brought him back to the US charts in 1969.

note: Manfred Mann's version went to number one in the UK in early 1968.

note: Peter, Paul and Mary released it as a single in late 1967, years before Dylan's own recording came out.

note: The Byrds recorded it for their 1968 country album Sweetheart of the Rodeo.

note: Fairport Convention recorded it for their 1969 album Unhalfbricking.

note: Joe Cocker included it on his second album, Joe Cocker!, released in 1969.

note: Joan Baez recorded it for Any Day Now, her 1968 double album of Dylan songs.

note: Manfred Mann's Earth Band recorded a long, heavy version for their 1973 album Solar Fire.

note: The O'Jays made it the title track of their 1991 album Emotionally Yours.

note: Stevie Wonder's soul single of the song reached the US top ten.

title: Blowin' in the Wind
note: Sam Cooke sang the song on his live album Sam Cooke at the Copa.

note: The trio's version was a US top-ten single in 1963.

note: The couple sang it as a duet on Cash's album Orange Blossom Special.

note: Bryan Ferry's glam reworking was his first solo single.

note: The duo included it on their first album, Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.

note: Nina Simone recorded it on her album To Love Somebody.

note: Nina Simone recorded it on her album Here Comes the Sun.

note: Eric Clapton released a reggae-tinged single of the song.

title: Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door
note: Warren Zevon recorded it on The Wind, made while he was terminally ill.

note: Billy Joel released it as To Make You Feel My Love on his third greatest-hits set.

title: To Make You Feel My Love
note: Garth Brooks recorded it for the film Hope Floats, and it topped the country chart.

note: U2's live version appears on Rattle and Hum.

note: Jimi Hendrix played the song at the Monterey Pop Festival.

note: The Isley Brothers stretched it into a long soul track on Givin' It Back.

note: It was Olivia Newton-John's first hit single.

note: Joan Baez recorded it on her album Farewell, Angelina.

note: Joan Baez recorded it on Diamonds & Rust.

note: Joan Baez recorded it on Any Day Now, an album entirely of Dylan songs.

note: The Byrds recorded it on their debut album Mr. Tambourine Man.

title: Chimes of Freedom
note: Bruce Springsteen released a live version on an EP tied to the Amnesty International tour.

note: Faces opened their first album, First Step, with the song.

note: The duet was a UK top-ten hit.

note: The Band opened Music from Big Pink with the song, which Dylan wrote with Richard Manuel.

note: The Band recorded it on Music from Big Pink; Rick Danko co-wrote the music.

note: The White Stripes included it on their first album.

note: Patti Smith recorded it on Twelve, her album of covers.

note: The Neville Brothers recorded it on Yellow Moon.

note: Madeleine Peyroux recorded it on Careless Love.

note: Folk singer Paul Clayton's adaptation of an older folk song.

title: Joe Hill
note: A song about the executed labor organizer Joe Hill, set by Earl Robinson to a poem by Alfred Hayes.

title: Pretty Polly
note: An old murder ballad from Britain and Appalachia.

title: Down on Penny's Farm
note: A song about a hard-hearted landlord that was later reissued on the Anthology of American Folk Music.

title: Trouble No More
note: Muddy Waters' Chess single, itself reworked from Sleepy John Estes' Someday Baby Blues.

title: All Your Love (I Miss Loving)
note: A Chicago blues single by Otis Rush on the Cobra label.

title: The Lonesome Road
note: A ballad written by Gene Austin and Nathaniel Shilkret that became a standard.

title: Where the Blue of the Night (Meets the Gold of the Day)
note: Bing Crosby's theme song, which he co-wrote.

title: New Danville Girl
note: An unreleased song Dylan wrote with playwright Sam Shepard and recorded during the Empire Burlesque sessions.

title: Jokerman
note: The opening track, it was also released as a single with a music video.
preview: A shape-shifting figure drifts through a landscape of biblical and political images, admired and doubted at once.
summary: The singer addresses a mysterious, ever-changing figure who moves freely through a crowded dreamscape of biblical scenes, false prophets and looming tyrants. Each verse piles up vivid images, and the chorus calls out to the Jokerman directly, half in admiration and half in frustration that he does nothing to stop what is coming. Whether he is a savior, a trickster or the singer himself is left open. The opening track rides a light, reggae-inflected groove.

title: Sweetheart Like You
note: It was the album's first single.
preview: The singer asks a woman what she is doing in a world of corrupt and dangerous men.
summary: The singer meets a woman in a dim, unwelcoming place run by men who are absent or not to be trusted, and asks why someone like her is there at all. He offers observations about power, ambition and the roles people are pushed into, mixing admiration with something close to condescension. The tone is gentle and wry, a quiet conversation more than a story. It was the album's first single, built on a slow, easy groove.

title: Neighborhood Bully
note: It is widely heard as a defense of the state of Israel.
preview: A small nation surrounded by enemies is blamed for defending itself.
summary: Using one extended, sarcastic metaphor, the singer describes a small figure scorned as a bully for refusing to be wiped out, though outnumbered and surrounded by hostile neighbors. Verses trace a long history of exile and persecution and mock the double standard by which survival itself is condemned. The irony never breaks; the narrator keeps repeating the accusation while showing how unfair it is. The song is widely heard as a defense of the state of Israel, set to a forceful rock arrangement.

title: License to Kill
note: Dylan played it on Late Night with David Letterman in March 1984 with the punk band the Plugz.
preview: Mankind's urge to conquer and destroy is held up against a woman who sees it clearly.
summary: The song looks at humanity's drive to conquer, from reaching into space to waging war, and suggests that man has been taught to think of himself as master of everything. Against that sweeping indictment stands a single woman who watches and understands, and who keeps asking who will finally take away his power to destroy. The tone is grave and accusing. Dylan later played it on Late Night with David Letterman in March 1984 with the punk band the Plugz.

title: Union Sundown
note: It targets the shift of American manufacturing to cheap labor overseas.
preview: Everyday goods are made abroad while workers at home lose their jobs to corporate greed.
summary: The singer takes an inventory of everyday goods, from clothes to cars, and notes that almost none of it is made at home anymore. He blames corporate greed that ships work abroad to cheap labor, but also turns a skeptical eye on unions that have lost their way. The tone is sardonic and combative, with each verse adding new examples before the chorus tolls the end of an era. It plays as a hard, punchy rocker with backing singers.

title: I and I
note: Its title borrows a Rastafarian expression for the self joined with God.
preview: A restless man walks out at dawn, weighing his own guilt against a stern, unseen judge.
summary: The singer slips out at daybreak, leaving a woman asleep, and walks through a stark landscape while turning over questions of guilt, justice and the impossibility of facing God directly. The verses wander between small observations and heavy moral thought, and the refrain returns to the title, borrowed from a Rastafarian expression for the self joined with God. The mood is uneasy and solitary, set to a loping, reggae-tinged rhythm.

title: Don't Fall Apart on Me Tonight
note: It closes the album.
preview: A tired man pleads with a lover to hold together with him for one more night.
summary: Late at night, a tired and uncertain man talks to the woman beside him, admitting regrets about the life he has led and the person he might have been. He wonders aloud about what has passed and what might still come, but keeps circling back to one simple request that she stay strong with him until morning. The mood is tender, worn and a little wry. It closes the album on a quiet, intimate note.

title: Tight Connection to My Heart (Has Anybody Seen My Love)
note: He reworked it from an unreleased Infidels-era song.
preview: A man trapped in a tense, mistrustful affair keeps asking where the love has gone.
summary: The singer is caught in a relationship full of suspicion and unease, where he feels watched, misread and unsure of where he stands. The verses jump between fragments of scenes, some tense and some oddly comic, while the chorus keeps asking whether anyone has seen the love he has lost. The tone is restless and a little paranoid. He reworked it from an unreleased Infidels-era song, giving it a polished mid-eighties sound with backing singers.

title: When the Night Comes Falling From the Sky
note: At seven and a half minutes it is the longest song on the album.
preview: A spurned lover warns that a reckoning is coming when darkness falls.
summary: The singer addresses a woman who turned him away, and his hurt hardens into a warning that she will see him again when darkness finally falls. The verses mix wounded pride with images of upheaval and judgment, so a personal grudge starts to feel like something larger. The tone is brooding and insistent, building rather than resolving. At seven and a half minutes it is the longest song on the album.

title: Dark Eyes
note: The closing track is just Dylan with acoustic guitar and harmonica.
preview: A man feels out of step with the violent, money-driven world around him, with only a woman's gaze to steady him.
summary: The singer moves through a night world where people chase money, fight and forget each other, and he feels like a stranger to all of it. Instead of joining in or condemning it, he steps back, troubled and detached, and the one thing that holds him is the steady gaze of the dark eyes in the title. The tone is hushed and haunted. The closing track is just Dylan with acoustic guitar and harmonica, a stark contrast to the rest of the album.

title: They Killed Him
note: A Kris Kristofferson song about Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesus, sung with a children's choir.
preview: Peacemakers who preached love are remembered, each cut down by violence.
summary: This is Dylan's version of a Kris Kristofferson song. Each verse remembers a man who preached peace and love, Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesus, and each ends the same way, with the man cut down by violence. The repetition turns three life stories into one lament about how the world treats those who ask it to be better. Dylan sings it plainly and earnestly, with a children's choir joining him.

title: Driftin' Too Far From Shore
note: One of the few songs on the album Dylan wrote by himself.
preview: A man tells a lover she has wandered too far from him to be brought back.
summary: The singer tells a lover that she has wandered so far from him that there may be no bringing her back. He sounds frustrated and a little bitter, puzzled by her moods and tired of trying, though he cannot quite let her go. The verses circle the same distance between them rather than telling a story, and the tone stays restless throughout. It is one of the few songs on the album Dylan wrote by himself.

title: Brownsville Girl
note: Co-written with playwright Sam Shepard, it runs past eleven minutes and is framed around the Gregory Peck western The Gunfighter.
preview: A rambling tale of a road trip, an old movie and a lost woman blurs memory and myth.
summary: The narrator recalls watching the Gregory Peck western The Gunfighter and lets the film bleed into his memories of a road trip across Texas with a woman he has since lost. The story drifts between past and present, scenes from the movie and scenes from his own life, until it is hard to tell myth from memory. Wry, rambling and tender, it was co-written with playwright Sam Shepard and runs past eleven minutes, with backing singers answering his lines.

title: Death Is Not the End
note: It was an outtake from the 1983 Infidels sessions.
preview: In the face of grief and fear, the song offers the plain comfort that death is not final.
summary: The singer speaks to someone overwhelmed by sorrow, fear and confusion, whose hopes have collapsed and who no longer knows whom to trust. Verse by verse he names more of the world's troubles, from crime to loneliness, then answers each with the same steady reassurance that death does not have the final word. The tone is grave and consoling rather than triumphant. It was an outtake from the 1983 Infidels sessions, sung slowly and solemnly.

title: Silvio
note: Written with Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter, it became a regular in his concerts.
preview: A drifter sets off to learn what fate holds for him.
summary: A restless narrator announces that he is setting out to learn what fate holds for him, ready to take whatever he finds. The verses are boastful and a bit cryptic, full of hints at trouble and mystery, while the chorus turns his search into a journey toward knowledge the living do not have. The tone is swaggering and carefree. Written with Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter, it is an upbeat rocker that became a regular in his concerts.

title: Rank Strangers to Me
note: An Albert E. Brumley song best known from the Stanley Brothers.
preview: A man returns to his home place and finds no one there who knows him.
summary: In this Albert E. Brumley song, best known from the Stanley Brothers, a man returns to the place where he grew up hoping to find old friends. Everyone he meets is a stranger, and he slowly realizes that the people he knew are gone. In the end he takes comfort in the hope of meeting them again in a life beyond this one. Dylan sings it slowly and simply, letting the loneliness of the story carry it.

title: Political World
note: The opening track sets the album's mood of a corrupt world.
preview: A world run by politics leaves no room for wisdom, love or peace.
summary: The singer describes a world where politics governs everything and leaves no room for wisdom, love, mercy or peace. Each verse adds another virtue that has been pushed aside or locked away, building a picture of a society that has lost its moral center. The tone is blunt and bleak, delivered with steady force rather than outrage. The opening track sets the album's mood of a corrupt world, on a driving, insistent rhythm.

title: Everything Is Broken
note: It was released as a single with a music video.
preview: A rolling list of broken things paints a world falling apart piece by piece.
summary: The singer reels off a long, rolling list of things that no longer work, from household objects and machinery to laws, promises and people. The catalogue starts small and keeps widening until the whole world seems to be coming apart, yet the delivery is wry rather than despairing, almost a shrug. There is no story, just the steady pile-up of damage. It was released as a single with a music video and moves on a swampy, rhythmic groove.

title: Ring Them Bells
note: A slow, hymn-like song built around piano.
preview: Bells are called to ring out for the lost and the faithful as the world nears its end.
summary: The singer calls for bells to ring out across a world that seems close to its end, on behalf of the lost, the blind, the faithful and those who have been forgotten. Each verse widens the circle of who needs to hear them, mixing sorrow with a stubborn hope. The tone is solemn and prayerful. It is a slow, hymn-like song built around piano, one of the most quietly moving moments on the album.

title: Man in the Long Black Coat
note: Its recording opens with the sound of crickets, adding to Lanois's swampy atmosphere.
preview: A woman vanishes with a mysterious stranger, leaving a haunted town behind.
summary: A woman has gone off with a mysterious stranger, and the song sketches the empty, uneasy place she left behind. The singer gathers fragments: a sermon about conscience, rumors, the silent landscape, and the lingering question of whether she was lured away or went willingly. Nothing is explained, and the stranger remains a shadow. The recording opens with the sound of crickets, adding to Daniel Lanois's swampy, dreamlike atmosphere.

title: Most of the Time
note: It was used in the 2000 film High Fidelity.
preview: A man insists he is over a past love, and the insistence gives him away.
summary: The singer insists he has moved on from a past love: he is clear-headed, steady, and hardly thinks of her at all. Yet every claim of calm comes with the same small qualifier, and the more he repeats it, the more obvious it becomes that he has not let go. The tone is soft and self-deceiving, which makes it quietly sad. The slow, atmospheric track was used in the 2000 film High Fidelity.

title: What Good Am I?
note: One of the album's quietest songs.
preview: The singer asks himself whether he is worth anything if he turns away from others' suffering.
summary: Speaking to himself, the singer asks a string of hard questions about his own conduct. Would he be worth anything if he looked away from people in need, kept silent when he should speak, or shut himself off from the pain around him? Each verse adds another test of conscience, and none is answered outright, so the listener is left to weigh them too. It is one of the quietest songs on Oh Mercy, sung softly over a hushed, sparse backing.

title: Shooting Star
note: It closes the album.
preview: Watching a falling star, he thinks of a lover he may have failed and of the last chances slipping away.
summary: The singer sees a star fall across the night sky and thinks of a woman he once loved, wondering whether he ever became the man she hoped for or simply let her down. From there the song widens into a sense of last things: chances closing, an ending drawing near, one final call to change. Its tone is gentle and regretful rather than bitter, and as the closing track of Oh Mercy it leaves the album on a quiet, reflective note.

title: Wiggle Wiggle
note: Slash of Guns N' Roses plays guitar on the opening track.
preview: A childlike chant urges someone to wiggle through a series of absurd images.
summary: In a nursery-rhyme chant, the singer keeps telling someone to wiggle, piling up nonsense comparisons that grow odder and slightly more menacing as they go. There is no real story, only a run of playful commands repeated with cheerful insistence. The song works more as a rhythm and a mood than as a message, a deliberately silly opener. It starts Under the Red Sky, with Slash of Guns N' Roses playing guitar.

title: Under the Red Sky
note: George Harrison plays slide guitar on the title track.
preview: A fairy-tale about a boy and girl in a small town that ends in loss.
summary: Told like a fairy tale, the song follows a boy and a girl who live in a little town, and the singer seems to address one of them as if recalling a shared childhood. Its simple, riddling verses hint at danger beneath the surface, and by the end the place and its innocence are gone and the world they knew has come undone. The childlike telling makes the sadness underneath feel stranger. George Harrison adds slide guitar to the title track.

title: Born in Time
note: Dylan first tried it during the Oh Mercy sessions.
preview: A man recalls a love that grew and faded in a single stretch of time.
summary: A man looks back on a love affair as if through a haze of memory, recalling how it began and how it seemed to belong to its own particular moment. He speaks to the woman directly, tender but aware that what they shared has passed. The verses drift between closeness and distance, dream and recollection, and the mood is wistful rather than angry. Dylan first tried the song during the Oh Mercy sessions before it appeared on Under the Red Sky.

title: Frankie & Albert
note: The opener is a version of the old murder ballad usually called Frankie and Johnny.
preview: A woman shoots the man who cheated on her and faces the consequences.
summary: This old murder ballad follows Frankie, who loves Albert devotedly until she learns he has been seeing another woman. She goes after him with a gun and shoots him, and then the law and its judgment close in on her. Each verse moves the story forward plainly, with a refrain that keeps returning to her sense of betrayal. Dylan's version opens Good as I Been to You, sung alone with acoustic guitar in a brisk, matter-of-fact way.

title: Arthur McBride
note: An Irish anti-recruiting song, which Dylan learned from Paul Brady's recording.
preview: Two cousins meet army recruiters on the road and send them packing.
summary: The narrator tells of a morning stroll with his cousin Arthur McBride, when the two meet a sergeant, a corporal and a young drummer out recruiting. The sergeant tempts them with talk of pay, fine clothes and glory, but the cousins reply that they know what soldiering really costs. When the recruiters turn threatening, the pair beat them soundly and send them off. Dylan sings this Irish anti-recruiting song alone with his acoustic guitar, having learned it from Paul Brady's recording.

title: Froggie Went a Courtin’
note: The centuries-old children's song closes the album at more than six minutes.
preview: A frog courts a mouse, and the wedding party ends badly.
summary: In this centuries-old children's song, a frog rides out to court a mouse, asks her uncle for permission to marry, and a wedding feast follows with a parade of animal guests. The festivities end in chaos when hungry predators arrive and scatter the party. Dylan tells the tale patiently, verse after verse, treating its nonsense with a straight face that makes it both funny and faintly sad. Sung alone over acoustic guitar, it closes the album at more than six minutes.

title: World Gone Wrong
note: The title song comes from the Mississippi Sheiks.
preview: The singer laments a world turned upside down, where nothing works as it should.
summary: Speaking to a lover, the singer explains that he can no longer behave as he once did, because the whole world around him has gone wrong. The verses touch on broken trust, trouble at home and his resolve to leave, each one returning to the same weary refrain. The tone is resigned rather than angry, more a shrug at ruin than a protest. The song comes from the Mississippi Sheiks, and Dylan performs it alone with acoustic guitar.

title: Delia
note: It is based on the real 1900 killing of a teenage girl in Savannah, Georgia.
preview: A young woman is shot by her lover, who is left to mourn in prison.
summary: Drawn from the real 1900 killing of a teenage girl in Savannah, Georgia, the song tells of Delia, shot by the young man who loved her. The verses move from the shooting to the courtroom and on to the prison cell, where he is left with nothing but his regret. Between them a mournful refrain grieves for friends who are gone. Dylan sings it slowly and plainly with acoustic guitar, letting the sorrow carry the story rather than the drama.

title: Stack a Lee
note: It tells the story of the 1895 killing of Billy Lyons by Lee Shelton in St. Louis.
preview: A gambler kills a man over a hat and passes into legend.
summary: The ballad retells the 1895 St. Louis killing of Billy Lyons by Lee Shelton, the man remembered as Stack a Lee. A quarrel over a hat turns deadly when Stack a Lee shoots Billy, who begs to be spared for the sake of his family. The story then follows the killer into the hands of the law, while the song turns him into a legend, part villain and part folk hero. Dylan performs it alone with acoustic guitar in a steady, unhurried telling.

title: Someone's Got a Hold of My Heart
note: An Infidels outtake, released in 1991 on The Bootleg Series Volumes 1–3.
preview: An early version of the song he later reworked for Empire Burlesque.
summary: The speaker is caught in a love he cannot shake, haunted by a woman who seems to have power over him and feeling watched and unsettled wherever he goes. The verses move through restless nights and vague threats, with the title returning as a confession of helplessness. The tone is brooding and tense. This Infidels outtake is the earlier version of the song that he later reworked for Empire Burlesque.

title: Death Is Not the End
by: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds
note: The band closed their 1996 album Murder Ballads with it, trading verses among several guest singers.

title: Man in the Long Black Coat
note: Osborne recorded it on her 1995 album Relish.

title: Born in Time
note: Clapton recorded it on his 1998 album Pilgrim.

title: Subterranean Homesick Blues
note: It became his first Top 40 hit in the US, and its cue-card promo clip opens Dont Look Back.
preview: A rapid-fire run of warnings about cops, fads and authority, telling a young listener to trust no leader.
summary: A rush of street-level warnings is aimed at a young listener trying to get by. The verses fly past in quick bursts, with police, informers, people mixing drugs, schooling that leads only to dull work, and fads that change by the hour. Running through it all is the advice not to trust anyone who claims to lead. It is fast, funny and paranoid, delivered almost as a chant over a rough electric band.

title: Maggie's Farm
note: It was the opening number of his electric set at Newport in 1965.
preview: A worker announces he is done laboring for a bossy family that treats him as property.
summary: A worker announces that he will no longer labor on Maggie's farm. In each verse he describes one member of the family that runs it: a brother who underpays and fines him, a father who bullies, a mother who lectures. He sings that he tries to be himself while they want him to be like them, so he is leaving. The refrain is a flat refusal, driven home by a loud, pounding electric band.

title: Love Minus Zero/No Limit
note: A quiet love song on the album's electric first side, with a title written as a fraction.
preview: A portrait of a calm, wise lover who stays above the noise and posturing of the world around her.
summary: The singer describes his lover, who speaks softly, needs no fuss and knows more than she says. Around her, people boast, argue, chase success and make empty promises, while she stays calm and untouched by it all. The song ends on a still, faintly ominous image of a wounded bird at the window. It is a quiet, admiring love song, set to a gentle band arrangement on the album's electric side.

title: Mr. Tambourine Man
note: The Byrds' electric version reached number one in 1965 before many listeners had heard Dylan's own.
preview: A sleepless singer asks a street musician to carry him off into music and forgetting.
summary: Tired but unable to sleep, the singer speaks to a street musician and begs him to play a song so that he can follow. He asks to be carried away from his own mind and worries for a while, out into a night of motion, music and forgetting. The verses drift through images of dancing, wandering and escape, always returning to the request in the refrain. Dylan's own version is gentle and mostly acoustic, with harmonica.

title: Gates of Eden
note: A long acoustic song of surreal images, it was the B-side of the single Like a Rolling Stone.
preview: A dreamlike set of scenes contrasting the false promises of the world with a paradise where those things vanish.
summary: The song moves through a series of strange, dreamlike scenes full of kings, soldiers, preachers, lovers and lost travelers. Each verse sets the confusion, greed and false promises of the world against a paradise where none of those things exist. In the last verse the singer's lover tells him her dreams, and he chooses not to explain them. It is solemn and hypnotic, a long solo performance for voice, guitar and harmonica.

title: It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding)
note: Running about seven and a half minutes, it is the longest song on the album.
preview: A relentless indictment of advertising, hypocrisy and power, told by someone who refuses to be shaken.
summary: The singer surveys a darkened world and lays out what he sees: advertising that deceives, preachers and politicians who manipulate, people who conform out of fear, and a society that worships money. The verses tumble forward in long chains of rhymes, broken by short refrains in which he insists he is unharmed, merely bleeding, and simply living. It is an unrelenting monologue over hard, insistent acoustic guitar, sustained across about seven and a half minutes.

title: It's All Over Now, Baby Blue
note: The album's closing song, it was later recorded by Them with Van Morrison.
preview: A farewell telling someone to leave the old life behind and start again.
summary: The singer tells someone that the time has come to leave, and urges them to take only what they need and let the rest go. Each verse brings a new image of an old life breaking up, from the people left behind to the ground shifting underfoot. The final verse tells them to strike a light and start over. It is a farewell that is both stern and tender, closing the album on a quiet, ringing acoustic note.

title: Like a Rolling Stone
note: Released as a single in July 1965 at over six minutes, it reached number two in the US.
preview: A sneering address to a once-privileged woman who has fallen and must now fend for herself.
summary: The singer turns on a woman who once lived in comfort and looked down on others, and who now finds herself alone, broke and without a home. Verse after verse he lists the friends and privileges she relied on and shows how each has failed her, then lands on a chorus that taunts and challenges at once. Beneath the scorn runs a strange sense of release, as if losing everything has set her free. Rolling organ and a long, surging band arrangement drive it.

title: Tombstone Blues
note: A fast electric blues featuring Mike Bloomfield on lead guitar.
preview: A chaotic parade of historical and biblical figures acting out a nightmare version of America.
summary: A fevered collage of America in which historical figures, biblical characters and pop-culture names collide in absurd, often violent scenes. There is no story as such; the verses pile up images of war, authority and madness, while a chorus returns the singer to his own household, where everyone is struggling to get by. The effect is satirical and breathless, propelled by a racing electric blues band and Mike Bloomfield's stinging lead guitar.

title: Ballad of a Thin Man
note: Built on Dylan's piano, it became a fixture of his 1966 live shows.
preview: A bewildered outsider, Mr. Jones, wanders through a strange scene he cannot understand.
summary: The song follows Mr. Jones, a respectable, educated man who walks into a room full of strange people and cannot make sense of anything. He asks questions, takes notes and appeals to his learning and connections, but every encounter leaves him more lost. The refrain mocks him for not knowing what is going on around him. The mood is menacing and sly, built on slow, heavy piano with organ.

title: Queen Jane Approximately
note: The song opens side two of the original LP.
preview: An invitation to a worn-out woman to come by when she tires of the people around her.
summary: Addressed to a woman worn down by her family, her admirers and the obligations of her position, the song offers a quiet alternative. Each verse names another source of her exhaustion, and each closes on the same refrain inviting her to come and see the singer once she has had enough. The mood is gentler than the songs around it on the album, half sympathy and half wry teasing, set to an easy mid-tempo band groove.

title: Highway 61 Revisited
note: Named after the highway that runs from Minnesota down to New Orleans, it features a police siren whistle.
preview: A string of absurd episodes, from a biblical sacrifice to a war, all staged on one American highway.
summary: In five short, comic verses, the song tells of absurd events that all end up on the same American highway. God orders Abraham to sacrifice a son there, a man with a bloody nose needs a place to go, odd goods need dumping, and finally a promoter decides to stage the next world war out there. Each tale lands in the same place, making the road a stage for everything. It is a rowdy, fast band performance punctuated by a police siren whistle.

title: Just Like Tom Thumb’s Blues
note: Set largely in Juarez, Mexico, it was recorded in the summer 1965 New York sessions.
preview: A traveler lost in a border town slides into sickness and despair and resolves to head back to New York.
summary: A drifter narrates his own unravelling in a Mexican border town, where the authorities are crooked, the women are dangerous and every comfort turns out to cost him something. The verses move like a slow hangover, each scene seedier and more sickly than the last, until he gives up on the place and decides to go back to New York. The tone is weary and darkly funny, carried by a loose, rolling band with piano well up in the mix.

title: Desolation Row
note: At over eleven minutes, it is the album's only acoustic track and its closer.
preview: A long carnival of literary, historical and invented characters in a ruined town where everything is upside down.
summary: The song wanders through a broken town where figures from history, literature and legend act out absurd scenes: Cinderella, Romeo, Einstein, the Phantom of the Opera and Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot among them. Each verse adds another strange tableau of violence, fear or foolishness, with Desolation Row standing for the place where the clear-sighted end up. In the last verse the singer answers a letter by asking for no more unless it comes from there. It is long, acoustic and hypnotic.

title: Rainy Day Women #12 & 35
note: Recorded in Nashville with a raucous brass-band feel, it reached number two in the US.
preview: A rowdy, laughing chorus about being attacked and judged by everyone no matter what you do.
summary: A boisterous romp in which the singer complains that people will attack and condemn you whatever you do, at home, at work or out in the street. Each verse lists another way of being judged, and each ends on a chorus that turns the persecution into a rowdy joke with a famous double meaning. Recorded in Nashville, it sounds like a marching brass band at a party, with laughter, shouting and loose, stumbling horns.

title: Visions of Johanna
note: Dylan first tried it in New York with the Hawks before cutting the album version in Nashville.
preview: A restless night in a cold room where the singer is with one woman but haunted by thoughts of another.
summary: Set during a sleepless night, the song finds the singer in a room with one lover, Louise, while his mind keeps drifting to an absent woman, Johanna, who seems more vivid to him than anyone present. The verses wander out into the city and through a gallery of minor figures, then return each time to that haunting pull of memory. There is no resolution; the longing only deepens as the night wears on. The Nashville recording is hushed and drifting, with organ and harmonica adding to its late-hour mood.

title: I Want You
note: It was released as a single ahead of the album and charted in the US and UK.
preview: A cheerful, plain declaration of desire set among a crowd of odd characters.
summary: A bright, simple confession of longing, set against a gallery of strange and sorrowful characters who pass through the verses. The singer moves briskly from one odd figure to the next, each a little sad or ridiculous, but every verse returns to the same direct refrain of desire. The contrast between the crowded, surreal scenery and the plainness of what he wants gives it charm. It bounces along on a cheerful, jangling band sound with bright guitar lines.

title: Stuck Inside of Mobile With the Memphis Blues Again
note: Cut in Nashville in early 1966, it runs about seven minutes.
preview: A man trapped in a strange town meets a series of eccentrics and wonders if he will ever get out.
summary: The narrator is stranded in a town where nothing makes sense, and each verse brings another odd character his way, from lawmen and would-be lovers to advisers offering strange counsel. Between these encounters comes a weary refrain that wonders if he is doomed to stay there for good while longing to be somewhere else. The mood is comic and exasperated rather than despairing. The Nashville musicians give it a loose, rolling bounce that carries it through its seven minutes.

title: Just Like a Woman
note: Manfred Mann released a hit version in the UK in 1966.
preview: A bitter-tender look at a lover who seems grown-up but breaks down like a child.
summary: The singer looks back on a relationship with a woman who presents herself as poised and grown-up but, in private, comes apart like a child. The verses move from the scene around her to his own exhaustion and his need to leave, and the chorus repeats his double-edged verdict on her. The tone sways between tenderness and resentment, which has made the song both loved and argued over. It is a slow, gentle ballad with acoustic guitar and harmonica.

title: 4th Time Around
note: Its waltz melody and story closely resemble the Beatles' Norwegian Wood.
preview: A wry tale of a tense romantic encounter that ends with the singer walking away.
summary: The singer recounts an uneasy encounter with a lover that turns on small, awkward exchanges and a sense that neither party is being straight with the other. The story unfolds coolly and with deadpan humour, and ends with him leaving and addressing someone else entirely. Its lilting waltz melody and storyline closely echo the Beatles' Norwegian Wood, which many hear as a playful reply. The arrangement is soft and spare, built on gently picked guitars.

title: Sad-Eyed Lady of the Lowlands
note: Over eleven minutes long, it filled the whole fourth side of the original double LP.
preview: A slow, hymn-like tribute to a mysterious woman, piling up images of her before asking whether he may wait for her.
summary: Dylan addresses a woman he holds in awe, describing her over several long verses in a cascade of surreal, devotional images that never settle into a plain portrait. Each verse builds slowly toward the same pleading refrain, in which he asks whether he should go on waiting for her. The tone is reverent and almost liturgical rather than casually romantic. The band plays softly and patiently, swelling at each chorus, and the song stretches past eleven minutes, filling the whole fourth side of the original double LP.

title: Mr. Tambourine Man
note: The Byrds' jangling 12-string version topped the US charts and helped launch folk rock.

title: It's All Over Now, Baby Blue
note: Van Morrison's band Them recorded the song in 1966.

title: Norwegian Wood (This Bird Has Flown)
note: John Lennon's song on Rubber Soul, with sitar played by George Harrison.

title: Just Like a Woman
note: Manfred Mann's single version charted in the UK in 1966.

title: Highway 61 Revisited
note: Johnny Winter's slide-guitar version appeared on his album Second Winter.

title: Maggie's Farm
note: Rage Against the Machine covered the song on their album Renegades.

title: Desolation Row
note: My Chemical Romance recorded a punk version for the Watchmen film soundtrack.

title: Like a Rolling Stone
note: The Rolling Stones released a live version on their album Stripped.

title: Gotta Serve Somebody
note: It won Dylan the 1980 Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Male.
preview: Whoever you are and however high you rise, you will end up answering to one master or another.
summary: The singer runs through a long list of people, from the powerful and famous to the ordinary and the poor, and tells each of them the same thing. Whatever their status, they will end up serving one master or another, either good or evil. The refrain hammers that choice home after every verse. The tone is steady and certain, almost preaching. It won Dylan the 1980 Grammy for Best Rock Vocal Performance, Male.

title: Precious Angel
note: Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits plays the lead guitar on the track.
preview: A thank-you to the woman who showed him the way to faith, mixed with warnings for a world he thinks has lost its bearings.
summary: The singer speaks to the woman who brought him to faith, grateful that she opened his eyes to what he had been missing. Between those thanks he turns outward, scolding friends and others who cling to comfortable illusions and warning that a spiritual battle is under way. The mood is bright and urgent rather than solemn, a love song and a sermon at once. Mark Knopfler's lead guitar threads through the full, buoyant band sound.

title: I Believe in You
note: It was one of three songs he played on Saturday Night Live in October 1979.
preview: He holds to his belief even as friends turn away and treat him as a stranger.
summary: The singer describes being shunned by friends and treated as an outsider because of his new faith. Each verse sets the rejection he faces against his determination to keep believing, whatever the cost. The tone is quiet and resolute rather than defiant, a private devotion spoken aloud. He played it on Saturday Night Live in October 1979 as one of three songs.

title: Slow Train
note: The album takes its name from this song.
preview: A survey of greed, false leaders and moral drift, with a reckoning steadily drawing closer.
summary: The singer looks around at his country and the wider world and does not like what he sees: greed, hollow preachers, leaders who serve themselves, and people who have traded conscience for comfort. Verse by verse the complaints pile up, some public and some personal, and each time the refrain points to something slow but unstoppable approaching. The tone is weary and stern, more warning than rage, carried by a patient, rolling groove that gives the album its name.

title: Gonna Change My Way of Thinking
note: He recorded a reworked version as a duet with Mavis Staples for a 2003 tribute album of his gospel songs.
preview: A vow to turn his life around and live by a new set of rules.
summary: The speaker announces that he is going to change how he thinks and lives, setting aside old habits for a new, stricter code rooted in his faith. The verses describe the corruption around him and his resolve to stand apart from it. The tone is tough and determined rather than gentle, delivered over a hard, bluesy groove. He later recorded a reworked version as a duet with Mavis Staples for a 2003 tribute album of his gospel songs.

title: When You Gonna Wake Up
note: He performed it on Saturday Night Live in October 1979.
preview: A list of society's hypocrisies, ending in a demand that the listener open their eyes.
summary: The singer runs through what he sees as the hypocrisies of modern life, from false teachers and self-serving leaders to people who chase pleasure while ignoring what matters. Each verse adds new targets, and each chorus comes back to the same blunt question of when the listener will finally rouse themselves and act. It is less a lament than a confrontation, delivered with the force of a preacher pounding the pulpit over a hard-driving band.

title: Man Gave Names to All the Animals
note: It was published as an illustrated children's picture book in 2010.
preview: A playful retelling of the first man naming each creature he meets in the garden.
summary: A playful retelling of the story of the first man naming the creatures in the garden. Each verse describes an animal he comes across, its look and its habits, and then the name he gives it, so the listener can guess along. In the final verse a snake appears, and the song stops before naming it, leaving a sly hint of trouble ahead. It was published as an illustrated picture book for children in 2010.

title: When He Returns
note: The album's closing track is just Dylan's voice and Barry Beckett's piano.
preview: A quiet hymn of surrender, waiting for a promised return that will set things right.
summary: Close to a prayer, the song has the singer reasoning with himself and with anyone listening about pride, struggle and the futility of resisting a greater power. He asks how long a person can keep fighting what they already know, then lets the argument rest in trust that a coming return will settle every question. It moves slowly and builds in intensity without ever raising the tempo. As the album's closer, it is only Dylan's voice and Barry Beckett's piano.

title: Saved
note: The title track is co-credited to Dylan and bassist Tim Drummond.
preview: A jubilant testimony of being pulled out of a lost life.
summary: A joyful testimony, the song has the singer looking back on a life he now sees as blind and headed for ruin, and celebrating the rescue that turned it around. The verses move from that old state to gratitude, with the title returning as a shout of relief. There is no doubt or hesitation in it, only celebration. The title track is co-credited to Dylan and bassist Tim Drummond, and it moves at a quick, exuberant gospel pace.

title: Solid Rock
note: It was a driving fixture of the 1979–80 gospel concerts.
preview: He declares he is holding on to an unshakable foundation no matter what the world throws at him.
summary: The singer insists he is holding on to a foundation that cannot be moved, whatever pressure, mockery or temptation the world puts in his way. The verses sketch the forces arrayed against him and recall the suffering that, in his belief, made his rescue possible, while the chorus hammers home his refusal to let go. It is fast, insistent and almost defiant in tone. It was a driving fixture of the 1979 to 1980 gospel concerts.

title: Pressing On
note: In the 2007 film I'm Not There it is sung by John Doe.
preview: A determined promise to keep moving toward a higher goal despite doubters.
summary: The singer describes people who doubt him, try to shake him or pull him back, and answers each with the same resolve to keep moving toward a higher calling. There is no turn in the story; the song works by repetition, its determination growing as it goes. It starts quietly and swells into a full gospel performance with backing voices. Years later, in the 2007 film I'm Not There, the song is sung by John Doe.

title: Shot of Love
note: The title track was produced by Bumps Blackwell, known for his work with Little Richard.
preview: A plea for the one kind of cure that can heal a troubled soul.
summary: The singer is surrounded by trouble: enemies plotting against him, people who misjudge him, and temptations that promise relief but deliver none. He rejects one easy fix after another and keeps returning to the one thing he says can truly heal him, the love named in the title. The tone is gritty and restless rather than serene. The title track was produced by Bumps Blackwell, known for his work with Little Richard, and has a raw, rocking edge.

title: Lenny Bruce
note: It is a tribute to the comedian Lenny Bruce, who died in 1966.
preview: A fond remembrance of a rule-breaking comic who was hounded in life and is missed now that he is gone.
summary: The singer remembers the comedian Lenny Bruce, who died in 1966, as someone who told uncomfortable truths and was punished for it. He argues that Bruce was no criminal, contrasts him with people who did real harm and went free, and recalls a brief personal encounter with him. The tone is fond and a little rueful rather than angry, a tribute from someone who admired his nerve. Dylan delivers it as a slow ballad led by piano.

title: Every Grain of Sand
note: It closes the album and is often counted among his finest songs.
preview: A humble meditation on finding a guiding design in every small detail of an imperfect life.
summary: In a quiet moment of reckoning, the singer looks back over his failings, temptations and regrets without excuses. He describes swinging between feeling watched over and feeling utterly alone, yet keeps finding signs of a guiding purpose in the smallest things around him. The song never preaches; it reads like a confession and a gentle act of acceptance. Unhurried and spacious, with harmonica, it closes the album and is often counted among his finest songs.

title: Serve Yourself
note: John Lennon recorded it as a home demo in 1980 and it was released after his death.

title: Every Grain of Sand
note: Emmylou Harris recorded it for her 1995 album Wrecking Ball.

title: Love Sick
