note: Dylan played it at the 1998 Grammy Awards, where a dancer with the words Soy Bomb painted on his chest jumped on stage beside him.
preview: A man walks through a world that has gone sour, sick from a love he can neither keep nor shake.
summary: A man walks through streets that feel empty and hostile, worn down by a love he wishes he had never known yet cannot give up. He sees couples around him and feels only the distance between himself and them. The verses circle the same restless mood, contradictory, weary and sick at heart, without offering relief. As the opening track of Time Out of Mind, it sets the album's dark, spare tone with a flickering organ and a slow, stalking beat.

title: Standing in the Doorway
note: A slow, drifting ballad that runs nearly eight minutes.
preview: Left behind by a lover, the singer lingers between staying and going, unable to let the feeling die.
summary: Left by a lover, the singer stands at a threshold, unsure whether to stay where she left him or move on. Over nearly eight minutes he drifts through memories, the small sounds of the night and flashes of bitterness, yet keeps returning to a love that will not fade. He insists he will get by, though he never sounds certain of it. The ballad moves slowly and loosely, matching the singer's hesitation.

title: Tryin' to Get to Heaven
note: Dylan reshaped the song often in concert in the years after the album came out.
preview: A weary traveler moves through river towns and train stations hoping to reach salvation before time runs out.
summary: A weary traveler passes through river towns, trains and stations, and every stop reminds him how far he still is from where he hopes to end up. The verses gather scenes from an old American landscape of journeys and departures, and the people he meets offer little comfort. The refrain holds on to his goal of reaching salvation while there is still time. The tone is tired but steady, and Dylan reshaped the song often in concert in the years after the album came out.

title: Not Dark Yet
note: It was released as a single from the album and became one of its most praised songs.
preview: An aging man takes stock of a life that is fading toward its end, though night has not quite fallen.
summary: An aging man takes stock of a life that is wearing out, admitting that he feels detached from the world and weighed down by everything he has seen and lost. The verses move slowly and evenly, each one coming back to the sense that the end is close but has not quite arrived. He speaks of failed love, of travel, and of understanding little more now than before. The tone is resigned and unhurried, sad without self-pity.

title: Cold Irons Bound
note: It won the 1998 Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance.
preview: Rejected and trapped, the singer feels himself carried away as if in chains, far from the one he loved.
summary: A man walks away from a love that has turned against him, feeling as though he is being hauled off in chains. The verses mix memories of the woman with images of a bleak, windswept country and a growing sense that the world he trusted has betrayed him. The refrain keeps returning him to his captivity, far from where he wants to be. The band plays a dark, pounding groove drenched in echo, and the song won the 1998 Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance.

title: Make You Feel My Love
note: Billy Joel released a version before Dylan's own appeared, and it went on to become one of his most covered songs.
preview: A plain promise that the singer will go to any length to comfort and stand by the person he loves.
summary: The singer speaks to someone he loves and promises to comfort them through any hardship, offering shelter, patience and steady devotion. Each verse adds another pledge of what he would do and endure for them, and he insists he knew from the start that they belonged together. The language is simple and the feeling direct, closer to a hymn than a confession. Billy Joel released a version before Dylan's own, and it became one of his most covered songs.

title: Highlands
note: At more than sixteen minutes it closes the album and was then the longest studio track Dylan had released.
preview: A man rambles through a city day, including a long exchange with a waitress, while his mind is set on a distant, longed-for place.
summary: Over a long, loping blues, a man drifts through an ordinary city day while his mind keeps returning to the highlands, a distant place where he feels he truly belongs. He watches people pass, grumbles about the times, and stops in a restaurant, where a waitress asks him to draw her and their exchange turns wry and prickly. The tone is dry, funny and weary all at once. At more than sixteen minutes it closes Time Out of Mind.

title: Tweedle Dee & Tweedle Dum
note: The opening track borrows its title characters from the old English nursery rhyme also used by Lewis Carroll.
preview: Two look-alike schemers roll through a carnival-like America, bound together and impossible to tell apart.
summary: A pair of near-identical partners travel through a sideshow version of America, inseparable and indistinguishable. The verses suggest plots, deceptions and crimes without ever explaining them, and the pair seem as wary of each other as of the world. The mood is comic but uneasy, a picture of shared ambition and mutual suspicion. The opening track borrows its title characters from the old English nursery rhyme also used by Lewis Carroll.

title: Mississippi
note: Dylan first tried it during the Time Out of Mind sessions, and Sheryl Crow released a version before his own appeared.
preview: A man who has stayed too long in one place looks back on lost chances and still offers his love.
summary: Having lingered somewhere past his time, a man reviews the mistakes and missed chances of his life. He speaks to a woman, admitting what he has lost and how little he can change, yet he still offers her his love and refuses to call himself finished. The verses mix regret with a weathered dignity. Dylan first tried the song during the Time Out of Mind sessions, and Sheryl Crow released a version before his own appeared.

title: Summer Days
note: A fast jump-blues number that became a lively fixture of his concerts.
preview: An older man insists the good times are not over and that the past can still be lived again.
summary: Refusing to accept that his best years are spent, an aging man boasts, jokes, flirts with a woman and argues with anyone who claims the past cannot be lived again, while hints of age and loss slip in at the edges. The verses tumble out quickly, mixing swagger with sly self-mockery. It is a fast jump-blues number that became a lively fixture of his concerts.

title: High Water (For Charley Patton)
note: It is dedicated to the Delta blues pioneer Charley Patton.
preview: A rising flood sweeps over a Southern landscape, and the people in its path scramble for safety.
summary: As floodwaters rise across the South, the singer surveys a scene of panic and ruin, crowded with blues singers, figures from old songs and stray characters each facing the deluge. The verses are fragmentary and ominous, threaded with dark humor and hints of judgment, and nobody seems sure where safety lies. A driving banjo pushes the band forward. The song is dedicated to the Delta blues pioneer Charley Patton, who sang of an earlier great flood.

title: Honest With Me
note: A hard-driving electric blues built on a slide-guitar riff.
preview: A restless man stuck in a city he dislikes demands straight talk from the woman he is with.
summary: Trapped in a town he despises, an uneasy man presses his companion to stop lying to him. He swings between boasts, threats, jokes and complaints, never settling long enough to explain himself, and the verses pile up odd details of his discontent. The refrain keeps pressing for straight talk he does not seem to expect. It is a hard-driving electric blues built on a slide-guitar riff, loud and relentless.

title: Po’ Boy
note: A light, jazzy tune filled with old vaudeville-style jokes.
preview: A poor wanderer moves from one odd scene to the next, making the best of hard luck.
summary: A poor wanderer drifts from one odd scene to the next, from cheap lodgings to strange family dramas, meeting each setback with a joke. The verses are full of wordplay, puns and old vaudeville gags, so that hardship and comedy sit side by side. Beneath the humor is a picture of someone with little to his name who keeps going anyway. The tune is light and jazzy, played gently with a relaxed, old-fashioned swing.

title: Sugar Baby
note: The slow, brooding closing track runs well over six minutes.
preview: A world-weary man tells a woman that the old days are gone and warns her to face what is coming.
summary: A world-weary man addresses a woman he calls Sugar Baby, telling her the old days are gone and that she should face what is coming. He looks over a dry, broken world full of hard lessons and false hopes, and warns her to make her peace before judgment arrives. His tone is tender and stern at once, more sorrowful than scolding. The slow, brooding closing track runs well over six minutes.

title: Thunder on the Mountain
note: The opening track famously name-checks the singer Alicia Keys.
preview: A rollicking vision of trouble brewing over the land, with the singer ready to ride out the storm.
summary: The singer watches a great disturbance gathering over the country and braces himself to meet it. The verses mix apocalyptic images with wisecracks, boasts and odd asides, so that dread and good humor run side by side. He seems both to welcome the coming upheaval and to stand apart from it. The opening track of Modern Times moves at a brisk, rollicking pace, and it famously name-checks the singer Alicia Keys.

title: Spirit on the Water
note: A gentle, swinging love song that runs more than seven minutes.
preview: A man shut out of paradise still can't stop thinking of the woman he adores.
summary: Barred for good from paradise, a man remains unable to stop dreaming of the woman he adores. He confesses his longing and his past mistakes, mixing tender declarations with jokes and boasts about himself, and wonders whether she feels the same. The song takes its time, letting the verses wander. It is a gentle, swinging love song that runs more than seven minutes.

title: Rollin’ and Tumblin’
note: Dylan built it on the old Delta blues tune best known from Muddy Waters' 1950 recording.
preview: A restless man rises early and wrestles with his troubles and a woman who has done him wrong.
summary: A restless man wakes early, unable to rest, and wrestles with his troubles and with a woman who has treated him badly. The verses complain, threaten and boast in turn, but the song is driven more by its rolling rhythm than by any story. Dylan built it on the old Delta blues tune best known from Muddy Waters' 1950 recording, and the band plays it as a loud, churning electric blues.

title: When the Deal Goes Down
note: A slow waltz in the style of the old crooner ballads.
preview: A man reflects on how short life is and pledges to be there for his love when the end comes.
summary: Thinking about how short and uncertain life is, a man promises the person he loves that he will be beside her at the finish. The verses are calm and measured, touching on the limits of knowledge, the passing of time and the comfort of love that remains. The tone is tender and accepting rather than fearful. It is a slow waltz in the style of the old crooner ballads.

title: Someday Baby
note: It won the 2007 Grammy for Best Solo Rock Vocal Performance.
preview: A man fed up with a lover's mistreatment says that one day she won't be able to hurt him anymore.
summary: Tired of being treated badly, a man warns his lover that a time is coming when her cruelty will no longer reach him. He lists her faults and his own frustrations, more weary than furious, and seems to be talking himself into leaving as much as warning her. The verses move at an easy, shuffling pace. It won the 2007 Grammy for Best Solo Rock Vocal Performance.

title: Workingman’s Blues #2
note: Its title nods to Merle Haggard's country song Workin' Man Blues.
preview: A laborer watches wages fall and the old order crumble, yet keeps faith with his love and his dignity.
summary: A working man speaks to the woman he loves while the economy turns against people like him: pay shrinks, jobs vanish and the powerful seem untouchable. The verses drift between plain talk about hardship, battlefield imagery, memories and tender promises, always circling back to a refrain that holds on to her as his anchor. The tone is weary but proud rather than bitter. It moves at a gentle, unhurried pace, led by piano and a soft band.

title: Ain’t Talkin’
note: At almost nine minutes it is the album's long, somber closer.
preview: A lone figure walks through a ruined, hostile world, keeping his thoughts to himself as he goes.
summary: A solitary traveler trudges across a broken, unfriendly landscape, refusing to share what is on his mind. He passes through gardens and fields nursing old wounds and grudges, swinging between prayer in one moment and thoughts of revenge in the next. The refrain returns again and again to his silence and his walking. At almost nine minutes it is the somber closer of Modern Times, slow and steady.

title: Beyond Here Lies Nothin'
note: The opening track was co-written with Grateful Dead lyricist Robert Hunter.
preview: Over a Latin-tinged groove the singer tells his love that there is nothing beyond what they have together.
summary: The singer addresses his lover as they move through a dark, deserted night, and he tells her that what they share is all there is; past it there is only emptiness. The verses sketch empty streets, closed doors and a sense of time running out, but the mood is tough and determined rather than despairing. The refrain lands like a vow. A rolling, Latin-flavored groove with prominent accordion gives the song a smoky, border-town swagger.

title: Life Is Hard
note: Dylan wrote it for the French director Olivier Dahan's film My Own Love Song, which led to the whole album.
preview: A lonely man drifts through his days missing someone and finding the world harder to bear alone.
summary: A lonely man moves through his days without the person he lost, and everything around him feels heavier for her absence. The verses are quiet and plain, describing evenings, memories and a resolve to keep going even though the world has grown harder to face alone. There is no dramatic turn, only a steady, resigned tenderness. Dylan croons it softly as a slow ballad, closer to an old-fashioned love song than to the bluesier tracks around it.

title: I Feel a Change Comin' On
note: Another co-write with Robert Hunter, it name-checks the country songwriter Billy Joe Shaver.
preview: An older man senses a shift in his life and hopes it will bring him closer to the woman he wants.
summary: An older man, half amused at himself, senses that something in his life is about to shift and hopes it will finally bring him the woman he has been watching. The verses wander through his days, his reading and his music, with a wry aside about the country singer Billy Joe Shaver, before returning to the feeling of change in the air. The tone is relaxed and teasing, carried by an easy, loping band sound.

title: Here Comes Santa Claus
note: Dylan's straight-faced take on the holiday standard first made popular by Gene Autry.
preview: A cheerful announcement that Santa is on his way down the road with gifts for everyone.
summary: Dylan plays the old holiday standard completely straight, announcing Santa's arrival as if passing on good news to the neighborhood. The verses picture the sleigh, the reindeer and children getting ready for bed, then widen into a note of goodwill that reminds listeners Santa treats everyone alike and that the season has a religious root. His rough, worn voice sits against a bright, old-fashioned arrangement with a warm backing chorus, which gives the cheer an oddly touching sincerity.

title: The Christmas Blues
note: A melancholy holiday song Dylan sings as a slow, bluesy lament.
preview: Someone alone at Christmas feels the season's cheer only deepen their sadness.
summary: Someone spends the holidays alone and finds that everything meant to bring joy only reminds them of what is missing. The verses walk through familiar seasonal sights and sounds, the decorations, the music, the good wishes of others, and set each against the speaker's empty feeling. There is no turn toward comfort; the song simply sits with the sadness. Dylan sings it slowly and quietly, letting the bluesy mood hang over the festive setting.

title: Must Be Santa
note: Dylan's raucous polka version, built on an arrangement by the Texas band Brave Combo, got a manic party music video.
preview: A rapid-fire game of clues that all point to one jolly visitor.
summary: This is a call-and-response game in which one voice asks a string of questions about a mysterious visitor and the answers pile up until there is only one possible guest. Each round adds another clue and repeats the earlier ones, so the song keeps speeding up and growing sillier as it goes. Dylan treats it as pure fun, roaring through a frantic polka with accordion and a crowd of party voices shouting the replies.

title: Duquesne Whistle
note: Co-written with Robert Hunter, it opens with a mock-vintage swing intro before the band kicks in.
preview: A train whistle sounds across the land as the singer rides toward home and the woman he loves.
summary: A train whistle sounds through the night as the singer travels toward home and the woman he loves, and the sound seems to carry both promise and warning. The verses mix romantic longing with hints of trouble along the line, so the cheerful surface never quite settles. After a mock-vintage swing opening that sounds like an old record, the full band kicks in and the song rolls along at a bright, rocking pace.

title: Tempest
note: The nearly fourteen-minute title song retells the sinking of the Titanic.
preview: A sweeping ballad of the great ship's last night, following passengers and crew as it goes down.
summary: This long narrative ballad retells the Titanic's last night, moving among passengers and crew as they dance, gamble, pray and face the end. There is no chorus; verse follows verse like an old folk ballad, returning to a watchman who dreams the disaster as it happens, and it even nods to the famous film. The tone is calm and fatalistic. It unfolds as a lilting waltz with fiddle and accordion, steady and almost soothing despite the subject.

title: Roll on John
note: The closing track is a tribute to John Lennon.
preview: A farewell that traces a fellow musician's life from his early days to his violent death.
summary: Dylan speaks directly to John Lennon, following him from his youth in Liverpool through the clubs of Hamburg, worldwide fame and his later life in New York, up to his sudden death. The verses mix scenes from Lennon's life with echoes of his own songs and of older poetry, while the refrain keeps urging him onward into whatever lies beyond. The tone is tender and mournful, set to a slow, hymn-like accompaniment that closes the album.

title: Make You Feel My Love
note: Adele recorded it for her debut album 19, and it became a major and lasting hit in the UK.

title: Mississippi
note: Crow included the song on her 1998 album The Globe Sessions.

title: Rollin' and Tumblin'
note: Muddy Waters' recording of the Delta blues tune became the standard version of the song.

title: Workin' Man Blues
note: Haggard's country hit is a tribute to the hard-working laborer.

title: High Water Everywhere
note: Patton's two-part blues describes the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927.

title: I’m a Fool to Want You
note: Frank Sinatra shares a writing credit on this 1951 torch song, which opens the album.
preview: A singer admits he cannot stop longing for someone he knows is bad for him.
summary: The singer confesses that he cannot stop longing for someone who has treated him badly, and he knows full well that the desire is foolish. The verses move between self-reproach and helpless need, never resolving the conflict, which is what gives the torch song its ache. Opening the album, Dylan sings it slowly and close to the microphone, with a sparse band and mournful pedal steel leaving plenty of space around his voice.

title: Full Moon and Empty Arms
note: Its melody comes from Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto, and Dylan released his version a year ahead of the album.
preview: A lonely lover spends a moonlit night wishing the absent one were there.
summary: A lover alone under a bright moon spends the night wishing the absent person were there, and turns the moonlight into a kind of promise that they will be together again. The song moves from longing toward hope, ending on a quiet wish rather than despair. Dylan sings the old standard with a small, hushed band, where gentle pedal steel takes the place of the lush strings of the classic versions.

title: That Lucky Old Sun
note: A 1949 hit for Frankie Laine, it closes the album.
preview: A worn-out laborer envies the sun, which rolls across the sky all day with no burden to carry.
summary: A worn-out laborer describes a life of toil for his family and his Lord, and compares himself bitterly with the sun, which crosses the sky every day without any burden. As the song goes on, his envy turns into a weary prayer for release and rest. The tone is tired but dignified, close to a spiritual. Closing the album, Dylan delivers it slowly, with a spare band behind him and the final lines left to linger.

title: Young at Heart
note: Frank Sinatra had a hit with it in 1954, and it opens the album.
preview: Staying hopeful and playful, the song argues, keeps a person young whatever their age.
summary: The song argues that staying hopeful, playful and open to wonder keeps a person young, whatever the calendar says. Its verses list the rewards of that outlook, from dreams that come true to a longer, happier life, and the cheerful message builds to a gentle conclusion. Coming from Dylan in his seventies, the advice sounds wistful as much as sunny. It opens the album at an easy, swaying pace with a soft small-band backing.

title: All the Way
note: Written for the 1957 film The Joker Is Wild, it won the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
preview: A promise of love that holds nothing back and lasts through good times and bad.
summary: The singer offers a love that holds nothing back, promising devotion that will last through good fortune and hard times alike. The verses explain what such love asks of a person, steady and unconditional rather than half-hearted, and the song builds gently toward its title as a final pledge. Dylan's aged voice gives the romantic standard a thoughtful, lived-in quality, backed by a small, quiet band in place of the big orchestra of earlier versions.

title: Melancholy Mood
note: It was the song on Frank Sinatra's first commercial record, made with Harry James's band in 1939.
preview: A singer sunk in gloom after love has gone wishes the clouds would lift.
summary: Someone sunk in gloom after a love has ended admits that the sadness has settled in and will not lift. The singer describes the low feeling and longs for the day the clouds part and happiness returns, so the song hangs between despair and a faint hope. Dylan sings the old standard with a light, swaying touch, and the small band keeps the melancholy soft rather than heavy.

title: September of My Years
note: Frank Sinatra made it the title song of his 1965 album about growing older.
preview: A man in later life looks back over the seasons of his years.
summary: A man in the autumn of his life looks back over the seasons of his years, weighing the joys and regrets they held. The verses move between fond memory and sober acceptance, treating age as both a loss and a kind of ripening. The tone is reflective and bittersweet rather than sad. Dylan's weathered voice suits the theme, and he sings it slowly over a soft, spare arrangement.

title: Stormy Weather
note: Harold Arlen and Ted Koehler wrote it in 1933, and Lena Horne made it her signature song.
preview: Since a lover left, it has felt as if the rain will never stop.
summary: Since the singer's lover left, it feels as though the rain has never stopped, and the gloom outside mirrors the gloom within. The verses describe a life gone gray, weariness and the hope that the sun will someday return with the lost love. The tone is heavy and patient, a slow lament rather than an outburst. Dylan takes the famous standard at a gentle, unhurried pace with a small band.

title: As Time Goes By
note: First heard in a 1931 Broadway show, it became famous through the 1942 film Casablanca.
preview: Whatever else changes, the simple truths of love stay the same.
summary: The singer reflects that whatever else in the world changes, the basic facts of love stay the same, and the old gestures between lovers keep their meaning. The song moves from these general truths to a hope that love will last against everything, ending on a note of quiet confidence. Dylan sings the standard from Casablanca tenderly and unhurriedly, with a light, understated band behind him.

title: I Contain Multitudes
note: Its title comes from Walt Whitman's Song of Myself, and it was released as a single in April 2020.
preview: An aging narrator describes himself as a bundle of contradictions holding many selves at once.
summary: An aging narrator describes himself as a bundle of contradictions, holding many selves and moods at once. The verses work like a self-portrait made of opposites and borrowed figures, naming people from Anne Frank and Indiana Jones to the Rolling Stones, as he admits to both tenderness and menace. The tone is calm, sly and quietly unsettling. It is a soft, almost hushed performance over gentle guitar, letting each verse unfold slowly.

title: False Prophet
note: Released in May 2020, its music is built on Billy "The Kid" Emerson's 1954 Sun Records blues "If Lovin' Is Believing".
preview: A defiant speaker insists he is no fake and stares down enemies and mortality alike.
summary: A defiant speaker insists that he is genuine, no fake, and warns off his enemies with a mix of boasting and grim humor. The verses pile up claims about his strength, his past and his readiness to face death, sounding at once like a gunfighter and an old preacher. The tone is swaggering and sardonic. Its music is built on Billy Emerson's 1954 Sun Records blues, played as a slow, snarling electric shuffle.

title: My Own Version of You
note: It imagines building a companion out of body parts, in the manner of Frankenstein.
preview: A narrator roams graveyards and history gathering pieces to assemble the perfect person.
summary: In the manner of Frankenstein, a narrator roams graveyards and history gathering body parts and borrowed qualities to build himself the perfect companion. The verses list the pieces he wants, drawn from famous figures and stories, and the project grows stranger and more macabre as it goes, while the speaker remains oddly calm. The tone is darkly comic and eerie. It moves at a slow, creeping pace with a menacing, low-lit band sound.

title: Goodbye Jimmy Reed
note: It is a tribute to the Chicago blues singer and harmonica player Jimmy Reed.
preview: A farewell to a blues hero that mixes religion, rough living and devotion to the music.
summary: Dylan bids farewell to the Chicago blues man Jimmy Reed, mixing praise for him with scenes of rough living, church and loyalty to the music. The verses jump between religion, violence and memories of hearing the blues, as if the speaker were explaining where his own life and faith came from. The tone is affectionate and rowdy. It rocks along as a lively, stomping blues that echoes Reed's own style.

title: Crossing the Rubicon
note: Its title refers to Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon river in 49 BC, a point of no return.
preview: Over a slow blues, a man announces he has made an irreversible choice and will not turn back.
summary: A man announces that he has made his irreversible choice and will not turn back, taking the ancient image of Caesar's crossing as his own. The verses swing between prayer, menace, dark humor and glimpses of his past, so it is never clear whether he is a pilgrim or a threat. Each verse ends by returning to the decision he has made. It grinds along as a slow, heavy blues, menacing and steady.

title: Key West (Philosopher Pirate)
note: Named for the island city at the tip of Florida, it runs over nine minutes with accordion throughout.
preview: The Florida island becomes a dreamlike refuge, a place of healing at the end of the road.
summary: The narrator tells of the island city at the tip of Florida as a dreamlike refuge, a place where he finds healing and peace at the end of the road. The verses drift through memories of radio, poets, a presidential assassination and his own wanderings, always returning to the island in the refrain. The tone is gentle and wistful, like a slow dream. Running over nine minutes, it floats along with accordion throughout.

title: Murder Most Foul
note: Nearly seventeen minutes long, it is his longest song and became his first to top a Billboard chart.
preview: The 1963 killing of John F. Kennedy is retold alongside a vast roll call of the music and films of the era.
summary: The killing of John F. Kennedy in Dallas in 1963 is retold in close, haunting detail, as if the event had never finished happening. Midway, the song widens into a long request to a disc jockey, calling up songs, films and performers of the era, so the national tragedy and its soundtrack become tangled together. The tone is solemn and incantatory. Nearly seventeen minutes long, it unfolds slowly over piano and strings with almost no beat.

title: If Lovin' Is Believing
note: A blues by Billy "The Kid" Emerson, recorded for Sun Records in Memphis.

title: Billy 1
note: One of several takes on the same ballad about Billy the Kid spread across the soundtrack.
preview: A ballad that follows the outlaw Billy as the law hunts him across the border country.
summary: The singer speaks directly to Billy the Kid, an outlaw on the run, as the law closes in. The verses follow him through lonely towns, card games, borrowed beds and the long ride toward the border, while a lawman who was once his friend draws nearer. Each verse returns to the same address to Billy, part warning and part lament, as if the outcome is already known. The mood is unhurried and fatalistic, a portrait of a young man living on borrowed time.

title: Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door
note: Written for a death scene in the film, it was a US top-20 single in 1973.
preview: A dying lawman asks to lay down his badge and guns as the end closes in.
summary: A dying lawman speaks to his mother, asking her to take away the badge and the guns he no longer has any use for. He describes the light failing around him and the sense that his time is over. The song is short, just two verses, each followed by a repeated refrain in which he says he is at the threshold of heaven. Gentle backing voices and a slow, steady rhythm give it the feel of a hymn sung at a deathbed.

title: Lily of the West
note: A traditional folk ballad, recorded during the 1970 sessions that produced Self Portrait and New Morning.
preview: An old ballad of a man undone by a woman he loved.
summary: An old ballad told by a man looking back on his ruin. He travels to a new town, falls hard for a beautiful woman, and believes she returns his love, until he finds her with another man. In a jealous rage he attacks his rival and ends up tried and locked away. The striking turn is that, even after her betrayal has cost him his freedom, he still cannot stop loving her, and the tale closes on that helpless devotion.

title: Can't Help Falling in Love
note: His version of the song Elvis Presley made a hit in 1961.
preview: A tender admission of falling in love despite better judgment.
summary: Dylan takes on a much-loved romantic standard and sings it as a simple confession. The speaker admits that sensible people would warn him against hurrying into love, yet he finds he cannot stop himself and gives in completely. He likens his feeling to a river that has no choice but to run to the sea. The song asks nothing of the listener except to accept that some feelings arrive whether or not they are wise.

title: On a Night Like This
note: The album's opening track, released as a single in 1974.
preview: A warm welcome home on a cold winter night.
summary: A man welcomes a lover home on a bitter winter night, delighted that she is back with him. He talks of shutting out the cold, building up the fire, and staying close together while the snow piles up outside. Rather than a story, the song is a single happy moment stretched out, full of easy affection and relief. The Band back him with a loose, rolling sound that feels like a party in a warm room.

title: Forever Young
note: The album includes two different recordings of it, one slow and one fast, and he has said he wrote it with one of his sons in mind.
preview: A parent's blessing wishing a child courage, truth and a lasting youthful spirit.
summary: A parent offers a blessing to a child, setting out hopes for the life ahead. Verse by verse the wishes pile up: that the child will be honest, brave, surrounded by love, sure of foot and strong in spirit, and will always have a song inside them. Each verse closes with the same refrain, a wish that the child keep a youthful heart however many years pass. The album holds two recordings of it, one slow and tender, the other quicker and more upbeat.

title: Wedding Song
note: It closes the album as a solo performance with acoustic guitar and harmonica.
preview: A fervent declaration of devotion to a partner who saved him.
summary: A man pours out his devotion to his partner, telling her she rescued him and gave his life meaning. He insists his love is greater now than ever and that he has no wish to return to the turmoil of the past. The verses build in intensity, moving from gratitude to vows that reach toward forever. It closes the album as a solo performance with only acoustic guitar and harmonica, which makes the passion sound raw and personal.

title: Tangled Up in Blue
note: He re-recorded it in Minneapolis in December 1974, and that version opens the album.
preview: A man retraces a love affair across years, jobs and cities, with the story shifting between viewpoints.
summary: A man retraces a love affair that keeps breaking off and starting again over many years. The verses jump between places and jobs, from a marriage that falls apart to drifting work, a chance reunion and an old book of poems that moves him. The pronouns slip between he, I and she, so the story feels like memory shifting as it is retold. By the end he is back on the road, still looking for her. The Minneapolis version opens the album.

title: Simple Twist of Fate
note: It was recorded at the original New York sessions in September 1974.
preview: A brief encounter with a woman ends when she leaves, and he is left blaming chance.
summary: The song begins in the third person, following a couple who meet one evening, walk together and spend the night in a cheap hotel. When he wakes she has gone, and he searches for her along the waterfront, hoping she will come back. In the last verse the voice shifts into the first person, revealing that the story is his own. Each verse ends by blaming chance for what happened, and the tone is sad and resigned.

title: Idiot Wind
note: He replaced the quiet New York take with a harder full-band version cut in Minneapolis.
preview: A bitter, furious outpouring at a former lover and the gossip around them, which finally turns back on himself.
summary: A man lashes out at a former lover and at the rumours and lies that have swirled around them. The verses heap up bitter accusations, wild images and jabs at the people spreading stories, with a chorus that names her as the source of all the foolishness. In the final chorus he turns the charge on both of them, admitting his own share of the blame. The released version is the harder full-band take cut in Minneapolis, loud and full of anger.

title: You’re Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go
note: A spare acoustic recording from the New York sessions.
preview: A light-hearted song that already feels the loneliness ahead while a love is still in bloom.
summary: A man in a new, happy romance already senses that it will not last and that he will miss her badly when she leaves. Rather than sinking into gloom, he sounds amused and tender, comparing this love favourably with a stormier one from his past and noticing the small sights of their days together. He imagines looking for her in distant places once she has gone. It is a spare acoustic recording from the New York sessions, light on its feet.

title: Lily, Rosemary and the Jack of Hearts
note: At close to nine minutes, it is the album's longest track and one of the five songs re-recorded in Minneapolis.
preview: A western caper in which a mysterious card player's arrival in a small town sets off robbery, jealousy and a killing.
summary: A western tale told across many verses, set in a small mining town. A stranger who seems to be the Jack of Hearts arrives at the cabaret, and his presence stirs up the showgirl Lily, the jealous wife Rosemary, and the powerful man who owns the town. While a robbery unfolds down the street, tensions in the room explode into a killing and a hanging. There is no chorus; the story simply rolls forward, and the mysterious stranger slips away at the end.

title: Shelter From the Storm
note: A solo performance from the New York sessions, later remade with a loud band arrangement on the live album Hard Rain.
preview: A weary man remembers a woman who once took him in and gave him refuge from a hostile world.
summary: A worn-out man looks back on the time a woman took him in when he had nowhere left to turn. The verses describe the hostile, violent world he was escaping and the calm she offered him, each closing with the memory of her welcome. As the song goes on, regret creeps in: he has lost that refuge and wishes he could return to it. The original is a solo performance; later he remade it with a loud band on Hard Rain.

title: Buckets of Rain
note: The album's closing track, a quiet acoustic blues.
preview: A playful, weary song about doing what you must and loving someone through hard times.
summary: A man tells his lover about the sorrow he carries and the simple pleasures she brings him. Between wry complaints about how hard and unfair life can be, he lists small, affectionate things he likes about her, and offers to do whatever she needs. The song settles on a shrug of acceptance: life is tough, so you get on with what has to be done. It ends the album as a quiet acoustic blues, gentle and slightly teasing.

title: Tears of Rage
note: Dylan wrote the words and Richard Manuel of the Band wrote the music.
preview: A parent laments being betrayed and forgotten by a child once cherished.
summary: A parent speaks to a grown child who has turned away, recalling the hopes and care given in the past and the hurt of being forgotten. The verses move from memories of raising the child to a bitter sense of betrayal, while the refrain dwells on grief and the lateness of the hour. The mood is slow and mournful, closer to a hymn than a complaint. Dylan wrote the words and Richard Manuel of the Band wrote the music.

title: You Ain’t Goin’ Nowhere
note: The Byrds released a cover of it in 1968, years before Dylan's own recording was officially issued.
preview: A cheerful, nonsense-laced song about waiting around until a loved one arrives.
summary: A cheerful song about waiting for a loved one to arrive. The speaker mixes everyday details with odd, playful nonsense, and the refrain urges patience and comfort, as if the wait itself might be enjoyed. Its tone is relaxed and good-humoured, a song of contentment rather than longing. The Byrds released a cover of it in 1968, years before his own recording was officially issued.

title: This Wheel’s on Fire
note: Dylan wrote the words and Rick Danko of the Band wrote the music.
preview: An ominous warning that a reckoning is coming and cannot be escaped.
summary: The speaker tells someone that he will return, and that when he does, the debts and promises between them will have to be settled. The images are mysterious and full of menace, building toward a refrain about a burning wheel rolling down the road that threatens to burst apart. Nothing is fully explained, which makes the warning feel all the more unavoidable. Dylan wrote the words and Rick Danko of the Band wrote the music.

title: Hurricane
note: Co-written with Jacques Levy, it argues that boxer Rubin Carter was wrongly convicted of a 1966 triple murder.
preview: A narrative of how a boxer was framed for murder by police and a prejudiced justice system.
summary: A long narrative that lays out the case that the boxer Rubin Carter was wrongly convicted of a triple murder. It opens on the night of the shootings and follows how police, witnesses and the courts built a case against him, presenting race and corruption as the real reasons for his conviction. The song is told with anger and urgency, ending with a plea for his freedom. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it drives forward with a prominent violin.

title: Isis
note: Co-written with Jacques Levy, it was a staple of the Rolling Thunder Revue shows.
preview: A man leaves his new wife for a strange quest through cold mountains and returns changed.
summary: A man marries a woman named Isis and then, restless, rides away from her. He falls in with a stranger who promises treasure, and the pair travel through cold, wild country to rob a tomb, only for his companion to die and the prize to prove empty. Changed by the ordeal, he returns to Isis, and the song ends on their reunion. It unfolds like a myth or dream. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it was a staple of the Rolling Thunder Revue shows.

title: One More Cup of Coffee
note: Emmylou Harris sings harmony on the recording.
preview: A farewell to a mysterious woman and her family before a journey down into the valley.
summary: A man prepares to leave a mysterious woman whose family seems wild and dangerous, and asks for one last drink before he sets off down into the valley. He describes her beauty and her strange household, and admits that she does not truly love him. Each verse returns to the same request, as if he is delaying the parting. The mood is dark and exotic, with Emmylou Harris singing harmony.

title: Oh, Sister
note: Co-written with Jacques Levy and sung as a duet with Emmylou Harris.
preview: A plea to a woman for closeness, framed in terms of shared faith and a short life.
summary: A man pleads with a woman to let him close, appealing to the faith and family bonds they share. He reminds her that they were raised under the same guiding hand and that life is short, so it would be wrong to hold back. The tone is earnest and slightly anxious, as though he fears she may refuse. Co-written with Jacques Levy, it is sung as a duet with Emmylou Harris, whose voice gives the plea added weight.

title: Joey
note: Co-written with Jacques Levy about the New York gangster Joey Gallo, killed in 1972.
preview: A sympathetic ballad about a mobster's life and violent death.
summary: A long, sympathetic ballad about the New York gangster Joey Gallo. It traces his rise in the underworld, his years in prison and his return to the streets, presenting him as a man who wanted peace and was hunted by rivals. It ends with his violent death in a restaurant, and the refrain asks why he had to die that way. The tone is mournful, treating him almost as a folk hero. Dylan co-wrote it with Jacques Levy.

title: Black Diamond Bay
note: Co-written with Jacques Levy, it is one of the album's long story songs.
preview: A cast of strangers at an island hotel meets disaster, while a man watching the news far away barely notices.
summary: A long story song set at a hotel on a tropical island. A cast of strangers, among them a mysterious woman, a soldier, a gambler and a desperate man, each pursue their own small dramas as a volcano begins to erupt. The island and everyone on it are swallowed up. In the final verse the scene cuts to a man far away who sees the news on television, shrugs and moves on. Dylan co-wrote it with Jacques Levy.

title: Sara
note: Written by Dylan alone and named for his wife, Sara Lownds, it closes the album.
preview: A husband recalls the years and children he shared with his wife and begs her not to leave.
summary: A husband speaks to his wife, recalling scenes from their life together: the children playing, places they visited, the early days of their love. The tender memories are mixed with a growing sense that she is slipping away, and his praise of her becomes a plea for her to stay. The song alternates verses of memory with a refrain that simply calls her name. Written by Dylan alone and named for his wife, it closes the album.

title: Changing of the Guards
note: The album's opening track, running more than six minutes.
preview: A dense allegory of a long struggle, a lost lover and an old order about to fall.
summary: A dense, dreamlike allegory that runs for more than six minutes and opens the album. It moves through images of a long struggle, a lost woman, merchants and thieves, and powers that seem ready to fall, without telling a straightforward story. The verses build toward the sense that an old order is ending and something new must take its place. The arrangement is big and full, with horns and backing singers driving it forward.

title: Is Your Love in Vain?
note: Released as a single in 1978.
preview: A wary man questions whether a new lover can really give him what he needs.
summary: A man who has been hurt before questions a new lover about what she really wants from him. He asks whether she needs him or just his company, whether she understands his life, and whether she could be the partner he hopes for. The questions sound cautious, even demanding, as he weighs up the risk. In the end he decides to take the chance and give his heart anyway.

title: Señor (Tales of Yankee Power)
note: Like the rest of the album, it was recorded at his Rundown Studios in Santa Monica with his 1978 touring band.
preview: A traveller asks a mysterious guide where they are heading and how long the ordeal will last.
summary: A weary traveller speaks to a mysterious guide he calls Señor, asking where they are heading and how long the journey will last. The verses are full of uneasy questions and scenes from a harsh landscape, hinting at a past love and a world close to catastrophe. By the end his patience runs out and he longs to break free and tear things down. The tone is brooding and tense, a dark journey with no clear destination.

title: Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door
note: Guns N' Roses released their hard-rock version on Use Your Illusion II in 1991.

title: You Ain’t Goin’ Nowhere
note: The Byrds put it on their 1968 country-rock album Sweetheart of the Rodeo and released it as a single.

title: This Wheel’s on Fire
by: Julie Driscoll, Brian Auger and the Trinity
note: Their psychedelic version was a top-five hit in the UK in 1968.

title: Talkin' New York
note: One of only two original songs on his debut album, it is a talking blues about his first days in the city.
preview: A newcomer's wry account of arriving in a cold, crowded city and scraping for gigs in the folk clubs.
summary: A young musician tells how he came east to New York in the dead of winter and tried to break into the folk scene. He rides the subway, gets turned away from a coffeehouse for sounding too rural, and ends up playing harmonica for very little pay. Along the way he jabs at the people who exploit musicians, and finally gives up on the city for now and heads off across the river. It is a talking blues, half spoken over guitar, full of deadpan jokes.

title: House of the Risin' Sun
note: Dylan's recording of the traditional song used an arrangement he learned from Dave Van Ronk.
preview: A ruined life looks back on a house of sin in New Orleans and warns others not to follow.
summary: The narrator looks back on a life wrecked in a notorious house in New Orleans. The verses trace how it happened, through a hard family background and a lover given to drink and gambling, and then turn outward into a warning to others, especially a younger sibling, not to make the same mistakes. It ends with the singer resigned to going back to that house for good. Dylan sings it with raw intensity over his own guitar, in an arrangement he learned from Dave Van Ronk.

title: Song to Woody
note: Written in 1961 as a tribute to Woody Guthrie, it is one of the two originals on his debut album.
preview: A young singer salutes his ailing hero and the hard-traveling people Guthrie sang about.
summary: A young singer far from home speaks directly to Woody Guthrie, his hero, who is now ill. He describes a world that seems weary and worn down, then thanks Guthrie and the singers who rode alongside him for the songs they left behind. The tone is humble rather than grand: he admits he cannot match them, but says he too is out on the road and trying. It is a plain, quiet performance for voice and guitar.

title: Blowin' in the Wind
note: Its melody adapts the spiritual "No More Auction Block", and it became a civil-rights anthem.
preview: A string of unanswerable questions about war, freedom and indifference, with the answers left drifting in the air.
summary: The singer puts a series of plain questions to the listener: how long people must suffer, how long war and injustice will go on, and how long others can look away. Each of the three verses gathers more questions and never answers them directly, and the refrain only says the answer is out there, moving and hard to hold. The tone is calm and searching rather than angry, which helped it become a civil-rights anthem. Dylan sings it simply, with guitar and harmonica.

title: Girl from the North Country
note: He wrote it after his first trip to England, drawing on the "Scarborough Fair" arrangement he learned from Martin Carthy.
preview: A traveler asks for news of a lost love living far north and hopes she is well cared for.
summary: The singer asks someone traveling north to carry a message to a woman he once loved who still lives there. He worries about small things: whether she is warm enough as the winter sets in, whether her hair is still long. As the verses go on, his care for her shows how much he still misses her, though he never asks for her back. The mood is hushed and tender, sung over a softly picked guitar.

title: Masters of War
note: It sets a furious attack on arms makers to the tune of the traditional "Nottamun Town".
preview: A bitter denunciation of the people who build weapons and profit from wars they never fight.
summary: The singer speaks straight to the people who build and sell weapons. Verse by verse he accuses them of hiding behind desks and walls, frightening the world into war, and sending the young to die while they stay safe and grow rich. There is no chorus and no softening; his anger grows until he says no amount of money can redeem them and wishes for their death. The tune is a stark, circling traditional melody under a bare guitar.

title: A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall
note: Dylan premiered it in 1962, and it borrows its question-and-answer frame from the old ballad "Lord Randal".
preview: A young traveler returns with a torrent of nightmarish images and vows to keep telling what he saw.
summary: A parent questions a beloved son about where he has been, what he saw and heard, and whom he met. Each answer pours out as a long list of images of suffering, ruin and warning, and every verse builds to the title's prophecy. In the last verse the son says what he will do next: go back into the darkness and keep telling the world what he has witnessed. Dylan delivers it alone with his guitar, steady and grave, the question-and-answer frame borrowed from an old ballad.

title: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right
note: A finger-picked breakup song, it became a hit for Peter, Paul and Mary in 1963.
preview: A man leaving a failed love tells her, with a mix of hurt and shrugging pride, not to dwell on it.
summary: A man leaving a relationship at daybreak speaks to the woman he is walking away from. He tells her not to wonder why, not to call after him, and not to blame herself too much, while making it clear he feels he gave more than he got back. Each verse mixes tenderness and resentment, and the refrain shrugs off the parting as if it costs him nothing. It is set to quick, rolling finger-picked guitar.

title: Bob Dylan's Dream
note: Its melody comes from the ballad "Lord Franklin", which he learned from Martin Carthy in London.
preview: A dreamer longs for the lost days of youthful friendship before the world got complicated.
summary: Riding a train, the singer falls asleep and dreams of an old room where he and his friends once sat together by a fire, talking, laughing and certain they would never grow old. As the song goes on, the dream gives way to the knowledge that those friends have scattered and the easy certainty is gone. He ends by saying he would give anything to sit in that room once more. It is a gentle, wistful song set to an old ballad melody.

title: Oxford Town
note: It is about the violence that met James Meredith when he enrolled at the University of Mississippi in 1962.
preview: A brisk, ironic look at a Southern town erupting in violence over one Black student's right to attend college.
summary: The song tells of a Southern college town turning to violence because one Black man has come to enroll. In short verses the singer describes the guns, the clubs, the tear gas and the deaths, and asks how anyone could accept it. A breezy, almost jaunty guitar tune runs underneath, so the cheerful sound sharpens the irony of the grim events. It is brief and pointed, a news story set to song.

title: The Times They Are a-Changin'
note: Written in 1963 as a deliberate anthem, it became one of the defining songs of the 1960s.
preview: A warning to politicians, critics and parents that a new generation is coming and the old order is giving way.
summary: The singer calls on everyone to gather round and face what is coming. Verse by verse he addresses writers and critics, senators and congressmen, and mothers and fathers, warning each not to stand in the way of change they cannot stop. The last verse declares that the order of things is about to be turned upside down. The tone is solemn and prophetic, like a hymn or a public proclamation, sung over plain guitar and harmonica.

title: Ballad of Hollis Brown
note: A grim ballad of rural poverty, it tells of a South Dakota farmer driven to despair.
preview: A starving farmer with no way out reaches a desperate and terrible end.
summary: The singer tells, mostly in direct address to Hollis Brown himself, the story of a South Dakota farmer with a wife and five children and nothing to feed them. The verses pile up his troubles: a barren farm, sick animals, no work and no help coming, until, pushed past hope, he spends his last money on shotgun shells and kills his family and himself. The bleak story ends by noting that somewhere else new lives begin. It moves over a relentless, droning guitar figure.

title: With God on Our Side
note: Its melody follows Dominic Behan's "The Patriot Game".
preview: A survey of American wars questions the habit of claiming divine approval for every killing.
summary: A young man from the Midwest recalls what his schoolbooks taught him: that in every American war, from the fighting against Native Americans through the World Wars, his country had God on its side. Verse by verse he sees how easily enemies become friends and back again, and how the arrival of weapons of mass death makes the claim more frightening. He ends troubled and uncertain, hoping that God would stop the next war. It is a long, slow ballad for voice, guitar and harmonica.

title: Only a Pawn in Their Game
note: Written about the 1963 murder of Medgar Evers, Dylan sang it at the March on Washington.
preview: It argues that the man who killed a civil-rights leader was a tool of politicians who stoke racial hatred.
summary: The song tells of the murder of a civil-rights leader, shot in the back, and then looks past the gunman to the people behind him. The singer argues that a poor white man has been taught hatred by politicians, sheriffs and leaders who use it to keep power, and that he is a tool in a bigger scheme. Each verse ends by naming him as just a pawn. The tone is cool and analytical rather than mournful, set to a plain, steady guitar.

title: Boots of Spanish Leather
note: It is written as an exchange of letters between a man and a woman who has sailed away.
preview: A lover offers gifts across the ocean and slowly realizes the one who left is not coming back.
summary: The song is a conversation between two lovers, one of whom has sailed across the sea. She keeps offering to send him a gift from abroad, and he keeps saying he wants nothing but her safe return. Then a letter arrives saying she cannot tell when she will be back, and he understands she is gone for good, and only then does he ask for a gift, a pair of Spanish leather boots. It is quiet and restrained, carried by gentle finger-picked guitar.

title: When the Ship Comes In
note: Dylan sang it at the March on Washington in 1963.
preview: A prophecy of a day of reckoning when the oppressed rise and their enemies are swept aside.
summary: The song imagines the day a great ship arrives and the world turns in favor of the downtrodden. Nature itself joins in, the seas and the sun greeting the change, and then the enemies of the righteous wake in disbelief and are swept away, like the army of Pharaoh in the Bible. The tone is joyful and triumphant rather than bitter. It moves with a bright, marching rhythm on guitar and harmonica, part sermon and part celebration.

title: The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll
note: It recounts the 1963 killing of Hattie Carroll, a Black barmaid, by William Zantzinger, who received a six-month sentence.
preview: A cool, exact account of a wealthy man's killing of a hotel worker and the light sentence that followed.
summary: The song tells how William Zantzinger, a rich young man with powerful family connections, killed Hattie Carroll, a Black woman who served tables, by striking her with a cane at a hotel gathering in Baltimore. The verses set his wealth beside her life of hard work. The refrain tells listeners to hold back their tears for now, and the last verse reveals why: the court gave him only six months. Dylan sings it calmly and precisely, and the restraint makes the anger hit harder.

title: Restless Farewell
note: Its tune is based on the traditional Irish song "The Parting Glass".
preview: The singer takes leave of old friends, quarrels and critics, determined to move on on his own terms.
summary: The singer takes stock of his life: the money he spent, the friends and lovers he leaves behind, the quarrels he fought and the critics who misread him. Each verse ends with the decision to say goodbye and move on. In the last verse he answers the gossip and the attacks by refusing to let them change him. The mood is weary but defiant, a slow, ceremonial farewell sung over guitar and harmonica to an Irish parting tune.

title: Chimes of Freedom
note: A long visionary song, it was covered by The Byrds on their 1965 debut album.
preview: Sheltering from a storm, two people imagine the storm tolling for every outcast and underdog in the world.
summary: Two people shelter in a doorway during a night thunderstorm, and the lightning seems to them like great bells ringing out. Each verse widens the list of those the bells ring for: the refugees, the gentle, the outcasts, the mistreated, the lonely and the misunderstood, all over the world. The refrain returns them to the simple act of watching the storm. It is long, hymn-like and visionary, sung over a steady acoustic strum.

title: My Back Pages
note: Widely heard as his farewell to protest songwriting, it was later a hit cover for The Byrds.
preview: The singer looks back on his own preachy certainties and finds that shedding them has renewed him.
summary: The singer looks back on a time when he was sure of everything, preaching about right and wrong and seeing the world in black and white. Verse by verse he admits how proud, rigid and self-righteous he had been, and how those certainties shut him in. The refrain makes the turn: he felt old and stiff back then and feels younger now that he has let them go. It is a reflective, self-mocking song for solo guitar and voice.

title: It Ain't Me Babe
note: It was a 1965 hit for The Turtles and became a duet favorite of Johnny Cash and June Carter.
preview: A man gently but firmly tells a woman he is not the perfect, devoted partner she is looking for.
summary: A man tells a woman to step away from his window and go on her way. She wants a partner who will never weaken, always protect her and give up everything for her, and he says plainly that he is not that person. The verses list what she hopes for, and the refrain turns each hope down. The tone is gentle rather than cruel, closer to honest warning than rejection, and his guitar and harmonica keep it light.

title: 1913 Massacre
note: Guthrie's ballad tells of the Italian Hall disaster in Calumet, Michigan, where dozens of striking miners' children died in a stampede.

title: No More Auction Block
note: A spiritual sung by formerly enslaved people, it was in Dylan's early repertoire.

title: Nottamun Town
note: An English-derived folk song of topsy-turvy riddles, popularized in the folk revival by Jean Ritchie.

title: Scarborough Fair
note: An English ballad of impossible tasks set for a former lover, which Martin Carthy taught Dylan in London.

title: Lord Franklin
note: A ballad lamenting Sir John Franklin's lost Arctic expedition, sung in the voice of his widow.

title: Lord Randal
note: An old Child ballad in which a mother questions her son, who has been poisoned.

title: The Patriot Game
note: Behan's song about a young IRA volunteer killed in a 1957 raid.

title: The Parting Glass
note: A traditional Scottish and Irish song of farewell sung at the end of a gathering.

title: Blowin' in the Wind
note: The trio's 1963 single was a major hit that carried Dylan's song to a mass audience.

title: My Back Pages
note: The Byrds recorded it for their 1967 album Younger Than Yesterday.
